title: MEASURES OF CENTRAL TENDENCY
introRaw:
BASIC IDEA (plain English)
A measure of central tendency answers: "What is a typical or central
value of this data?" Mean, median and mode are three different answers to
that question, and they can disagree. Which is appropriate depends on
the shape of the data and what you want to know.

sections.title: ARITHMETIC MEAN

blocks.title: ARITHMETIC MEAN
blocks.formulaBody:
Sample mean:        x_bar = (1/n) sum[i=1..n] x_i
     Population mean:   mu    = (1/N) sum[i=1..N] x_i

parts.B:
FORMULAS
     Sample mean:        x_bar = (1/n) sum[i=1..n] x_i
     Population mean:   mu    = (1/N) sum[i=1..N] x_i
parts.C:
SYMBOLS: x_i the i-th observation; n sample size (N population size);
   sum[i=1..n] the sum of all n values.
parts.D:
CONCEPT: the "balance point" of the data: if each value were a weight on
   a seesaw, x_bar is where it balances. Equivalent: the value each item
   would have if the total were shared equally.
parts.E:
CONDITIONS: needs numeric (interval/ratio) data. It uses every value, so
   it is SENSITIVE TO OUTLIERS (breakdown point 0: a single extreme
   value can move it arbitrarily).
   KEY PROPERTIES
     (1) sum (x_i - x_bar) = 0  (deviations balance).
     (2) x_bar minimizes sum (x_i - c)^2 over c (least squares).
     (3) Linear: mean(a x + b) = a x_bar + b.
     (4) mean(x + y) = mean(x) + mean(y) for paired data.
parts.F:
DERIVATION of (2): g(c) = sum (x_i - c)^2; g'(c) = -2 sum (x_i - c) = 0
   gives c = x_bar; g'' = 2n > 0 (a minimum). Property (1) follows from
   sum x_i - n x_bar = 0.
parts.G:
EXAMPLES
   Simple: 2, 4, 4, 4, 5, 5, 7, 9: sum = 40, n = 8, x_bar = 5.
      Deviations: -3, -1, -1, -1, 0, 0, 2, 4 (sum 0).
   Moderate: temperatures in Celsius 20, 22, 25 have mean 22.33. Convert to
      Fahrenheit F = 1.8 C + 32: mean = 1.8(22.33) + 32 = 72.2 (property 3).
parts.H:
INTERPRETATION: the mean is the natural summary for symmetric data and
   for totals (mean x n = total).
parts.J:
RELATED: weighted mean (F29.2), median (F29.3), expectation E[X]
   (Module 36): the population mean is the expectation of a random value
   drawn uniformly from the population.

blocks.rawText:
F29.1  ARITHMETIC MEAN
A. NAME: Arithmetic mean (average).
B. FORMULAS
     Sample mean:        x_bar = (1/n) sum[i=1..n] x_i
     Population mean:   mu    = (1/N) sum[i=1..N] x_i
C. SYMBOLS: x_i the i-th observation; n sample size (N population size);
   sum[i=1..n] the sum of all n values.
D. CONCEPT: the "balance point" of the data: if each value were a weight on
   a seesaw, x_bar is where it balances. Equivalent: the value each item
   would have if the total were shared equally.
E. CONDITIONS: needs numeric (interval/ratio) data. It uses every value, so
   it is SENSITIVE TO OUTLIERS (breakdown point 0: a single extreme
   value can move it arbitrarily).
   KEY PROPERTIES
     (1) sum (x_i - x_bar) = 0  (deviations balance).
     (2) x_bar minimizes sum (x_i - c)^2 over c (least squares).
     (3) Linear: mean(a x + b) = a x_bar + b.
     (4) mean(x + y) = mean(x) + mean(y) for paired data.
F. DERIVATION of (2): g(c) = sum (x_i - c)^2; g'(c) = -2 sum (x_i - c) = 0
   gives c = x_bar; g'' = 2n > 0 (a minimum). Property (1) follows from
   sum x_i - n x_bar = 0.
G. EXAMPLES
   Simple: 2, 4, 4, 4, 5, 5, 7, 9: sum = 40, n = 8, x_bar = 5.
      Deviations: -3, -1, -1, -1, 0, 0, 2, 4 (sum 0).
   Moderate: temperatures in Celsius 20, 22, 25 have mean 22.33. Convert to
      Fahrenheit F = 1.8 C + 32: mean = 1.8(22.33) + 32 = 72.2 (property 3).
H. INTERPRETATION: the mean is the natural summary for symmetric data and
   for totals (mean x n = total).
I. MISTAKES: averaging percentages or ratios without weights (Module 26);
   reporting the mean of heavily skewed data (income) as "typical";
   averaging ordinal codes (1-5 satisfaction) without noting the
   assumption.
J. RELATED: weighted mean (F29.2), median (F29.3), expectation E[X]
   (Module 36): the population mean is the expectation of a random value
   drawn uniformly from the population.

sections.title: WEIGHTED MEAN

blocks.title: WEIGHTED MEAN
blocks.formulaBody:
x_w = ( sum w_i x_i ) / ( sum w_i )
   Grouped data (frequency table): x_bar = ( sum f_j x_j ) / ( sum f_j ),
   with f_j the frequency of value (or class midpoint) x_j.

parts.B:
FORMULA:   x_w = ( sum w_i x_i ) / ( sum w_i )
   Grouped data (frequency table): x_bar = ( sum f_j x_j ) / ( sum f_j ),
   with f_j the frequency of value (or class midpoint) x_j.
parts.C:
SYMBOLS: w_i weights (importance, reliability, size), w_i >= 0, not all 0;
   f_j frequencies.
parts.D:
CONCEPT: some observations count more than others; each value is
   multiplied by its weight, and the total is divided by total weight so
   weights need not sum to 1. If all w_i are equal it reduces to the
   ordinary mean.
parts.E:
CONDITIONS: weights must be meaningful (credits, group sizes, inverse
   variances). Class midpoints in grouped data give an APPROXIMATION.
parts.G:
EXAMPLES
   Simple (GPA): grades 90 (3 credits), 80 (4 credits), 70 (2 credits):
      (90*3 + 80*4 + 70*2)/(3 + 4 + 2) = (270 + 320 + 140)/9 = 730/9
      = 81.11. (Unweighted mean would be 80.)
   Moderate (frequency table): values 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 9 with frequencies
      1, 2, 3, 2, 1, 1: sum f x = 2 + 6 + 12 + 10 + 6 + 9 = 45; sum f = 10;
      mean = 4.5.
   Combining groups: group means 4 (n = 3) and 9 (n = 2): (3*4 + 2*9)/5 = 6
      (Module 26).
parts.H:
INTERPRETATION: use weights equal to group sizes to recover the pooled
   mean; inverse-variance weights give the most precise combined
   estimate of a quantity measured with different precisions.
parts.I:
MISTAKES: weights that do not match the quantity (e.g. weighting
   rates by something other than their denominators); dividing by
   the number of items rather than the sum of weights.
parts.J:
RELATED: combining group means (F26.2), grouped data, expectation
   (F36.1).

sections.title: MEDIAN

blocks.title: MEDIAN
blocks.formulaBody:
sort the data x_(1) <= ... <= x_(n).
     n odd:   median = x_((n+1)/2)
     n even:  median = ( x_(n/2) + x_(n/2 + 1) ) / 2

parts.B:
FORMULA: sort the data x_(1) <= ... <= x_(n).
     n odd:   median = x_((n+1)/2)
     n even:  median = ( x_(n/2) + x_(n/2 + 1) ) / 2
parts.C: SYMBOLS: x_(k) the k-th smallest value (order statistic).
parts.D:
CONCEPT: the middle value: half the data lie at or below it, half at or
   above. It depends on the ORDER of values, not their magnitudes, so
   extreme values cannot drag it far (breakdown point 50%). It minimizes
   the sum of absolute deviations: sum |x_i - c| is smallest at c = median.
parts.E:
CONDITIONS: needs at least ordinal data. For even n, the average of the two
   middle values may not be an observed value (for discrete or categorical
   ordinal data some use the lower or upper median).
parts.G:
EXAMPLES
   Simple: 3, 9, 4, 1, 7 -> sorted 1, 3, 4, 7, 9 -> median 4.
           1, 2, 3, 4 -> (2 + 3)/2 = 2.5.
   Moderate (outlier): salaries (thousands) 30, 32, 35, 36, 38, 40, 300.
      Mean = 511/7 = 73.0 (pulled up by 300); median = 36 (the middle
      value of seven). The median describes the "typical" salary here.
      A 15% trimmed mean (drop the lowest and highest value) is
      (32 + 35 + 36 + 38 + 40)/5 = 36.2.
parts.H:
INTERPRETATION: a median salary of 36 means half of employees earn at
   most 36. Reports on incomes, house prices and waiting times
   usually use the median.
parts.I:
MISTAKES: forgetting to sort; mis-handling even n; assuming the median of
   combined groups equals a combination of group medians (Module 26.5).
parts.J:
RELATED: quartiles (Module 30/31), quantile of a distribution (Module
   35), L1 loss (the median minimizes mean absolute error).

sections.title: MODE

blocks.rawText:
DEFINITION: the most frequent value (or the most frequent class). 
   Data may have NO mode (all values distinct), ONE mode (unimodal), or
   several (bimodal, multimodal). For continuous data the mode is the
   location of a peak of the density.
USES: the only measure for NOMINAL data (most common color, most common
product category, most common class label: the "majority-class"
baseline classifier).
EXAMPLES: 2, 3, 3, 4, 4, 4, 5, 5, 6, 9: mode 4 (three times).
   1, 2, 2, 3, 3: modes 2 and 3 (bimodal in the data sense).
MISTAKES: reporting the mode of continuous raw data (usually every value is
unique; bin the data or estimate a density first); treating the mode as
unique; forgetting that the mode can be far from the center.

sections.rawText:

sections.title: RELATIONSHIP BETWEEN MEAN AND MEDIAN; OUTLIERS AND SKEWED DISTRIBUTIONS

blocks.rawText:
SYMMETRIC unimodal: mean = median = mode.
RIGHT-SKEWED (positive skew; long tail to the right, e.g. income):
   typically mean > median > mode (the tail pulls the mean toward it).
LEFT-SKEWED (negative skew; long tail to the left, e.g. age at death in
   developed countries): typically mean < median < mode.
!! CAUTION !! These orderings are TYPICAL, not laws; counter-examples
exist (multimodal or discrete data).
ROBUSTNESS: mean (breakdown 0%), median (50%), trimmed mean (as chosen).
EXAMPLE: data 2, 3, 3, 4, 4, 4, 5, 5, 6, 9 has mean 4.5 > median 4 = mode 4:
   right-skewed because of the 9. Pearson's 2nd skewness coefficient
   3 (mean - median)/s = 3 (0.5)/1.958 = 0.77 > 0.
TRANSFORMATIONS: for right-skewed positive data a log transform often makes
   the distribution more symmetric (mean and median closer).
OTHER MEANS [SUPPLEMENTARY]
   Geometric mean (growth factors): GM = (prod x_i)^(1/n). Growth of 10% then
      20%: factors 1.1 and 1.2: GM = sqrt(1.32) = 1.1489 -> average growth
      14.89% per period (arithmetic 15% overstates).
   Harmonic mean (rates over equal distances): HM = n / sum(1/x_i).
      Driving 120 km at 60 km/h and 120 km at 40 km/h: HM = 2/(1/60 + 1/40)
      = 48 km/h (total distance 240 km / total time 5 h = 48). The
      arithmetic mean 50 would be wrong.
   Inequality: HM <= GM <= AM (equal only if all values are equal).

blocks.title: COMPARISON TABLE: MEAN vs MEDIAN vs MODE
blocks.rawText:
Aspect              Mean                   Median                Mode
  Definition          sum / n                middle sorted value   most frequent value
  Data types          numeric                ordinal or numeric    any, incl. nominal
  Uses all values     yes                    no (order only)       no (frequency only)
  Outlier sensitivity high                   low (robust)          low
  Skewed data         pulled toward tail     stays near the bulk   at the peak
  Unique?             always                 always                may be none or many
  Algebra             easy (linear,          harder                hard
                      combinable)
  Minimizes           sum of squares         sum of absolute       (0-1 loss: number
                                             deviations            of misses)
  Typical use         symmetric data,        income, prices,       categories,
                      totals, modeling       skewed data           majority class

the mean is the best constant predictor under squared
error, the median under absolute error, the mode under 0-1 loss: these
are the baselines (mean-baseline regressor, majority classifier).
Imputation: median is safer for skewed features. Robust scaling uses
median and IQR.

Imputation: median is safer for skewed features. Robust scaling uses
median and IQR.

sections.title: FREQUENCY DISTRIBUTIONS

blocks.rawText:
DEFINITIONS (for data x_1..x_n)
   FREQUENCY f_j: number of observations equal to value x_j (or falling in
      class j).
   RELATIVE FREQUENCY f_j / n (a proportion; all sum to 1).
   CUMULATIVE FREQUENCY: running total of frequencies up to class j;
      cumulative relative frequency = running total / n.
WORKED EXAMPLE: data 2, 3, 3, 4, 4, 4, 5, 5, 6, 9 (n = 10)
   Value  Freq  Rel. freq  Cumulative freq  Cumulative rel.
    2      1     0.1        1                0.1
    3      2     0.2        3                0.3
    4      3     0.3        6                0.6
    5      2     0.2        8                0.8
    6      1     0.1        9                0.9
    9      1     0.1        10               1.0
FOR CONTINUOUS DATA: group into non-overlapping classes (bins); state the
boundary convention (e.g. [a, b), left-closed), otherwise boundary values are
double counted or lost.

sections.title: HISTOGRAMS AND DENSITY HISTOGRAMS

blocks.title: DENSITY HISTOGRAM
blocks.formulaBody:
height of the bar for bin j of width h_j:
        d_j = f_j / ( n h_j )
   so that  sum_j d_j h_j = 1  (total area 1).

parts.B:
FORMULA: height of the bar for bin j of width h_j:
        d_j = f_j / ( n h_j )
   so that  sum_j d_j h_j = 1  (total area 1).
parts.C: SYMBOLS: f_j count in bin j; n sample size; h_j bin width.
parts.D:
CONCEPT: the AREA of a bar (not its height) represents the proportion of
   data in the bin: area_j = d_j h_j = f_j/n. Thus the histogram
   approximates a probability density function (Module 35): the area
   over [a, b] approximates P(a <= X < b).
parts.E:
CONDITIONS: with UNEQUAL bin widths a count histogram is misleading (a
   wide bin looks tall merely because it is wide); use density heights.
parts.H:
INTERPRETATION: heights are "proportion per unit of x" (density), not
   proportions. Density values can exceed 1 if the bins are narrow
   (e.g. data in [0, 0.1]).
BIN CHOICE (a bias-variance trade-off: too few bins hide structure, too
many show noise)
     Sturges: k = ceil(log2 n) + 1 bins.
     Scott:   h = 3.49 s n^(-1/3).
     Freedman-Diaconis: h = 2 IQR n^(-1/3) (robust to outliers).
   Always try several bin widths; shape impressions depend on them.
   (NumPy: bins='auto' combines Sturges and FD.) KERNEL DENSITY
   ESTIMATES smooth the histogram [SUPPLEMENTARY].
parts.I:
MISTAKES: unequal widths without density scaling; unlabeled axes (counts
   vs density); extreme outliers stretching the x-axis; histogram of
   categorical data.
parts.J: RELATED: PDF (F35.3), ECDF (F30.2), kernel density estimates.

sections.title: EMPIRICAL DISTRIBUTIONS

blocks.title: EMPIRICAL CUMULATIVE DISTRIBUTION FUNCTION (ECDF)

parts.B: FORMULA:   F_n(x) = (1/n) * #{ i : x_i <= x } = (1/n) sum 1[x_i <= x]
parts.C:
SYMBOLS: 1[condition] equals 1 if true, else 0; #{...} counts the
   observations at most x.
parts.D:
CONCEPT: the proportion of the sample at or below x. A step function that
   starts at 0, rises by 1/n at each data point (by k/n at a value
   repeated k times) and reaches 1. It is the CDF of the "distribution
   that puts probability 1/n on each observed value".
parts.E:
CONDITIONS: right-continuous, non-decreasing, between 0 and 1. By the
   Glivenko-Cantelli theorem [SUPPLEMENTARY] F_n converges uniformly to the
   true CDF F as n grows. Quantiles are read by inverting F_n.
parts.G:
EXAMPLE (data above): F_n(3) = 3/10 = 0.3; F_n(4) = 0.6; F_n(4.5) = 0.6
   (flat between jumps); F_n(9) = 1; F_n(1) = 0.
   Median: smallest x with F_n(x) >= 0.5 -> 4.
parts.H:
INTERPRETATION: "60% of observations are at most 4". The ECDF needs no
   binning, so it is the cleanest honest picture of a sample; the
   bootstrap resamples from F_n (Module 37); the KS statistic compares F_n
   with a theoretical CDF.
parts.I:
MISTAKES: reading values of the ECDF as densities; forgetting the
   jump-size rule for ties.
parts.J:
RELATED: CDF (Module 35), quantiles, histograms (ECDF = cumulative
   version).

QUARTILES AND THE FIVE-NUMBER SUMMARY
   Q1 (25th percentile), Q2 = median, Q3 (75th percentile). Minimum, Q1,
   median, Q3, maximum form the five-number summary, drawn as a BOX PLOT
   (box from Q1 to Q3, line at the median, whiskers to the most extreme
   values within the fences, points beyond as outliers).
   For the data above (linear-interpolation rule): Q1 = 3.25, Q2 = 4,
   Q3 = 5 (position 2.25 in 0-based sorted values: 3 + 0.25(4 - 3) = 3.25;
   position 6.75: both neighbors 5).

sections.title: DISTRIBUTION SHAPE AND SKEWNESS

blocks.rawText:
SHAPE VOCABULARY
   Modality: unimodal (one peak), bimodal (two peaks; often two
      sub-populations mixed), uniform (flat), multimodal.
   Symmetry: left side mirrors right (normal-like) vs skewed.
   Tails: heavy tails (more extremes than a normal), light tails.
   Spread and center.

blocks.title: SKEWNESS COEFFICIENTS
blocks.formulaBody:
Moment coefficient:  g1 = m3 / m2^(3/2),
        m2 = (1/n) sum (x_i - x_bar)^2,  m3 = (1/n) sum (x_i - x_bar)^3
     Adjusted (Fisher-Pearson, as in Excel/SciPy bias=False):
        G1 = sqrt(n(n - 1)) / (n - 2) * g1
     Pearson's second coefficient: Sk2 = 3 (x_bar - median) / s.

parts.B:
FORMULAS
     Moment coefficient:  g1 = m3 / m2^(3/2),
        m2 = (1/n) sum (x_i - x_bar)^2,  m3 = (1/n) sum (x_i - x_bar)^3
     Adjusted (Fisher-Pearson, as in Excel/SciPy bias=False):
        G1 = sqrt(n(n - 1)) / (n - 2) * g1
     Pearson's second coefficient: Sk2 = 3 (x_bar - median) / s.
parts.C: SYMBOLS: m2, m3 the second and third central moments; s sample SD.
parts.D:
CONCEPT: cubing the standardized deviations keeps their SIGN, so a
   long tail on one side makes that side dominate the sum. g1 > 0:
   right-skewed; g1 < 0: left-skewed; g1 approx 0: roughly symmetric.
   (Excess kurtosis g2 = m4/m2^2 - 3 measures tail heaviness relative to the
   normal: 0 for a normal.)
parts.E:
CONDITIONS: skewness is sensitive to outliers; needs adequate n
   (unstable for small samples); several definitions exist, so state
   which one.
parts.G:
EXAMPLE: data 2, 3, 3, 4, 4, 4, 5, 5, 6, 9: g1 = 1.12 (calculated with
   the 1/n moment form), G1 = 1.33 (adjusted); both positive:
   right-skewed. Symmetric data 1, 2, 3, 4, 5: g1 = 0.
parts.H:
INTERPRETATION: rough guide |g1| < 0.5 approximately symmetric;
   0.5-1 moderately skewed; > 1 highly skewed (rule of thumb only).
parts.I:
MISTAKES: calling a distribution symmetric because the mean equals the
   median (not sufficient); confusing the direction ("right skew" means
   the TAIL is on the right, the bulk on the left).
parts.J:
RELATED: moments (F36.4), transformations (F36.5), normality checks
   (section 40.4).

sections.title: OUTLIERS

blocks.rawText:
DEFINITION: an observation far from the bulk of the data. It may be an
error, a different population, or a genuine extreme: investigate before
removing.
RULES OF THUMB
   TUKEY FENCES (box plot rule): flag values below Q1 - 1.5 IQR or above
      Q3 + 1.5 IQR; "far out" beyond 3 IQR.
      Example (data above): IQR = 5 - 3.25 = 1.75. Fences:
      3.25 - 2.625 = 0.625 and 5 + 2.625 = 7.625. The value 9 lies
      above 7.625: flagged as an outlier.
   Z-SCORE: z = (x - x_bar)/s; |z| > 3 flags. Weakness: outliers inflate x_bar
      and s, masking themselves.
   MODIFIED Z-SCORE: M = 0.6745 (x - median)/MAD, MAD = median |x_i - median|;
      |M| > 3.5 flags (robust).
TREATMENT: verify the data; keep if genuine; use robust methods (median,
   IQR, Huber loss); winsorize (cap at percentiles); transform; analyze
   with and without; do not delete simply to improve a model fit.
EXAMPLE (impact): salaries 30, 32, 35, 36, 38, 40, 300: the mean jumps from
   35.2 (without 300) to 73.0 (with), the median from 35.5 to 36.
   (Without 300: six values 30, 32, 35, 36, 38, 40: mean 35.17, median 35.5.)

sections.title: INTERPRETING SCATTER PLOTS

blocks.rawText:
A scatter plot shows each observation as a point (x_i, y_i). Describe:
   DIRECTION: upward (positive association), downward (negative), none.
   FORM: linear, curved (quadratic, exponential, saturating), clusters.
   STRENGTH: how tightly points follow the pattern.
   OUTLIERS and INFLUENTIAL POINTS: unusual points; high-leverage points far
      in x can pull a fitted line.
   SPREAD PATTERN: constant vertical spread (homoscedastic) or a funnel
      (heteroscedastic: variance grows with x).
   OVERPLOTTING: with many points use transparency, hexbin or 2D
      histograms; DISCRETE values create stripes.
WARNINGS: correlation coefficient hides shape; ANSCOMBE'S QUARTET: four
   datasets with the same means, variances, correlation (0.816) and
   regression line but completely different scatter plots (linear,
   curved, an outlier, a single leverage point). ALWAYS plot.
GROUPS: color by category; Simpson's paradox can reverse the overall trend
   relative to within-group trends.

blocks.text:
scatter plots reveal nonlinearity (add polynomial or
tree features), heteroscedasticity (weighted or log-transformed
regression), clusters (unsupervised methods), and leakage (suspiciously
perfect relationships).

   SPREAD PATTERN: constant vertical spread (homoscedastic) or a funnel
      (heteroscedastic: variance grows with x).
   OVERPLOTTING: with many points use transparency, hexbin or 2D
      histograms; DISCRETE values create stripes.
WARNINGS: correlation coefficient hides shape; ANSCOMBE'S QUARTET: four
   datasets with the same means, variances, correlation (0.816) and
   regression line but completely different scatter plots (linear,
   curved, an outlier, a single leverage point). ALWAYS plot.
GROUPS: color by category; Simpson's paradox can reverse the overall trend
   relative to within-group trends.
DATA SCIENCE LINK: scatter plots reveal nonlinearity (add polynomial or
tree features), heteroscedasticity (weighted or log-transformed
regression), clusters (unsupervised methods), and leakage (suspiciously
perfect relationships).

title: MEASURES OF DISPERSION
introRaw:
BASIC IDEA (plain English)
Two datasets can have the same mean but be very different: test scores
all near 70 versus scores spread from 20 to 100. Measures of dispersion
(spread, variability) quantify how far values typically lie from each
other or from the center.

sections.title: VARIANCE AND STANDARD DEVIATION

blocks.title: POPULATION VARIANCE AND STANDARD DEVIATION
blocks.formulaBody:
sigma^2 = (1/N) sum[i=1..N] (x_i - mu)^2
     sigma   = sqrt(sigma^2)
     Computational form: sigma^2 = (1/N) sum x_i^2 - mu^2

parts.A: NAME: Population variance and standard deviation.
parts.B:
FORMULAS
     sigma^2 = (1/N) sum[i=1..N] (x_i - mu)^2
     sigma   = sqrt(sigma^2)
     Computational form: sigma^2 = (1/N) sum x_i^2 - mu^2
parts.C:
SYMBOLS: mu population mean; N population size; (x_i - mu) the deviation
   of observation i from the mean; sigma^2 the average squared deviation.
parts.D:
CONCEPT: the AVERAGE squared distance from the mean. Squaring makes all
   deviations positive and penalizes large deviations more. The
   standard deviation returns to the original units.
parts.E:
CONDITIONS: use when the data are the ENTIRE population of interest.
   Properties: sigma^2 >= 0 (= 0 iff all values equal); Var(a x + b) =
   a^2 Var(x) (shifting does not matter, scaling squares);
   units of variance are squared units; SD has the original units.
parts.H:
INTERPRETATION: sigma = 2 means a typical value lies about 2 units
   from the mean (for 2, 4, 4, 4, 5, 5, 7, 9).
parts.I:
MISTAKES: using this formula on a sample (underestimates, see below);
   forgetting the square root for SD; confusing variance units.
parts.J:
RELATED: sample variance (F31.4); the expectation form E[X^2] - mu^2
   (F36.3).

B. FORMULAS
     sigma^2 = (1/N) sum[i=1..N] (x_i - mu)^2
     sigma   = sqrt(sigma^2)
     Computational form: sigma^2 = (1/N) sum x_i^2 - mu^2

   standard deviation returns to the original units.

   Properties: sigma^2 >= 0 (= 0 iff all values equal); Var(a x + b) =
   a^2 Var(x) (shifting does not matter, scaling squares);
   units of variance are squared units; SD has the original units.
G. EXAMPLE: 2, 4, 4, 4, 5, 5, 7, 9 as a whole population: mu = 5.
   Deviations -3, -1, -1, -1, 0, 0, 2, 4; squares 9, 1, 1, 1, 0, 0, 4, 16;
   sum = 32. sigma^2 = 32/8 = 4; sigma = 2.
   Computational check: sum x^2 = 4 + 16 + 16 + 16 + 25 + 25 + 49 + 81 = 232;
   232/8 - 25 = 29 - 25 = 4. OK.

   from the mean (for 2, 4, 4, 4, 5, 5, 7, 9).

blocks.title: SAMPLE VARIANCE AND SAMPLE STANDARD DEVIATION
blocks.formulaBody:
s^2 = (1/(n - 1)) sum[i=1..n] (x_i - x_bar)^2
     s   = sqrt(s^2)
     Computational form: s^2 = ( sum x_i^2 - n x_bar^2 ) / (n - 1)

parts.A: NAME: Sample variance (unbiased) and sample standard deviation.
parts.B:
FORMULAS
     s^2 = (1/(n - 1)) sum[i=1..n] (x_i - x_bar)^2
     s   = sqrt(s^2)
     Computational form: s^2 = ( sum x_i^2 - n x_bar^2 ) / (n - 1)
parts.C: SYMBOLS: x_bar the SAMPLE mean (not mu); n - 1 "degrees of freedom".
parts.D:
CONCEPT: an ESTIMATE of the unknown population variance sigma^2 from a
   sample. The divisor n - 1 corrects a systematic underestimate that
   appears because the deviations are measured from x_bar (which is
   calculated from the same data and sits closer to the data than the
   true mu does).
parts.E:
CONDITIONS: needs n >= 2. Assumes the sample is random from the
   population. s^2 is UNBIASED for sigma^2 (E[s^2] = sigma^2); s is NOT
   unbiased for sigma (slightly underestimates, by Jensen's inequality,
   because sqrt is concave).
parts.F:
DERIVATION OF THE n - 1 (WHY BESSEL'S CORRECTION)
   Let X_1..X_n be independent with mean mu and variance sigma^2, and
   x_bar their mean. Identity (add and subtract mu):
        sum (x_i - x_bar)^2 = sum (x_i - mu)^2 - n (x_bar - mu)^2.
   Take expectations:
        E[ sum (x_i - mu)^2 ] = n sigma^2,
        E[ n (x_bar - mu)^2 ] = n Var(x_bar) = n (sigma^2/n) = sigma^2.
   Hence E[ sum (x_i - x_bar)^2 ] = n sigma^2 - sigma^2 = (n - 1) sigma^2.
   So dividing by n - 1 gives an unbiased estimator; dividing by n gives
   expectation (n - 1)/n times sigma^2: too small.
   Degrees-of-freedom view: the deviations x_i - x_bar must sum to 0, so only
   n - 1 of them are free to vary; the n-th is determined.
parts.G:
EXAMPLES
   Simple: sample 2, 4, 4, 4, 5, 5, 7, 9 (n = 8): x_bar = 5; sum of squared
      deviations 32; s^2 = 32/7 = 4.571; s = 2.138.
      (Population version for the same numbers: 4 and 2.)
   Moderate (simulation evidence): draw 200,000 samples of size 5 from a
      normal with sigma^2 = 4. The average of the divide-by-n variance is
      about 3.2 (= (4/5)*4); the divide-by-(n - 1) version averages about
      4.0.
   Moderate 2: scores 70, 75, 80, 85, 90: x_bar = 80; deviations -10, -5, 0, 5,
      10; squares 100, 25, 0, 25, 100 = 250; s^2 = 250/4 = 62.5; s = 7.91.
parts.H:
INTERPRETATION: s = 7.91 means scores typically lie about 8 points from
   the mean. For roughly bell-shaped data about 68% of values lie within
   +/- 1 s and 95% within +/- 2 s (empirical rule). Chebyshev's
   inequality (any distribution): at least 1 - 1/k^2 of the data lie
   within k standard deviations (k = 2: at least 75%).
parts.I:
COMMON MISTAKES: dividing by n for a sample; dividing by n - 1 for a
   complete population; software defaults (NumPy np.var and np.std:
   ddof = 0; pandas .var/.std: ddof = 1; statistics.variance: n - 1,
   statistics.pvariance: n); computing the computational form with huge
   means (cancellation; Module 26); n = 1 (undefined).
parts.J:
RELATED: standard error (Module 37), unbiased estimation (Module 38),
   t-distribution df = n - 1 (Module 39), regression residual variance
   (divide by n - p, Module 40).

blocks.title: COMPARISON TABLE: POPULATION vs SAMPLE VARIANCE
blocks.rawText:
Aspect               Population variance sigma^2        Sample variance s^2
  Formula              (1/N) sum (x_i - mu)^2             (1/(n-1)) sum (x_i - x_bar)^2
  Center used          true mean mu (fixed, known)        sample mean x_bar (estimated)
  Purpose              DESCRIBE the whole population      ESTIMATE sigma^2 from a sample
  Divisor              N                                  n - 1 (degrees of freedom)
  Bias as estimator    n/a                                unbiased
  Dividing sample by n biased low: E = (n-1)/n sigma^2    corrected by n - 1
  Python default       np.var(x) (ddof=0)                 pd.Series.var() / np.var(x, ddof=1)
  Use when             you hold ALL the data of interest  data are a sample
  (Large n: the two nearly coincide.)

sections.title: WHY SQUARED DEVIATIONS ARE USED

blocks.rawText:
THE PROBLEM: raw deviations x_i - x_bar sum to ZERO (positive and negative
cancel), so their average is useless as a spread measure.
FIXES: (1) take absolute values: the mean absolute deviation
(1/n) sum |x_i - x_bar|; or (2) square them: variance.
WHY SQUARES ARE PREFERRED IN STATISTICS
   1. SMOOTH and differentiable everywhere (|x| has a kink at 0): easy
      calculus; closed-form minimizers (least squares).
   2. The mean is exactly the value minimizing the sum of squares (the
      median minimizes the sum of absolute values).
   3. ADDITIVITY: for independent variables Var(X + Y) = Var(X) + Var(Y)
      (SDs do not add). Variances decompose into explained and unexplained
      parts (ANOVA, R^2).
   4. Geometry: sum of squares is squared Euclidean distance; Pythagoras
      and orthogonal projections (Module 10) work with it.
   5. Natural for the NORMAL distribution (its density has the squared term
      in the exponent) and the Central Limit Theorem.
COSTS OF SQUARING: (a) units are squared (hence the SD); (b) outliers are
heavily penalized (a deviation of 10 counts 100x a deviation of 1), so
the variance is NOT robust; (c) alternative: MAD / mean absolute error
when robustness matters (L1 loss).
EXAMPLE: deviations 1, 1, 1, 1 versus 0, 0, 0, 4: both have mean absolute
deviation 1, but variance (taking squared deviations / n) is 1 versus 4:
squaring is sensitive to one large deviation.
OTHER SPREAD MEASURE: coefficient of variation CV = s / x_bar (ratio scale,
positive mean); unit-free relative spread. Example: heights SD 7 cm at mean
170 cm: CV = 4.1%; weights SD 12 kg at mean 70 kg: CV = 17%.

title: CORRELATION
introRaw:
BASIC IDEA (plain English)
Correlation measures how consistently two variables move together: when
one is above its average, is the other usually above (positive), usually
below (negative), or unrelated?

blocks.title: COVARIANCE
blocks.formulaBody:
Population: Cov(X, Y) = E[ (X - mu_X)(Y - mu_Y) ] = E[XY] - mu_X mu_Y
     Sample: s_xy = (1/(n - 1)) sum (x_i - x_bar)(y_i - y_bar)
                  = ( sum x_i y_i - n x_bar y_bar ) / (n - 1)

parts.B:
FORMULAS

     Sample: s_xy = (1/(n - 1)) sum (x_i - x_bar)(y_i - y_bar)
                  = ( sum x_i y_i - n x_bar y_bar ) / (n - 1)
parts.C:
SYMBOLS: x_i, y_i paired observations; x_bar, y_bar the sample means;
   mu_X, mu_Y population means; E[.] expectation (Module 36).
parts.D:
CONCEPT: multiply the two deviations for each pair. If both are above
   (or both below) their means the product is positive; if one is above
   and the other below, negative. The average product captures the
   joint tendency. Cov(X, X) = Var(X).
parts.G:
EXAMPLE: x = 1, 2, 3, 4, 5; y = 2, 4, 5, 4, 5. x_bar = 3, y_bar = 4.
   dx: -2, -1, 0, 1, 2; dy: -2, 0, 1, 0, 1.
   Products: 4, 0, 0, 0, 2: sum 6. s_xy = 6/4 = 1.5 (positive).
   Doubling y plus 10 (y' = 2y + 10): s_xy' = 2*1.5 = 3.0 (covariance
   changes with units).
parts.H:
INTERPRETATION: the sign gives the direction of linear association; the
   size depends on units and variances (so cannot compare strength).
parts.I:
MISTAKES: reading magnitude as strength; dividing by n vs n - 1
   inconsistently (state the convention); concluding independence from
   zero covariance.
parts.J: RELATED: covariance matrix (Module 10), correlation.

sections.title: PEARSON CORRELATION COEFFICIENT

blocks.title: PEARSON CORRELATION COEFFICIENT
blocks.formulaBody:
rho = Cov(X, Y) / (sigma_X sigma_Y)                      (population)
     r = s_xy / (s_x s_y)
       = sum (x_i - x_bar)(y_i - y_bar) / sqrt( sum (x_i - x_bar)^2 *
                                              sum (y_i - y_bar)^2 )
       = (1/(n - 1)) sum z_xi z_yi   (z = standardized values)

parts.B:
FORMULAS
     rho = Cov(X, Y) / (sigma_X sigma_Y)                      (population)
     r = s_xy / (s_x s_y)
       = sum (x_i - x_bar)(y_i - y_bar) / sqrt( sum (x_i - x_bar)^2 *
                                              sum (y_i - y_bar)^2 )
       = (1/(n - 1)) sum z_xi z_yi   (z = standardized values)
parts.C:
SYMBOLS: s_x, s_y sample standard deviations; z_xi = (x_i - x_bar)/s_x.
   The n or n - 1 factors cancel between numerator and denominator, so r
   is the same whichever convention is used consistently.
parts.D:
CONCEPT: covariance rescaled to be UNIT-FREE: the average product of
   standardized values. Geometrically, r is the COSINE of the angle
   between the centered data vectors (Module 10): r = cos(theta). Hence
   -1 <= r <= 1 by Cauchy-Schwarz.
parts.E:
CONDITIONS & PROPERTIES
     - Measures LINEAR association only.
     - r = +1 or -1 iff all points lie exactly on a straight line (positive or
       negative slope); r = 0 means NO LINEAR association (not
       independence).
     - Symmetric: r(X, Y) = r(Y, X).
     - Needs non-zero variance in both variables.
     - Sensitive to outliers and to restricted range (selecting only high
       values of x lowers r).
     - In simple linear regression r^2 = R^2, the share of variance of y
       explained by x; slope b1 = r s_y / s_x.
parts.F:
DERIVATION OF THE BOUNDS: the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality
   |sum a_i b_i|^2 <= sum a_i^2 sum b_i^2, applied to a_i = x_i - x_bar,
   b_i = y_i - y_bar, gives |r| <= 1, with equality iff b is a multiple of a.
parts.G:
EXAMPLES
   Simple: x = 1..5, y = 2, 4, 5, 4, 5:
      sum dx dy = 6; sum dx^2 = 4 + 1 + 0 + 1 + 4 = 10;
      sum dy^2 = 4 + 0 + 1 + 0 + 1 = 6.
      r = 6/sqrt(10 * 6) = 6/7.746 = 0.7746.
      r^2 = 0.6: 60% of the variance of y is linearly explained by x.
   Moderate 1 (nonlinear): x = -2, -1, 0, 1, 2 and y = x^2 = 4, 1, 0, 1, 4:
      x_bar = 0, y_bar = 2; sum dx dy = (-2)(2) + (-1)(-1) + 0 + (1)(-1) + (2)(2)
      = -4 + 1 - 1 + 4 = 0, so r = 0 although y is a perfect function of x.
      (Correlation misses symmetric nonlinear dependence.)
   Moderate 2 (perfect line): y = 3 - 2x gives r = -1 exactly.
parts.H:
INTERPRETATION: sign = direction; |r| = strength of the LINEAR
   relationship. Rough guide (context-dependent!): |r| < 0.3 weak,
   0.3-0.7 moderate, > 0.7 strong. In noisy social data r = 0.3 can be
   notable; in physics r = 0.95 might be poor.
parts.I:
MISTAKES: interpreting r as a percentage of association (r = 0.5 is not
   "50% related": r^2 = 0.25); interpreting r = 0 as independence;
   computing r on data with an outlier/leverage point without looking at
   the scatter plot; correlating ratios sharing a common denominator
   (spurious correlation); using it for categorical or strongly
   nonlinear relations.
parts.J:
RELATED: Spearman's rank correlation [SUPPLEMENTARY] = Pearson r on the
   RANKS: robust to outliers and detects monotonic (not only linear)
   relations; for the example above it is 0.738. Kendall's tau is another
   rank correlation. Point-biserial and phi coefficients for binary data.

sections.title: POSITIVE AND NEGATIVE CORRELATION; STRENGTH

blocks.rawText:
r > 0: as x increases y tends to increase (height and weight).
  r < 0: as x increases y tends to decrease (price and quantity demanded).
  |r| near 1: points close to a line; |r| near 0: little linear pattern.
  Strength is about the SCATTER around the line, not about the slope:
  two datasets can have the same slope but different r.
  r = 0.9 with slope 0.01 means a very tight, nearly flat line.

sections.title: CORRELATION vs CAUSATION

blocks.rawText:
STATEMENT: a correlation between X and Y does NOT establish that X causes Y.
POSSIBLE EXPLANATIONS for an observed correlation
   1. X causes Y.
   2. Y causes X (REVERSE CAUSATION): cities with more police have more
      crime; more crime leads to more police.
   3. A CONFOUNDER Z causes both: ice-cream sales and drownings correlate
      because hot weather increases both.
   4. COINCIDENCE or data dredging (test many pairs and some will appear
      correlated by chance; Module 39 multiple testing); trending series
      (two increasing time series correlate spuriously).
   5. Selection bias or collider conditioning.
   6. Aggregation effects (Simpson's paradox).
HOW CAUSAL CLAIMS ARE SUPPORTED: RANDOMIZED CONTROLLED EXPERIMENTS (A/B
tests) break links with confounders; observational causal inference
(adjustment, matching, instrumental variables, difference-in-differences,
causal graphs) needs explicit assumptions.
DATA SCIENCE EXAMPLE: a model finds that customers who use the premium
support feature churn less. Support may not cause retention: engaged
customers may be both likelier to use the feature and to stay (a
confounder). A feature importance is not a causal effect.
MISTAKES: "x predicts y, therefore x causes y"; policy action from
correlational features; ignoring lurking variables.

sections.title: EFFECT OF SCALING AND TRANSFORMATIONS; INVARIANCE

blocks.title: INVARIANCE OF CORRELATION UNDER LINEAR TRANSFORMATIONS
blocks.formulaBody:
for constants a, b, c, d with a != 0, c != 0:
        r(aX + b, cY + d) = sign(a c) * r(X, Y).
   Thus r is UNCHANGED by any shift and by positive rescaling (a, c > 0),
   and only changes sign if exactly one scale factor is negative.
   By contrast Cov(aX + b, cY + d) = a c Cov(X, Y) (changes magnitude).

parts.A: NAME: Invariance under positive linear scaling (and shifts).
parts.B:
FORMULA: for constants a, b, c, d with a != 0, c != 0:
        r(aX + b, cY + d) = sign(a c) * r(X, Y).
   Thus r is UNCHANGED by any shift and by positive rescaling (a, c > 0),
   and only changes sign if exactly one scale factor is negative.
   By contrast Cov(aX + b, cY + d) = a c Cov(X, Y) (changes magnitude).
parts.C:
SYMBOLS: a, c scale factors; b, d shifts; X, Y variables; r the
   correlation.
parts.D:
CONCEPT: correlation is computed from standardized values, and standardizing
   removes shifts (subtract mean) and positive scalings (divide by SD).
parts.E:
CONDITIONS: holds exactly for linear changes of units; not for
   nonlinear transformations.
parts.F:
DERIVATION: Cov(aX + b, cY + d) = a c Cov(X,Y); SDs scale by |a| and |c|:
   r' = a c Cov / (|a| |c| s_x s_y) = sign(a c) r.
parts.G:
EXAMPLE: x = 1..5, y = 2, 4, 5, 4, 5 with r = 0.7746.
   Convert y to y' = 2y + 10: r = 0.7746 (same), covariance 3.0 (doubled).
   Convert y to y'' = -y: r = -0.7746; covariance -1.5.

A. NAME: Invariance under positive linear scaling (and shifts).

title: PROBABILITY FOUNDATIONS
introRaw:
BASIC IDEA (plain English)
Probability is a number between 0 and 1 that measures how likely an
uncertain outcome is. 0 means impossible, 1 means certain. It gives a
consistent language for reasoning about uncertainty, which is the basis
of statistics and machine learning.

BASIC IDEA (plain English)

uncertain outcome is. 0 means impossible, 1 means certain. It gives a

of statistics and machine learning.

sections.title: SAMPLE SPACES AND EVENTS

blocks.rawText:
DEFINITIONS
   RANDOM EXPERIMENT: a process whose result is uncertain but whose
      possible results are known (roll a die, test a patient, observe
      tomorrow's temperature).
   OUTCOME: one possible result of the experiment.
   SAMPLE SPACE (Omega): the set of ALL possible outcomes.
   EVENT: a subset of the sample space (a collection of outcomes). The
      event "occurs" if the outcome is one of its members.
   ELEMENTARY (simple) EVENT: a single outcome.
   CERTAIN event: Omega. IMPOSSIBLE event: the empty set.
EXAMPLES
   Die: Omega = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6}. Event A = "even" = {2, 4, 6}.
   Two coin tosses: Omega = {HH, HT, TH, TT} (4 equally likely outcomes).
      "At least one head" = {HH, HT, TH}. NOTE: the outcomes HT and TH are
      different; treating "one head, one tail" as a single outcome gives
      wrong probabilities.
   Two dice: Omega has 36 ordered pairs (d1, d2). Event "sum = 7" has 6
      outcomes: (1,6), (2,5), (3,4), (4,3), (5,2), (6,1).
   Continuous: time until a customer arrives: Omega = [0, infinity).
      Probabilities are then assigned to intervals, not single points
      (Module 35).
   Classifier output: Omega = {spam, not spam}.

blocks.title: PROBABILITY AXIOMS (KOLMOGOROV) AND CONSEQUENCES
blocks.formulaBody:
A probability measure P assigns a number to each event so that
     (1) P(A) >= 0 for every event A;
     (2) P(Omega) = 1;
     (3) if A_1, A_2, ... are MUTUALLY EXCLUSIVE (pairwise disjoint) events,
         P(A_1 U A_2 U ...) = P(A_1) + P(A_2) + ...
   CONSEQUENCES: P(empty set) = 0; 0 <= P(A) <= 1; if A is a subset of B then
   P(A) <= P(B); P(A^c) = 1 - P(A).

parts.B:
A probability measure P assigns a number to each event so that
     (1) P(A) >= 0 for every event A;
     (2) P(Omega) = 1;
     (3) if A_1, A_2, ... are MUTUALLY EXCLUSIVE (pairwise disjoint) events,
         P(A_1 U A_2 U ...) = P(A_1) + P(A_2) + ...
   CONSEQUENCES: P(empty set) = 0; 0 <= P(A) <= 1; if A is a subset of B then
   P(A) <= P(B); P(A^c) = 1 - P(A).
parts.C: SYMBOLS: U union ("or"); A^c complement ("not A").
parts.D: CONCEPT: everything else in probability follows from these three rules.
parts.E:
HOW PROBABILITIES ARE ASSIGNED
     CLASSICAL (equally likely outcomes, finite Omega):
         P(A) = |A| / |Omega|  (number of favorable / total outcomes).
         Valid ONLY if the outcomes are genuinely equally likely.
     EMPIRICAL (relative frequency): P(A) approx (times A occurred)/(number
         of trials), converging as trials grow (law of large numbers).
     SUBJECTIVE: degree of belief (Bayesian).
parts.G:
EXAMPLES
   Simple: fair die, P(even) = 3/6 = 0.5. Two dice: P(sum = 7) = 6/36 = 1/6.
   Moderate: loaded die with P(1) = 0.1, P(2) = 0.1, P(3) = 0.1, P(4) = 0.1,
      P(5) = 0.1, P(6) = 0.5 (sums to 1): P(even) = 0.1 + 0.1 + 0.5 = 0.7:
      the classical formula would be wrong because outcomes are not
      equally likely.
parts.H:
INTERPRETATION: every rule of probability follows from three simple
   axioms.
parts.I:
MISTAKES: assuming outcomes are equally likely when they are not (e.g.
   "it either rains or it does not, so 50%"); unordered outcomes for
   multi-object experiments; probabilities that do not sum to 1.
parts.J:
RELATED: complement rule (F33.2), addition rule (F33.3), conditional
   probability (F34.1).

sections.title: EVENT OPERATIONS, COMPLEMENTS

blocks.rawText:
UNION A U B: A occurs OR B occurs (or both).
   INTERSECTION A n B (written AB): BOTH occur.
   COMPLEMENT A^c: A does NOT occur. A U A^c = Omega, A n A^c = empty.
   DIFFERENCE A \ B (A and not B) = A n B^c.
   MUTUALLY EXCLUSIVE (disjoint): A n B = empty (cannot both occur).
   EXHAUSTIVE: A_1 U ... U A_k = Omega. A PARTITION is a collection that is
      both mutually exclusive and exhaustive.
   DE MORGAN (sets): (A U B)^c = A^c n B^c; (A n B)^c = A^c U B^c.
   SUBSET: A subset of B means A occurring forces B to occur.
EXAMPLE (die): A = {2, 4, 6} (even), B = {4, 5, 6} (greater than 3).
   A U B = {2, 4, 5, 6}; A n B = {4, 6}; A^c = {1, 3, 5};
   A \ B = {2}; (A U B)^c = {1, 3} = A^c n B^c = {1,3,5} n {1,2,3} = {1, 3}. OK.
Venn diagrams help, but write out the event as a set.

blocks.title: COMPLEMENT RULE

parts.C:
SYMBOLS: A an event; A^c its complement; P(none) the probability that
   no event occurs.
parts.D:
CONCEPT: either A happens or it does not. Powerful for "at least one"
   problems: P(at least one) = 1 - P(none).
parts.E:
CONDITIONS: always valid; for 'at least one of independent events'
   use 1 minus the product of the (1 - p_i).
parts.G:
EXAMPLES
   Simple: P(not 6 on a die) = 1 - 1/6 = 5/6.
   Moderate: P(at least one 6 in 4 rolls) = 1 - (5/6)^4 = 1 - 625/1296
      = 671/1296 = 0.5177.
   Moderate 2 (birthday problem): in a group of 23 people the probability
      that at least two share a birthday (365 equally likely days, ignore
      leap years) is 1 - (365/365)(364/365)...(343/365) = 0.5073. Counting
      the complement ("all different") is far easier than counting all
      the ways to have matches.
parts.H:
INTERPRETATION: counting the complement is often far easier (birthday
   problem, system reliability).
parts.I:
MISTAKE: computing "at least one" by adding single-event
   probabilities (double counts; see addition rule).
parts.J: RELATED: addition rule (F33.3), independence (F34.2).

sections.title: ADDITION AND MULTIPLICATION RULES

blocks.title: ADDITION RULE
blocks.formulaBody:
P(A U B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A n B)
     If A and B are mutually exclusive: P(A U B) = P(A) + P(B).
     Three events: P(A U B U C) = P(A) + P(B) + P(C) - P(AB) - P(AC) - P(BC)
                                  + P(ABC).

parts.B:
FORMULAS
     P(A U B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A n B)
     If A and B are mutually exclusive: P(A U B) = P(A) + P(B).
     Three events: P(A U B U C) = P(A) + P(B) + P(C) - P(AB) - P(AC) - P(BC)
                                  + P(ABC).
parts.C: SYMBOLS: P(A n B) probability both occur.
parts.D:
CONCEPT: adding P(A) and P(B) counts the overlap A n B twice, so subtract
   it once.
parts.E: CONDITIONS: always valid (the disjoint form needs mutual exclusivity).
parts.F:
DERIVATION: A U B = A + (B \ A) (disjoint), and B = (A n B) + (B \ A);
   so P(A U B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A n B).
parts.G:
EXAMPLES
   Simple: die, A = even {2,4,6}, B = greater than 3 {4,5,6}:
      P(A U B) = 3/6 + 3/6 - 2/6 = 4/6 = 2/3 (check: {2,4,5,6}, 4 outcomes).
   Moderate: 60% of customers buy product X, 50% buy Y, 30% buy both.
      P(X or Y) = 0.6 + 0.5 - 0.3 = 0.8; P(neither) = 0.2.
      P(only X) = 0.6 - 0.3 = 0.3.
parts.H:
INTERPRETATION: subtract the overlap to avoid double counting; the
   three-event version alternately adds and subtracts.
parts.I:
MISTAKES: forgetting to subtract the overlap; using the disjoint form
   when events overlap (can give probability above 1: a warning sign).
parts.J: RELATED: counting (F33.5 to F33.7), conditional probability (F34.1).

blocks.rawText:
F33.3  ADDITION RULE
A. NAME: Addition rule (inclusion-exclusion).
B. FORMULAS
     P(A U B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A n B)
     If A and B are mutually exclusive: P(A U B) = P(A) + P(B).
     Three events: P(A U B U C) = P(A) + P(B) + P(C) - P(AB) - P(AC) - P(BC)
                                  + P(ABC).
C. SYMBOLS: P(A n B) probability both occur.
D. CONCEPT: adding P(A) and P(B) counts the overlap A n B twice, so subtract
   it once.
E. CONDITIONS: always valid (the disjoint form needs mutual exclusivity).
F. DERIVATION: A U B = A + (B \ A) (disjoint), and B = (A n B) + (B \ A);
   so P(A U B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A n B).
G. EXAMPLES
   Simple: die, A = even {2,4,6}, B = greater than 3 {4,5,6}:
      P(A U B) = 3/6 + 3/6 - 2/6 = 4/6 = 2/3 (check: {2,4,5,6}, 4 outcomes).
   Moderate: 60% of customers buy product X, 50% buy Y, 30% buy both.
      P(X or Y) = 0.6 + 0.5 - 0.3 = 0.8; P(neither) = 0.2.
      P(only X) = 0.6 - 0.3 = 0.3.
H. INTERPRETATION: subtract the overlap to avoid double counting; the
   three-event version alternately adds and subtracts.
I. MISTAKES: forgetting to subtract the overlap; using the disjoint form
   when events overlap (can give probability above 1: a warning sign).
J. RELATED: counting (F33.5 to F33.7), conditional probability (F34.1).

blocks.title: MULTIPLICATION RULE (INTRODUCTION)
blocks.formulaBody:
P(A n B) = P(A) P(B | A) = P(B) P(A | B)  (general, Module 34)
   If A and B are INDEPENDENT: P(A n B) = P(A) P(B).

parts.B:
P(A n B) = P(A) P(B | A) = P(B) P(A | B)  (general, Module 34)
   If A and B are INDEPENDENT: P(A n B) = P(A) P(B).
parts.C:
SYMBOLS: P(A n B) the joint probability; P(B | A) the conditional
   probability; independence makes P(B | A) = P(B).

sections.title: COUNTING PRINCIPLES

blocks.rawText: For equally likely outcomes, probability is a counting problem.

blocks.title: FUNDAMENTAL COUNTING PRINCIPLES
blocks.formulaBody:
MULTIPLICATION PRINCIPLE: if a task has two stages, with m ways for stage 1
   and n ways for stage 2 (independent of stage 1), there are m * n ways
   overall. Extends to any number of stages.
   ADDITION PRINCIPLE: if a task can be done in one of two DISJOINT ways,
   with m and n options respectively, there are m + n options.
   FACTORIAL: n! = n (n-1) ... 2 * 1; 0! = 1. Number of ways to arrange n
   distinct objects in a row.

parts.B:
MULTIPLICATION PRINCIPLE: if a task has two stages, with m ways for stage 1
   and n ways for stage 2 (independent of stage 1), there are m * n ways
   overall. Extends to any number of stages.
   ADDITION PRINCIPLE: if a task can be done in one of two DISJOINT ways,
   with m and n options respectively, there are m + n options.
   FACTORIAL: n! = n (n-1) ... 2 * 1; 0! = 1. Number of ways to arrange n
   distinct objects in a row.
parts.C: SYMBOLS: m, n the numbers of options; n! the factorial.
parts.D: CONCEPT: independent stages multiply; exclusive alternatives add.
parts.E:
CONDITIONS: the number of options at a later stage must not depend on
   earlier choices (otherwise count case by case).
parts.G:
EXAMPLES: a license code of 3 letters then 2 digits: 26^3 * 10^2 = 1,757,600.
   An outfit from 4 shirts, 3 trousers, 2 shoes: 4 * 3 * 2 = 24.
   Arrangements of 5 distinct people in a line: 5! = 120.
parts.H:
INTERPRETATION: counting is the engine of classical probability and
   of complexity analysis (2^n subsets).
parts.I:
MISTAKES: adding when stages should be multiplied (and vice versa);
   forgetting restrictions (no repeats).
parts.J: RELATED: permutations (F33.6), combinations (F33.7).

sections.title: PERMUTATIONS AND COMBINATIONS

blocks.title: PERMUTATIONS
blocks.formulaBody:
Ordered selections of k from n DISTINCT objects, no repetition:
        P(n, k) = n! / (n - k)! = n (n-1) ... (n-k+1)
     With repetition allowed: n^k.
     Arrangements of n objects with repeats (n_1 identical of type 1, ...):
        n! / (n_1! n_2! ... n_r!)

parts.B:
FORMULAS
     Ordered selections of k from n DISTINCT objects, no repetition:
        P(n, k) = n! / (n - k)! = n (n-1) ... (n-k+1)
     With repetition allowed: n^k.
     Arrangements of n objects with repeats (n_1 identical of type 1, ...):
        n! / (n_1! n_2! ... n_r!)
parts.C: SYMBOLS: n number of objects available; k number chosen; n! factorial.
parts.D:
CONCEPT: ORDER MATTERS. Choose the first (n ways), second (n-1), ... k-th
   (n-k+1) and multiply; the formula packages that product.
parts.E: CONDITIONS: distinct objects for the first two formulas; 0 <= k <= n.
parts.G:
EXAMPLES
   Simple: 1st, 2nd, 3rd prizes among 5 runners: P(5,3) = 5*4*3 = 60.
   Moderate: distinct arrangements of the letters of MISSISSIPPI (M 1, I 4,
      S 4, P 2; 11 letters): 11!/(1! 4! 4! 2!) = 39,916,800/(24*24*2)
      = 34,650.
   Moderate 2: 4-digit PIN with digits allowed to repeat: 10^4 = 10,000;
      with no repeated digit: P(10, 4) = 5,040.
parts.H:
INTERPRETATION: P(n, k) counts ordered lists: arrangements of a
   ranking or a sequence.
parts.I:
MISTAKES: using this when order does not matter; forgetting the division
   for identical items.
parts.J: RELATED: combinations (F33.7), factorial growth (Module 17).

blocks.title: COMBINATIONS

parts.A: NAME: Combinations (unordered selections) and binomial coefficients.
parts.B:
FORMULAS
     C(n, k) = n! / ( k! (n - k)! ) = P(n, k) / k!
     Properties: C(n, k) = C(n, n - k); C(n, 0) = C(n, n) = 1;
        C(n, 1) = n; C(n, k) = C(n-1, k-1) + C(n-1, k) (Pascal);
        sum[k=0..n] C(n, k) = 2^n.
     Multisets (choose k from n types WITH repetition, order irrelevant):
        C(n + k - 1, k)  [SUPPLEMENTARY]
parts.C: SYMBOLS: C(n, k) "n choose k" (also written with n over k, or nCk).
parts.D:
CONCEPT: choose which k items form the group; each group of k can be
   arranged in k! orders, which we do NOT want to count separately, so
   divide the permutations by k!.
parts.E: CONDITIONS: 0 <= k <= n; selections without repetition (basic version).
parts.G:
EXAMPLES
   Simple: choose a committee of 3 from 10 people: C(10, 3) = 120.
   Moderate: committee of 4 from 6 men and 5 women with at least 2 women:
      exactly 2 women: C(5,2) C(6,2) = 10 * 15 = 150; 3 women: C(5,3) C(6,1)
      = 10 * 6 = 60; 4 women: C(5,4) = 5. Total 215.
      (Check by complement: all C(11,4) = 330, minus 0 women C(6,4) = 15
      and 1 woman C(5,1) C(6,3) = 100: 330 - 115 = 215. OK.)
   Moderate 2: lottery pick 6 numbers from 49: C(49, 6) = 13,983,816, so
      P(jackpot) = 1/13,983,816 = 7.15 x 10^-8.
parts.H:
INTERPRETATION: C(n, k) counts groups; it appears as the binomial
   coefficients and in the binomial distribution.
parts.I:
MISTAKES: using permutations when the problem says "group", "committee",
   "hand", "subset"; double counting by treating a combination as ordered.
parts.J:
RELATED: binomial theorem (F1.7), binomial distribution (F35.7),
   hypergeometric (F33.8).

blocks.title: COMPARISON TABLE: PERMUTATIONS vs COMBINATIONS
blocks.rawText:
Aspect               Permutation                  Combination
  Order matters?       YES                          NO
  Counts               arrangements/sequences       groups/subsets
  Formula (no repeat)  n!/(n-k)!                    n!/(k!(n-k)!)
  Relationship         P(n,k) = C(n,k) * k!         C(n,k) = P(n,k)/k!
  Keywords             arrange, rank, schedule,     choose, select, committee,
                       PIN, race positions          hand, team, sample
  Example n=5, k=3     60                           10
  Test question: "Would swapping two chosen items give a different result?"
  If yes: permutation; if no: combination.

sections.title: SAMPLING WITHOUT REPLACEMENT

blocks.rawText:
DEFINITIONS
   WITH REPLACEMENT: each selected item is returned before the next draw, so
      the draws are INDEPENDENT with unchanged probabilities.
   WITHOUT REPLACEMENT: items are not returned; the composition changes,
      making the draws DEPENDENT.
   (Simple random sample of n units from N is drawn without replacement.)

blocks.title: PROBABILITY FOR SAMPLING WITHOUT REPLACEMENT (HYPERGEOMETRIC)
blocks.formulaBody:
POPULATION of N items with K "successes". Draw n WITHOUT replacement.
        P( exactly k successes ) = C(K, k) C(N - K, n - k) / C(N, n).
   Sequence form (chain rule): P(first two are successes) =
        (K/N) * ((K - 1)/(N - 1)).

parts.B:
POPULATION of N items with K "successes". Draw n WITHOUT replacement.
        P( exactly k successes ) = C(K, k) C(N - K, n - k) / C(N, n).
   Sequence form (chain rule): P(first two are successes) =

sections.title: CONDITIONAL PROBABILITY

blocks.rawText:
BASIC IDEA (plain English)
Probabilities change when you learn something. The probability that a
card is a king is 4/52, but if you learn that it is a face card, it
becomes 4/12. Conditional probability is "the probability of A, given
that we know B has happened".

blocks.title: CONDITIONAL PROBABILITY
blocks.formulaBody: P(A | B) = P(A n B) / P(B),   P(B) > 0.

parts.B: FORMULA:   P(A | B) = P(A n B) / P(B),   P(B) > 0.
parts.C:
SYMBOLS: P(A | B) read "probability of A given B"; P(A n B) probability of
   both; P(B) the probability of the conditioning event.
parts.D:
CONCEPT: restrict attention to the outcomes in B (B becomes the new,
   smaller sample space) and ask what fraction of them also lie in A.
   Dividing by P(B) re-normalizes so that P(B | B) = 1.
parts.E:
CONDITIONS: requires P(B) > 0. Conditional probabilities obey all the
   axioms (e.g. P(A^c | B) = 1 - P(A | B)). In general P(A | B) != P(B | A).
parts.G:
EXAMPLES
   Simple (die): A = {5, 6} (at least 5), B = {2, 4, 6} (even).
      P(A n B) = P({6}) = 1/6; P(B) = 1/2; P(A | B) = (1/6)/(1/2) = 1/3.
      (Directly: of the 3 even outcomes only 6 is in A.)
   Moderate (two-way table): 200 customers: 120 are subscribers; 80 are
      not. Of the subscribers, 30 churned; of the non-subscribers, 40
      churned. P(churn) = 70/200 = 0.35.
      P(churn | subscriber) = 30/120 = 0.25.
      P(churn | not subscriber) = 40/80 = 0.5.
      P(subscriber | churn) = 30/70 = 0.4286 (different from
      P(churn | subscriber) = 0.25: direction matters).
   Moderate 2 (two cards): P(second is an ace | first was an ace) = 3/51.
parts.I:
COMMON MISTAKES: the "confusion of the inverse" (treating P(A | B) as
   P(B | A)): "most terrorists are X" is not "most X are terrorists";
   conditioning on the wrong event; forgetting to restrict the sample
   space; dividing by P(A) instead of P(B).
parts.J: RELATED: multiplication rule, Bayes' theorem.

   axioms (e.g. P(A^c | B) = 1 - P(A | B)). In general P(A | B) != P(B | A).

   Simple (die): A = {5, 6} (at least 5), B = {2, 4, 6} (even).

sections.title: INDEPENDENT AND DEPENDENT EVENTS

blocks.title: INDEPENDENCE
blocks.formulaBody:
A and B are INDEPENDENT iff
        P(A n B) = P(A) P(B)
   equivalently P(A | B) = P(A) (if P(B) > 0) and P(B | A) = P(B):
   knowing one tells nothing about the other.
   Several events A_1..A_n are MUTUALLY independent if the product rule
   holds for EVERY sub-collection (pairwise independence alone is not
   enough). If A and B are independent so are A and B^c, A^c and B^c.
   CONDITIONAL independence: A and B independent GIVEN C if
   P(A n B | C) = P(A | C) P(B | C).

parts.B:
FORMULAS: A and B are INDEPENDENT iff
        P(A n B) = P(A) P(B)
   equivalently P(A | B) = P(A) (if P(B) > 0) and P(B | A) = P(B):
   knowing one tells nothing about the other.
   Several events A_1..A_n are MUTUALLY independent if the product rule
   holds for EVERY sub-collection (pairwise independence alone is not
   enough). If A and B are independent so are A and B^c, A^c and B^c.
   CONDITIONAL independence: A and B independent GIVEN C if
   P(A n B | C) = P(A | C) P(B | C).
parts.C: SYMBOLS: as above.
parts.D: CONCEPT: the occurrence of B does not shift the probability of A.
parts.E:
CONDITIONS: independence is an ASSUMPTION to be justified (by the physical
   process, e.g. separate dice, or tested from data), not something to
   assume because the events "feel unrelated".
parts.G:
EXAMPLES
   Independent (die): A = even {2,4,6}, B = at most 4 {1,2,3,4}: P(A) = 1/2,
      P(B) = 2/3, P(A n B) = P({2,4}) = 1/3 = (1/2)(2/3): INDEPENDENT.
   Dependent (die): A = even, B = at least 4 {4,5,6}: P(A n B) = P({4,6})
      = 1/3, but P(A) P(B) = (1/2)(1/2) = 1/4: DEPENDENT.
   Coins: each toss independent: P(HHH) = 1/8.
   Dependent draws: two cards without replacement: P(both aces) =
      (4/52)(3/51) = 1/221 = 0.00452, not (4/52)^2 = 0.00592.
parts.H:
INTERPRETATION: independence means that learning one event tells
   nothing about the other.
parts.I:
COMMON MISTAKES (very frequent)
   - Confusing MUTUALLY EXCLUSIVE with INDEPENDENT. If A and B are mutually
     exclusive and both have positive probability they are DEPENDENT
     (if A occurs, B cannot: P(B | A) = 0 != P(B)).
   - The gambler's fallacy: after 5 heads in a row the next toss is still
     50% heads (independent tosses).
   - Assuming independence for convenience (multiplying probabilities of
     correlated events understates joint risk).
parts.J:
RELATED: conditional probability (F34.1), multiplication rule
   (F34.3), covariance (F32.1).

"naive" Bayes assumes features are conditionally
independent given the class; i.i.d. data (independent and identically
distributed) is the standard modeling assumption; time series and
clustered data violate independence (inflating confidence).

blocks.title: LAW OF TOTAL PROBABILITY
blocks.formulaBody:
if B_1, ..., B_n form a PARTITION of the sample space (mutually
   exclusive, exhaustive, each with P(B_i) > 0), then for any event A:
        P(A) = sum[i=1..n] P(A | B_i) P(B_i)
   Two-part version: P(A) = P(A | B) P(B) + P(A | B^c) P(B^c).

parts.B:

parts.C:

parts.D:

   the case-wise probabilities, weighted by how likely each case is.
parts.E:
CONDITIONS: the B_i MUST partition the whole space (no gaps, no
   overlaps), and the weights sum to 1.
parts.F:
DERIVATION: A = (A n B_1) U ... U (A n B_n), disjoint, so P(A) = sum P(A n
   B_i) = sum P(A | B_i) P(B_i).
parts.G:
EXAMPLES
   Simple (factories): machine M1 makes 60% of items with 2% defective;
      machine M2 makes 40% with 5% defective.
      P(defective) = 0.02 * 0.6 + 0.05 * 0.4 = 0.012 + 0.020 = 0.032.
   Moderate (three sources): a model is trained on data from regions R1, R2,
      R3 with shares 50%, 30%, 20% and error rates 10%, 20%, 40%.
      Overall error = 0.5 * 0.10 + 0.3 * 0.20 + 0.2 * 0.40 = 0.05 + 0.06
      + 0.08 = 0.19.
parts.H:
INTERPRETATION: the overall rate is a mixture; the same arithmetic
   gives the marginal distribution P(x) = sum_y P(x | y) P(y) in
   classification (the "evidence" in Bayes' theorem).
parts.I:

   P(B_i | A) instead of P(A | B_i).
parts.J:

   distributions (Module 35).

sections.title: BAYES' THEOREM

blocks.title: BAYES' THEOREM
blocks.formulaBody:
P(A | B) = P(B | A) P(A) / P(B)
     With a partition A_1..A_n of the sample space:
        P(A_j | B) = P(B | A_j) P(A_j) / sum_i P(B | A_i) P(A_i)
     Odds form:  posterior odds = prior odds x likelihood ratio,
        P(A | B)/P(A^c | B) = [P(A)/P(A^c)] * [P(B | A)/P(B | A^c)]

parts.B:
FORMULAS
     P(A | B) = P(B | A) P(A) / P(B)
     With a partition A_1..A_n of the sample space:
        P(A_j | B) = P(B | A_j) P(A_j) / sum_i P(B | A_i) P(A_i)
     Odds form:  posterior odds = prior odds x likelihood ratio,
        P(A | B)/P(A^c | B) = [P(A)/P(A^c)] * [P(B | A)/P(B | A^c)]
parts.C:
SYMBOLS
   P(A)      PRIOR probability of A (before seeing B).
   P(B | A)  LIKELIHOOD of the evidence B if A is true.
   P(B)      EVIDENCE / marginal probability of B (from total probability).
   P(A | B)  POSTERIOR probability of A after seeing B.
parts.D:
CONCEPT: Bayes reverses a conditional probability. We often know
   P(evidence | cause) (how a test behaves if the disease is present) but
   need P(cause | evidence) (how likely the disease is given a positive
   test). The answer depends on BOTH the test's characteristics and the
   prior (base rate).
parts.E:
CONDITIONS: P(B) > 0; priors must be meaningful and sum to 1 over the
   partition. The posterior is only as good as the prior and the
   likelihood model.
parts.F:
DERIVATION: from the multiplication rule P(A n B) = P(A | B) P(B) =
   P(B | A) P(A); divide by P(B). Expand P(B) by total probability.
parts.G:
EXAMPLES
   Simple (factories continued): an item is defective. P(it came from M1) =
      P(def | M1) P(M1)/P(def) = 0.012/0.032 = 0.375. (M1 makes 60% of
      items but only 37.5% of the defects.)
   Moderate (spam filter): 20% of mail is spam. The word "free" appears in
      40% of spam and 5% of non-spam. P(spam | "free")
      = 0.4 * 0.2 / (0.4 * 0.2 + 0.05 * 0.8) = 0.08/(0.08 + 0.04) = 0.667.
      Odds form: prior odds 0.2/0.8 = 0.25; LR = 0.4/0.05 = 8; posterior
      odds 2 -> probability 2/3. OK.
parts.H:
INTERPRETATION: evidence with a likelihood ratio of 8 multiplies the odds by
   8. Updating can be repeated: posterior becomes the next prior.
parts.I:
COMMON MISTAKES: ignoring the prior (BASE RATE FALLACY); equating
   P(A | B) with P(B | A) (PROSECUTOR'S FALLACY: P(evidence | innocent)
   small does not mean P(innocent | evidence) small); not summing over
   ALL alternative explanations in the denominator.
parts.J:
RELATED: Bayesian estimation and priors (Module 38), naive Bayes classifier
   (Module 48), posterior predictive distributions.

sections.title: DIAGNOSTIC TESTING EXAMPLES

blocks.rawText:
TERMS (D = condition present, + = positive test)
   PREVALENCE: P(D) (the prior / base rate).
   SENSITIVITY (true positive rate, recall): P(+ | D).
   SPECIFICITY (true negative rate): P(- | not D).
   FALSE POSITIVE RATE: P(+ | not D) = 1 - specificity.
   POSITIVE PREDICTIVE VALUE (PPV, precision): P(D | +).
   NEGATIVE PREDICTIVE VALUE (NPV): P(not D | -).

blocks.title: PREDICTIVE VALUES FROM SENSITIVITY, SPECIFICITY AND PREVALENCE
blocks.formulaBody:
PPV = (Se * Pr) / ( Se * Pr + (1 - Sp)(1 - Pr) )
   NPV = (Sp (1 - Pr)) / ( Sp (1 - Pr) + (1 - Se) Pr )

parts.B:
PPV = (Se * Pr) / ( Se * Pr + (1 - Sp)(1 - Pr) )
   NPV = (Sp (1 - Pr)) / ( Sp (1 - Pr) + (1 - Se) Pr )
parts.C: SYMBOLS: Se sensitivity; Sp specificity; Pr prevalence.
parts.D:
CONCEPT: a direct application of Bayes' theorem with the partition
   {D, not D}. The PPV depends strongly on prevalence.
parts.E:
CONDITIONS: assumes sensitivity and specificity are the same across
   the population and that Pr is the prevalence in the population where
   the test is applied.
parts.H:
INTERPRETATION: predictive values depend on prevalence: the same test
   has a high PPV in a high-risk group and a low PPV in general
   screening.
parts.I: COMMON MISTAKES: treating sensitivity as PPV; ignoring prevalence.
parts.J:
RELATED: Bayes (F34.5), precision and recall (F46.3), accuracy
   paradox (section 46.8).

blocks.rawText:
F34.6  PREDICTIVE VALUES FROM SENSITIVITY, SPECIFICITY AND PREVALENCE
B. PPV = (Se * Pr) / ( Se * Pr + (1 - Sp)(1 - Pr) )
   NPV = (Sp (1 - Pr)) / ( Sp (1 - Pr) + (1 - Se) Pr )
C. SYMBOLS: Se sensitivity; Sp specificity; Pr prevalence.
D. CONCEPT: a direct application of Bayes' theorem with the partition
   {D, not D}. The PPV depends strongly on prevalence.
E. CONDITIONS: assumes sensitivity and specificity are the same across
   the population and that Pr is the prevalence in the population where
   the test is applied.
G. EXAMPLE: Se = 0.95, Sp = 0.90, Pr = 0.01: PPV = 0.0095/(0.0095 +
   0.099) = 0.0876; NPV = 0.891/(0.891 + 0.0005) = 0.9994.
H. INTERPRETATION: predictive values depend on prevalence: the same test
   has a high PPV in a high-risk group and a low PPV in general
   screening.
I. COMMON MISTAKES: treating sensitivity as PPV; ignoring prevalence.
J. RELATED: Bayes (F34.5), precision and recall (F46.3), accuracy
   paradox (section 46.8).

WORKED EXAMPLE: prevalence 1%, sensitivity 95%, specificity 90%.
   Method 1 (formula):
      P(+) = 0.95 * 0.01 + 0.10 * 0.99 = 0.0095 + 0.099 = 0.1085.
      PPV = 0.0095/0.1085 = 0.0876 (8.76%).
   Method 2 (natural frequencies, imagine 10,000 people):
      100 have the condition: 95 test positive (true positives), 5 test
      negative. 9,900 do not: 990 test positive (false positives), 8,910
      test negative.
      Positives in total: 95 + 990 = 1,085. PPV = 95/1,085 = 8.76%.
      NPV = 8,910/(8,910 + 5) = 8,910/8,915 = 99.94%.
   Interpretation: although the test seems accurate (95% / 90%), a positive
   result means only about a 9% chance of having the condition, because
   the condition is rare and false positives from the large healthy group
   outnumber true positives roughly 10 to 1.
   Repeat testing: after a first positive the new prior is 0.0876. A second
   independent positive result (same test; assumes conditional
   independence of test errors) gives posterior
   0.95 * 0.0876/(0.95 * 0.0876 + 0.10 * 0.9124) = 0.0832/(0.0832 +
   0.0912) = 0.477.
   Effect of prevalence: at prevalence 20%, PPV = 0.19/(0.19 + 0.08) = 0.704.
H. INTERPRETATION: in screening for rare conditions, even good tests give many
   false alarms; confirmation tests are needed.
I. MISTAKES: reporting "the test is 95% accurate, so a positive means 95%
   likely"; using sensitivity where PPV is needed; forgetting that
   PPV changes when the test is used in a different population.
DATA SCIENCE LINK
   - Precision of a classifier = PPV; recall = sensitivity. With imbalanced
     classes (fraud: 0.1% prevalence) even a model with 99% specificity
     has low precision (check: Se = 0.9, Sp = 0.99, Pr = 0.001 gives
     PPV = 0.0009/(0.0009 + 0.00999) = 8.3%).
   - Accuracy can be misleading when classes are imbalanced (Module 46).
   - Bayesian updating, naive Bayes classifiers, A/B testing posteriors,
     and recommender models all use these rules.
MONTY HALL [SUPPLEMENTARY]: three doors, one car. You pick door 1; the host,
who knows where the car is, opens a goat door among the others. Switching
wins with probability 2/3 (staying 1/3) because the host's action is
informative. Simulation confirms 0.667.

   NPV = (Sp (1 - Pr)) / ( Sp (1 - Pr) + (1 - Se) Pr )
C. SYMBOLS: Se sensitivity; Sp specificity; Pr prevalence.
D. CONCEPT: a direct application of Bayes' theorem with the partition
   {D, not D}. The PPV depends strongly on prevalence.
E. CONDITIONS: assumes sensitivity and specificity are the same across
   the population and that Pr is the prevalence in the population where
   the test is applied.
G. EXAMPLE: Se = 0.95, Sp = 0.90, Pr = 0.01: PPV = 0.0095/(0.0095 +
   0.099) = 0.0876; NPV = 0.891/(0.891 + 0.0005) = 0.9994.
H. INTERPRETATION: predictive values depend on prevalence: the same test
   has a high PPV in a high-risk group and a low PPV in general
   screening.
I. COMMON MISTAKES: treating sensitivity as PPV; ignoring prevalence.
J. RELATED: Bayes (F34.5), precision and recall (F46.3), accuracy
   paradox (section 46.8).
WORKED EXAMPLE: prevalence 1%, sensitivity 95%, specificity 90%.
   Method 1 (formula):
      P(+) = 0.95 * 0.01 + 0.10 * 0.99 = 0.0095 + 0.099 = 0.1085.
      PPV = 0.0095/0.1085 = 0.0876 (8.76%).
   Method 2 (natural frequencies, imagine 10,000 people):
      100 have the condition: 95 test positive (true positives), 5 test
      negative. 9,900 do not: 990 test positive (false positives), 8,910
      test negative.
      Positives in total: 95 + 990 = 1,085. PPV = 95/1,085 = 8.76%.
      NPV = 8,910/(8,910 + 5) = 8,910/8,915 = 99.94%.
   Interpretation: although the test seems accurate (95% / 90%), a positive
   result means only about a 9% chance of having the condition, because
   the condition is rare and false positives from the large healthy group
   outnumber true positives roughly 10 to 1.
   Repeat testing: after a first positive the new prior is 0.0876. A second
   independent positive result (same test; assumes conditional
   independence of test errors) gives posterior
   0.95 * 0.0876/(0.95 * 0.0876 + 0.10 * 0.9124) = 0.0832/(0.0832 +
   0.0912) = 0.477.
   Effect of prevalence: at prevalence 20%, PPV = 0.19/(0.19 + 0.08) = 0.704.
H. INTERPRETATION: in screening for rare conditions, even good tests give many
   false alarms; confirmation tests are needed.
I. MISTAKES: reporting "the test is 95% accurate, so a positive means 95%
   likely"; using sensitivity where PPV is needed; forgetting that
   PPV changes when the test is used in a different population.
DATA SCIENCE LINK
   - Precision of a classifier = PPV; recall = sensitivity. With imbalanced
     classes (fraud: 0.1% prevalence) even a model with 99% specificity
     has low precision (check: Se = 0.9, Sp = 0.99, Pr = 0.001 gives
     PPV = 0.0009/(0.0009 + 0.00999) = 8.3%).
   - Accuracy can be misleading when classes are imbalanced (Module 46).
   - Bayesian updating, naive Bayes classifiers, A/B testing posteriors,
     and recommender models all use these rules.
MONTY HALL [SUPPLEMENTARY]: three doors, one car. You pick door 1; the host,
who knows where the car is, opens a goat door among the others. Switching
wins with probability 2/3 (staying 1/3) because the host's action is
informative. Simulation confirms 0.667.

sections.title: RANDOM VARIABLES: DISCRETE AND CONTINUOUS

blocks.rawText:
BASIC IDEA (plain English)
A random variable turns the uncertain outcome of an experiment into a
NUMBER, so that we can use algebra and calculus on it. "The number of
heads in 10 tosses", "tomorrow's temperature", "the time until the next
customer" are random variables.

blocks.title: RANDOM VARIABLE
blocks.formulaBody:
a function X : Omega -> R that assigns a real number X(w) to
   every outcome w of the sample space.
   Notation: capital letter X = the random variable (before the
   experiment); lower-case x = a particular value it may take; the
   event {X = x} means "X takes the value x"; P(X <= x) is the
   probability of the event {w : X(w) <= x}.

parts.B:
DEFINITION: a function X : Omega -> R that assigns a real number X(w) to
   every outcome w of the sample space.
   Notation: capital letter X = the random variable (before the
   experiment); lower-case x = a particular value it may take; the
   event {X = x} means "X takes the value x"; P(X <= x) is the
   probability of the event {w : X(w) <= x}.
parts.C: SYMBOLS: Omega sample space; w an outcome; R the real numbers.
parts.D:
CONCEPT: the randomness is in the outcome w; X is an ordinary function that
   reports a numerical feature of it. Two coin tosses: X = number of
   heads takes X(HH) = 2, X(HT) = X(TH) = 1, X(TT) = 0.
KINDS
   DISCRETE: takes a finite or countably infinite set of values (counts,
      categories coded as numbers): number of heads, defects per
      batch, die roll. Described by a PMF.
   CONTINUOUS: takes values in an interval (uncountably many): height,
      time, temperature, error. Described by a PDF.
   (Mixed variables exist: e.g. rainfall is 0 with positive probability
   and continuous otherwise [SUPPLEMENTARY].)
   TEST: if you can list the possible values (even an infinite list
   0, 1, 2, ...), it is discrete; if between any two values there is
   another possible value, it is continuous.
   Note: a measurement recorded to the nearest cm is DISCRETE in practice
   but modeled as continuous when the resolution is fine.
parts.E:
CONDITIONS: X must be a function for which P(X <= x) is defined; its
   type (discrete or continuous) determines how probabilities are
   described.
parts.G:
EXAMPLES: the number of heads in 2 tosses (values 0, 1, 2); the sum
   of two dice; the height of a random adult; tomorrow's rainfall.
parts.H:
INTERPRETATION: random variables let us compute averages, spreads and
   probabilities with algebra and calculus.
parts.I:
COMMON MISTAKES: confusing the random variable X with an observed
   value x (a fixed number); treating category labels as numbers without
   justification.
parts.J: RELATED: PMF, PDF and CDF (F35.2 to F35.4), expectation (F36.1).

sections.title: PROBABILITY MASS FUNCTION (PMF)

blocks.title: PMF
blocks.formulaBody:
p(x) = P(X = x)
   Requirements: p(x) >= 0 for all x;  sum over all x of p(x) = 1.
   Probability of an event: P(X in S) = sum[x in S] p(x).

parts.B:
FORMULA:   p(x) = P(X = x)
   Requirements: p(x) >= 0 for all x;  sum over all x of p(x) = 1.
   Probability of an event: P(X in S) = sum[x in S] p(x).
parts.C: SYMBOLS: p(x) (also p_X(x)) the probability that X equals exactly x.
parts.D:
CONCEPT: a table (or formula) listing each possible value with its
   probability: the probability "mass" placed at each point.
parts.E:
CONDITIONS: only for discrete variables; each p(x) is a genuine probability
   (between 0 and 1).
parts.H:
INTERPRETATION: the heights of the bars of a bar chart of
   probabilities.
parts.I:
MISTAKES: PMF values not summing to 1; using a PMF for a continuous
   variable.
parts.J: RELATED: CDF (F35.4), binomial (F35.7), expectation (F36.1).

blocks.rawText:
F35.2  PMF
A. NAME: Probability mass function (discrete variables).
B. FORMULA:   p(x) = P(X = x)
   Requirements: p(x) >= 0 for all x;  sum over all x of p(x) = 1.
   Probability of an event: P(X in S) = sum[x in S] p(x).
C. SYMBOLS: p(x) (also p_X(x)) the probability that X equals exactly x.
D. CONCEPT: a table (or formula) listing each possible value with its
   probability: the probability "mass" placed at each point.
E. CONDITIONS: only for discrete variables; each p(x) is a genuine probability
   (between 0 and 1).
G. EXAMPLES
   Simple: fair die: p(x) = 1/6 for x = 1..6; P(X >= 5) = 2/6.
   Moderate: sum S of two fair dice: values 2..12 with counts
      1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 5, 4, 3, 2, 1 out of 36:
      p(2) = 1/36, p(7) = 6/36, p(12) = 1/36. P(S >= 10) = (3 + 2 + 1)/36
      = 1/6. P(S is even) = (1 + 3 + 5 + 5 + 3 + 1)/36 = 18/36 = 1/2.
H. INTERPRETATION: the heights of the bars of a bar chart of
   probabilities.
I. MISTAKES: PMF values not summing to 1; using a PMF for a continuous
   variable.
J. RELATED: CDF (F35.4), binomial (F35.7), expectation (F36.1).

sections.title: PROBABILITY DENSITY FUNCTION (PDF)

blocks.title: PDF
blocks.formulaBody:
f(x) is a PDF of X if
        f(x) >= 0 for all x;   int[-inf..inf] f(x) dx = 1;
        P(a <= X <= b) = int[a..b] f(x) dx.
   Interpretation of the value: f(x) dx approx P(x <= X <= x + dx).

parts.B:
FORMULA: f(x) is a PDF of X if
        f(x) >= 0 for all x;   int[-inf..inf] f(x) dx = 1;
        P(a <= X <= b) = int[a..b] f(x) dx.
   Interpretation of the value: f(x) dx approx P(x <= X <= x + dx).
parts.C:
SYMBOLS: f(x) (also f_X(x)) the density at x; the integral gives AREA under
   the curve.
parts.D:
CONCEPT: probability is AREA under the density curve, not the height.
   Density = probability per unit length: like the density of a material
   (mass per volume), whose mass requires integrating over a region.
   The density height can exceed 1 (e.g. U(0, 0.5) has f = 2 on its
   support); only the AREA must be at most 1.
parts.E:
CONDITIONS: the density must integrate to 1 (normalization); non-negative;
   improper integrals must converge (Module 4). Distinguish the density
   f(x) (not a probability) from the probability P(X = x) = 0 for any
   single x (Module 36).
parts.G:
EXAMPLES
   Simple: f(x) = 2x for 0 <= x <= 1 (0 elsewhere). Check: int[0..1] 2x dx = 1.
      P(0.5 <= X <= 0.8) = [x^2] from 0.5 to 0.8 = 0.64 - 0.25 = 0.39.
   Moderate: find c so that f(x) = c x^2 on [0, 3] is a density:
      int[0..3] c x^2 dx = c * 9 = 1 -> c = 1/9. P(X <= 2) = (1/9)(8/3)
      = 8/27 = 0.296.
   Normalization constants in practice: the normal density's factor
      1/(sigma sqrt(2 pi)) exists to make the integral 1 (F4: Gaussian
      integral).
parts.H:
INTERPRETATION: a density shows where probability is concentrated;
   areas, not heights, are probabilities.
parts.I:
MISTAKES: treating f(x) as a probability (it may exceed 1); forgetting
   to check normalization; integrating over the wrong limits; confusing
   f with the CDF F.
parts.J: RELATED: histogram (F30.1), CDF (F35.4), improper integrals (F4.8).
