sections.title: CUMULATIVE DISTRIBUTION FUNCTION (CDF)

blocks.title: CDF
blocks.formulaBody:
(valid for both discrete and continuous X)
     F(x) = P(X <= x)
     Discrete:    F(x) = sum[t <= x] p(t)       (a STEP function)
     Continuous:  F(x) = int[-inf..x] f(t) dt    (a continuous curve)
                  f(x) = F'(x) wherever F is differentiable
     Interval probability: P(a < X <= b) = F(b) - F(a)
     Properties: non-decreasing; right-continuous; F(-inf) = 0, F(+inf) = 1;
        0 <= F(x) <= 1; P(X > x) = 1 - F(x) (SURVIVAL function).
     Quantile (inverse CDF): the p-quantile is x_p with F(x_p) = p; the median
        solves F(x) = 0.5.

parts.B:
FORMULAS (valid for both discrete and continuous X)
     F(x) = P(X <= x)
     Discrete:    F(x) = sum[t <= x] p(t)       (a STEP function)
     Continuous:  F(x) = int[-inf..x] f(t) dt    (a continuous curve)
                  f(x) = F'(x) wherever F is differentiable
     Interval probability: P(a < X <= b) = F(b) - F(a)
     Properties: non-decreasing; right-continuous; F(-inf) = 0, F(+inf) = 1;
        0 <= F(x) <= 1; P(X > x) = 1 - F(x) (SURVIVAL function).
     Quantile (inverse CDF): the p-quantile is x_p with F(x_p) = p; the median
        solves F(x) = 0.5.
parts.C: SYMBOLS: F(x) running total of probability up to x; t the dummy variable.
parts.D:
CONCEPT: "how much probability lies at or below x". It always exists
   (even for mixed variables) and is the most general description of a
   distribution. Jumps in F correspond to point masses (discrete part);
   the size of a jump at x equals P(X = x).
parts.E:
CONDITIONS: F always exists; it is right-continuous; for continuous X
   it is continuous, for discrete X it jumps.
parts.G:
EXAMPLES
   Simple (discrete): die: F(3) = 3/6 = 0.5; F(3.7) = 0.5 (flat between
      jumps); F(0) = 0; F(6) = 1.
   Moderate (continuous): f(x) = 2x on [0, 1]: F(x) = 0 for x < 0;
      F(x) = x^2 on [0, 1]; F(x) = 1 for x > 1.
      P(0.5 < X <= 0.8) = F(0.8) - F(0.5) = 0.64 - 0.25 = 0.39 (as before).
      Median: x^2 = 0.5 -> x = 0.7071. 90th percentile: x = sqrt(0.9) = 0.9487.
      Differentiating F gives back f(x) = 2x.
parts.H:
INTERPRETATION: reading quantiles from a CDF gives percentiles; the
   inverse CDF is used to simulate random numbers (inverse-transform
   sampling, Module 36); the ECDF (Module 30) estimates F from data;
   the ROC curve and the Kolmogorov-Smirnov test are CDF-based.
parts.I:
MISTAKES: forgetting that F accumulates from the left; using P(a < X < b)
   = F(b) - F(a) for discrete variables without care about endpoints
   (P(a < X <= b) is the exact version); confusing the CDF with the PDF.
parts.J: RELATED: ECDF (F30.2), quantiles, inverse-transform sampling (F36.5).

   the size of a jump at x equals P(X = x).

   it is continuous, for discrete X it jumps.

   Simple (discrete): die: F(3) = 3/6 = 0.5; F(3.7) = 0.5 (flat between

sections.rawText:
F35.4  CDF
A. NAME: Cumulative distribution function.
B. FORMULAS (valid for both discrete and continuous X)
     F(x) = P(X <= x)
     Discrete:    F(x) = sum[t <= x] p(t)       (a STEP function)
     Continuous:  F(x) = int[-inf..x] f(t) dt    (a continuous curve)
                  f(x) = F'(x) wherever F is differentiable
     Interval probability: P(a < X <= b) = F(b) - F(a)
     Properties: non-decreasing; right-continuous; F(-inf) = 0, F(+inf) = 1;
        0 <= F(x) <= 1; P(X > x) = 1 - F(x) (SURVIVAL function).
     Quantile (inverse CDF): the p-quantile is x_p with F(x_p) = p; the median
        solves F(x) = 0.5.

   (even for mixed variables) and is the most general description of a
   distribution. Jumps in F correspond to point masses (discrete part);
   the size of a jump at x equals P(X = x).

sections.title: UNIFORM DISTRIBUTION

blocks.title: CONTINUOUS UNIFORM DISTRIBUTION U(a, b)
blocks.formulaBody:
f(x) = 1/(b - a) for a <= x <= b (0 otherwise)
     F(x) = (x - a)/(b - a) for a <= x <= b
     mean = (a + b)/2;   variance = (b - a)^2 / 12;   median = (a + b)/2.

parts.B:
FORMULAS
     f(x) = 1/(b - a) for a <= x <= b (0 otherwise)
     F(x) = (x - a)/(b - a) for a <= x <= b
     mean = (a + b)/2;   variance = (b - a)^2 / 12;   median = (a + b)/2.
parts.C: SYMBOLS: a, b the lower and upper limits (a < b).
parts.D:
CONCEPT: every subinterval of the same length is equally likely: complete
   ignorance within the range. The height is constant 1/(b - a) so that the
   area (b - a) * 1/(b - a) = 1.
parts.E: CONDITIONS: bounded support; values outside [a, b] impossible.
parts.F:
DERIVATION of the variance: E[X^2] = int[a..b] x^2/(b - a) dx = (a^2 + ab +
   b^2)/3; Var = E[X^2] - ((a + b)/2)^2 = (b - a)^2/12.
parts.G:
EXAMPLES
   Simple: waiting time X ~ U(0, 10) minutes. P(2 < X < 5) = 3/10 = 0.3;
      mean 5; variance 100/12 = 8.33; sd 2.887. P(X > 7) = 0.3.
   Moderate: random numbers: U(0, 1) is the basic output of random number
      generators; it is transformed into other distributions (F36.5).
   Discrete uniform on {1, ..., n}: p = 1/n; die: mean 3.5, variance
      (n^2 - 1)/12 = 35/12 = 2.917.
parts.H:
INTERPRETATION: p-values are uniformly distributed on (0, 1) when the
   null hypothesis is true (Module 39).
parts.I:
MISTAKES: forgetting the density is zero outside [a, b]; using the
   continuous variance formula for the discrete uniform.
parts.J:
RELATED: density (F35.3), p-values under H0 (F39.5), random number
   generation (section 41.6).

sections.title: BERNOULLI DISTRIBUTION

blocks.title: BERNOULLI(p)
blocks.formulaBody:
P(X = 1) = p, P(X = 0) = 1 - p;  PMF: p(x) = p^x (1 - p)^(1 - x), x in {0, 1}
     mean E[X] = p;  variance Var(X) = p (1 - p).

parts.C:
SYMBOLS: p the success probability (0 <= p <= 1); X = 1 "success", 0
   "failure".
parts.D:
CONCEPT: a single yes/no trial; the building block of the binomial
   distribution. X is an INDICATOR variable: X = 1[event].
parts.E: CONDITIONS: exactly two outcomes with fixed probability p.
parts.G:
EXAMPLES: click on an advert with p = 0.03: mean 0.03; variance 0.03 * 0.97
   = 0.0291; sd = 0.1706. A spam label (1 = spam) with p = 0.2.
parts.H:
INTERPRETATION: the mean of Bernoulli outcomes in a sample is the observed
   proportion.
parts.I:
COMMON MISTAKES: using p as a percentage (0 to 100) instead of a
   number in [0, 1]; forgetting that the variance is largest at p = 0.5.
parts.J:
RELATED: binomial (F35.7), logistic regression (F48.1), log-loss
   (F46.5).

blocks.rawText:
F35.6  BERNOULLI(p)
A. NAME: Bernoulli distribution.
B. FORMULAS
     P(X = 1) = p, P(X = 0) = 1 - p;  PMF: p(x) = p^x (1 - p)^(1 - x), x in {0, 1}
     mean E[X] = p;  variance Var(X) = p (1 - p).
C. SYMBOLS: p the success probability (0 <= p <= 1); X = 1 "success", 0
   "failure".
D. CONCEPT: a single yes/no trial; the building block of the binomial
   distribution. X is an INDICATOR variable: X = 1[event].
E. CONDITIONS: exactly two outcomes with fixed probability p.
F. DERIVATION: E[X] = 1 * p + 0 * (1 - p) = p; E[X^2] = p (since X^2 = X);
   Var = p - p^2 = p (1 - p). The variance is largest at p = 0.5 (0.25) and
   zero at p = 0 or 1 (no uncertainty).
G. EXAMPLES: click on an advert with p = 0.03: mean 0.03; variance 0.03 * 0.97
   = 0.0291; sd = 0.1706. A spam label (1 = spam) with p = 0.2.
H. INTERPRETATION: the mean of Bernoulli outcomes in a sample is the observed
   proportion.
I. COMMON MISTAKES: using p as a percentage (0 to 100) instead of a
   number in [0, 1]; forgetting that the variance is largest at p = 0.5.
J. RELATED: binomial (F35.7), logistic regression (F48.1), log-loss
   (F46.5).

sections.title: BINOMIAL DISTRIBUTION

blocks.title: BINOMIAL(n, p)
blocks.formulaBody:
P(X = k) = C(n, k) p^k (1 - p)^(n - k),    k = 0, 1, ..., n
     mean E[X] = n p;   variance Var(X) = n p (1 - p);   sd = sqrt(n p (1-p)).
     Mode approx floor((n + 1) p).
     CDF: P(X <= k) = sum[j=0..k] C(n, j) p^j (1 - p)^(n - j).

parts.B:
FORMULAS
     P(X = k) = C(n, k) p^k (1 - p)^(n - k),    k = 0, 1, ..., n
     mean E[X] = n p;   variance Var(X) = n p (1 - p);   sd = sqrt(n p (1-p)).
     Mode approx floor((n + 1) p).
     CDF: P(X <= k) = sum[j=0..k] C(n, j) p^j (1 - p)^(n - j).
parts.C:
SYMBOLS: n number of trials; p success probability per trial; k number of
   successes; C(n, k) the number of ways to choose which trials succeed.
parts.D:
CONCEPT: the number of successes in n independent Bernoulli(p) trials;
   X = X_1 + ... + X_n with each X_i ~ Bernoulli(p).
parts.E:
CONDITIONS (BINS): Binary outcome per trial; Independent trials;
   Number of trials fixed in advance; Same probability p on every trial.
   Violations: sampling WITHOUT replacement from a small population
   (hypergeometric instead); p changing over time; clustered/dependent
   data; unknown n.
parts.F:
DERIVATION of the PMF: one particular sequence with k successes and n - k
   failures has probability p^k (1 - p)^(n - k) by independence; there are
   C(n, k) such sequences (choose the positions of the successes),
   mutually exclusive, so add. Mean and variance: sums of n independent
   Bernoulli: E = n p; Var = n p (1 - p) (variances add for independent
   variables).
parts.G:
EXAMPLES
   Simple: 10 tosses of a fair coin: P(X = 3) = C(10, 3)/2^10 = 120/1024
      = 0.1172. P(X >= 8) = (45 + 10 + 1)/1024 = 56/1024 = 0.0547.
   Moderate: a component fails with probability 0.3; test 5 independent
      components. P(at most 1 fails) = 0.7^5 + 5(0.3)(0.7^4)
      = 0.16807 + 0.36015 = 0.52822. Mean failures 1.5, variance
      5 * 0.3 * 0.7 = 1.05.
   Moderate 2 (normal approximation): n = 100, p = 0.5: X approx
      N(50, 5^2). P(X >= 60) exact = 0.0284. Approximation with continuity
      correction: P(X >= 59.5): z = (59.5 - 50)/5 = 1.9: 1 - Phi(1.9) = 0.0287.
      Rule of thumb: need n p >= 10 and n (1 - p) >= 10 (some use 5).
   Data science: a classifier with true accuracy 0.8 on 200 test items:
      the number correct ~ Binomial(200, 0.8): mean 160, sd 5.66 (so
      accuracy has standard error sqrt(0.8 * 0.2/200) = 0.0283).
parts.H:
INTERPRETATION: sd = sqrt(n p (1 - p)) grows like sqrt(n) while the mean grows
   like n, so the PROPORTION X/n has sd sqrt(p (1 - p)/n): precision
   improves like 1/sqrt(n) (Module 37).
parts.I:
MISTAKES: using the binomial when trials are dependent; forgetting the
   binomial coefficient; confusing P(X = k) with P(X <= k); using the
   normal approximation for small n p or extreme p.
parts.J:
RELATED: Bernoulli (n = 1); hypergeometric (without replacement);
   Poisson approximation for large n, small p [SUPPLEMENTARY]: Poisson(lambda)
   has P(X = k) = e^(-lambda) lambda^k / k!, mean = variance = lambda
   (events in a fixed interval, e.g. P(2 events | lambda = 3) =
   e^(-3) * 9/2 = 0.224).

B. FORMULAS
     P(X = k) = C(n, k) p^k (1 - p)^(n - k),    k = 0, 1, ..., n
     mean E[X] = n p;   variance Var(X) = n p (1 - p);   sd = sqrt(n p (1-p)).
     Mode approx floor((n + 1) p).
     CDF: P(X <= k) = sum[j=0..k] C(n, j) p^j (1 - p)^(n - j).
C. SYMBOLS: n number of trials; p success probability per trial; k number of
   successes; C(n, k) the number of ways to choose which trials succeed.
D. CONCEPT: the number of successes in n independent Bernoulli(p) trials;
   X = X_1 + ... + X_n with each X_i ~ Bernoulli(p).
E. CONDITIONS (BINS): Binary outcome per trial; Independent trials;
   Number of trials fixed in advance; Same probability p on every trial.
   Violations: sampling WITHOUT replacement from a small population
   (hypergeometric instead); p changing over time; clustered/dependent
   data; unknown n.
F. DERIVATION of the PMF: one particular sequence with k successes and n - k
   failures has probability p^k (1 - p)^(n - k) by independence; there are
   C(n, k) such sequences (choose the positions of the successes),
   mutually exclusive, so add. Mean and variance: sums of n independent
   Bernoulli: E = n p; Var = n p (1 - p) (variances add for independent
   variables).
G. EXAMPLES
   Simple: 10 tosses of a fair coin: P(X = 3) = C(10, 3)/2^10 = 120/1024
      = 0.1172. P(X >= 8) = (45 + 10 + 1)/1024 = 56/1024 = 0.0547.
   Moderate: a component fails with probability 0.3; test 5 independent
      components. P(at most 1 fails) = 0.7^5 + 5(0.3)(0.7^4)
      = 0.16807 + 0.36015 = 0.52822. Mean failures 1.5, variance
      5 * 0.3 * 0.7 = 1.05.
   Moderate 2 (normal approximation): n = 100, p = 0.5: X approx
      N(50, 5^2). P(X >= 60) exact = 0.0284. Approximation with continuity
      correction: P(X >= 59.5): z = (59.5 - 50)/5 = 1.9: 1 - Phi(1.9) = 0.0287.
      Rule of thumb: need n p >= 10 and n (1 - p) >= 10 (some use 5).
   Data science: a classifier with true accuracy 0.8 on 200 test items:
      the number correct ~ Binomial(200, 0.8): mean 160, sd 5.66 (so
      accuracy has standard error sqrt(0.8 * 0.2/200) = 0.0283).
H. INTERPRETATION: sd = sqrt(n p (1 - p)) grows like sqrt(n) while the mean grows
   like n, so the PROPORTION X/n has sd sqrt(p (1 - p)/n): precision
   improves like 1/sqrt(n) (Module 37).
I. MISTAKES: using the binomial when trials are dependent; forgetting the
   binomial coefficient; confusing P(X = k) with P(X <= k); using the
   normal approximation for small n p or extreme p.
J. RELATED: Bernoulli (n = 1); hypergeometric (without replacement);
   Poisson approximation for large n, small p [SUPPLEMENTARY]: Poisson(lambda)
   has P(X = k) = e^(-lambda) lambda^k / k!, mean = variance = lambda
   (events in a fixed interval, e.g. P(2 events | lambda = 3) =
   e^(-3) * 9/2 = 0.224).

sections.title: NORMAL (GAUSSIAN) DISTRIBUTION

blocks.title: NORMAL DISTRIBUTION N(mu, sigma^2)
blocks.formulaBody:
f(x) = 1/(sigma sqrt(2 pi)) * exp( -(x - mu)^2 / (2 sigma^2) ),  x in R
     mean = median = mode = mu;   variance = sigma^2.
     Standardization:  Z = (X - mu)/sigma ~ N(0, 1)  (standard normal)
     Standard normal CDF: Phi(z) = P(Z <= z)  (no closed form; tables or
        software).
     P(a <= X <= b) = Phi( (b - mu)/sigma ) - Phi( (a - mu)/sigma ).
     Symmetry: Phi(-z) = 1 - Phi(z).
     Empirical rule: P(|X - mu| <= sigma) = 0.6827; within 2 sigma = 0.9545;
        within 3 sigma = 0.9973.
     Key quantiles: z = 1.645 (two-sided 90%, one-sided 95%), 1.960 (95%
        two-sided), 2.576 (99% two-sided).

parts.B:
FORMULAS
     f(x) = 1/(sigma sqrt(2 pi)) * exp( -(x - mu)^2 / (2 sigma^2) ),  x in R
     mean = median = mode = mu;   variance = sigma^2.
     Standardization:  Z = (X - mu)/sigma ~ N(0, 1)  (standard normal)
     Standard normal CDF: Phi(z) = P(Z <= z)  (no closed form; tables or
        software).
     P(a <= X <= b) = Phi( (b - mu)/sigma ) - Phi( (a - mu)/sigma ).
     Symmetry: Phi(-z) = 1 - Phi(z).
     Empirical rule: P(|X - mu| <= sigma) = 0.6827; within 2 sigma = 0.9545;
        within 3 sigma = 0.9973.
     Key quantiles: z = 1.645 (two-sided 90%, one-sided 95%), 1.960 (95%
        two-sided), 2.576 (99% two-sided).
parts.C:
SYMBOLS: mu the center (location); sigma > 0 the scale (standard
   deviation); sigma^2 the variance; exp(.) = e^(.); z the standardized
   value ("z-score"): how many standard deviations x is from the mean.
   NOTATION WARNING: N(mu, sigma^2) lists the VARIANCE (convention here); in
   software, scipy.stats.norm(loc = mu, scale = sigma) uses the SD.
parts.D:
CONCEPT: the bell curve. Symmetric about mu; inflection points at mu +/- sigma;
   tails decay extremely fast (squared term in the exponent). The
   term (x - mu)^2/(2 sigma^2) measures squared distance in SD units.
   WHY IT IS EVERYWHERE: the Central Limit Theorem (Module 37): sums/averages
   of many small independent effects are approximately normal. Also: the
   normal maximizes entropy for a given mean and variance; linear
   combinations of independent normals are normal.
parts.E:
CONDITIONS: a MODEL; real data are only approximately normal. Check with
   histograms, Q-Q plots, tests. Heavy-tailed data (financial returns)
   violate it. Sum rule: if X ~ N(mu1, s1^2) and Y ~ N(mu2, s2^2) are
   independent then X + Y ~ N(mu1 + mu2, s1^2 + s2^2) (VARIANCES add, not
   SDs); aX + b ~ N(a mu + b, a^2 sigma^2).
parts.F:
DERIVATION (normalization): int e^(-z^2/2) dz = sqrt(2 pi) (polar-coordinate
   trick, F13.2), which is why the constant 1/sqrt(2 pi) appears.
parts.G:
EXAMPLES
   Simple: IQ ~ N(100, 15^2). P(X > 130): z = (130 - 100)/15 = 2;
      1 - Phi(2) = 0.0228 (about 2.3%).
      P(85 < X < 115) = P(-1 < Z < 1) = 0.6827.
   Moderate 1: the 90th percentile of IQ: x = mu + z_0.90 sigma =
      100 + 1.2816 * 15 = 119.2.
   Moderate 2: exam scores ~ N(70, 10^2). P(X < 55): z = -1.5, Phi(-1.5) =
      0.0668. P(60 < X < 85) = Phi(1.5) - Phi(-1) = 0.9332 - 0.1587 = 0.7745.
   Moderate 3 (sum): two independent measurement errors N(0, 3^2) and
      N(0, 4^2): the total error ~ N(0, 25): sd 5 (not 7).
parts.H:
INTERPRETATION: z = 2 means two standard deviations above the mean (top 2.3%).
   Z-scores let you compare values on different scales.
parts.I:
COMMON MISTAKES: using sigma vs sigma^2 inconsistently (software scale =
   SD); applying the empirical rule to non-normal data; treating the
   density value as a probability; adding SDs instead of variances;
   forgetting to standardize before using tables; assuming "large
   sample" makes the DATA normal (only the MEAN becomes approximately
   normal).
parts.J:
RELATED: t-distribution (Module 39), multivariate normal (mean vector and
   covariance matrix Sigma: density proportional to
   exp(-(1/2)(x - mu)^T Sigma^(-1) (x - mu))), log-normal (log X is normal),
   Gaussian noise in regression (Module 40), standardization of features.

sections.title: EXPONENTIAL DISTRIBUTION

blocks.title: EXPONENTIAL(lambda)
blocks.formulaBody:
f(x) = lambda e^(-lambda x),  x >= 0 (0 for x < 0)
     F(x) = 1 - e^(-lambda x);   survival P(X > x) = e^(-lambda x)
     mean = 1/lambda;  variance = 1/lambda^2;  sd = 1/lambda;
     median = ln(2)/lambda.
     MEMORYLESS property: P(X > s + t | X > s) = P(X > t).

parts.B:
FORMULAS
     f(x) = lambda e^(-lambda x),  x >= 0 (0 for x < 0)
     F(x) = 1 - e^(-lambda x);   survival P(X > x) = e^(-lambda x)
     mean = 1/lambda;  variance = 1/lambda^2;  sd = 1/lambda;
     median = ln(2)/lambda.
     MEMORYLESS property: P(X > s + t | X > s) = P(X > t).
parts.C:
SYMBOLS: lambda > 0 the RATE (events per unit time); 1/lambda the mean
   waiting time. NOTATION WARNING: some books/software use the scale
   beta = 1/lambda (scipy.stats.expon(scale = 1/lambda)).
parts.D:
CONCEPT: the waiting time until the next event when events occur
   independently at a constant average rate (a Poisson process). Density
   is highest at 0 and decays: short waits are the most likely, long
   waits rare.
parts.E:
CONDITIONS: constant rate, independent events; support x >= 0. Real
   lifetimes often have increasing/decreasing hazard (use Weibull
   etc.). The exponential is the only continuous distribution with the
   memoryless property.
parts.F:
DERIVATION: P(X > x) = P(no event in [0, x]); for a Poisson process with
   rate lambda that is e^(-lambda x). Hence F(x) = 1 - e^(-lambda x) and
   f = F'. Memoryless: P(X > s + t)/P(X > s) = e^(-lambda(s+t))/e^(-lambda s)
   = e^(-lambda t). Mean by integration by parts (F4.6): int x lambda
   e^(-lambda x) dx = 1/lambda.
parts.G:
EXAMPLES
   Simple: customers arrive at rate lambda = 0.5 per minute (mean wait 2
      minutes). P(wait > 3 min) = e^(-1.5) = 0.2231.
   Moderate: P(1 < X < 4) = F(4) - F(1) = e^(-0.5) - e^(-2) = 0.6065 - 0.1353
      = 0.4712. Median wait = ln 2/0.5 = 1.386 minutes (less than the mean
      2: right-skewed).
   Moderate 2 (memoryless): given you have already waited 5 minutes, the
      probability of waiting at least 3 more is still e^(-1.5) = 0.2231.
   Variance: 1/lambda^2 = 4; sd = 2 minutes = mean (a signature of the
      exponential: coefficient of variation 1).
parts.H: INTERPRETATION: "the past does not matter" for the remaining wait.
parts.I:
MISTAKES: mixing rate and scale; using it for lifetimes with wear-out
   (not memoryless); forgetting x >= 0.

sections.title: EXPECTED VALUE

blocks.title: EXPECTED VALUE (MEAN) OF A RANDOM VARIABLE
blocks.formulaBody:
Discrete:    E[X] = sum[x] x p(x)
     Continuous:  E[X] = int[-inf..inf] x f(x) dx
     Law of the unconscious statistician (LOTUS), for a function g:
        E[g(X)] = sum g(x) p(x)   or   int g(x) f(x) dx
     (no need to find the distribution of g(X)).

parts.A: NAME: Expectation / expected value / population mean.

sections.title: LINEARITY OF EXPECTATION

blocks.title: LINEARITY OF EXPECTATION
blocks.formulaBody:
E[a X + b] = a E[X] + b
     E[X + Y] = E[X] + E[Y]            ALWAYS (no independence needed)
     E[a_1 X_1 + ... + a_n X_n] = a_1 E[X_1] + ... + a_n E[X_n]
     If X and Y are independent: E[X Y] = E[X] E[Y]. More generally,
        E[X Y] = E[X] E[Y] + Cov(X, Y), so the product rule holds exactly
        when Cov(X, Y) = 0 (X and Y uncorrelated), which is weaker than
        independence.

parts.B:
FORMULAS
     E[a X + b] = a E[X] + b
     E[X + Y] = E[X] + E[Y]            ALWAYS (no independence needed)
     E[a_1 X_1 + ... + a_n X_n] = a_1 E[X_1] + ... + a_n E[X_n]
     If X and Y are independent: E[X Y] = E[X] E[Y]. More generally,
        E[X Y] = E[X] E[Y] + Cov(X, Y), so the product rule holds exactly
        when Cov(X, Y) = 0 (X and Y uncorrelated), which is weaker than
        independence.
parts.C: SYMBOLS: a, b constants; X, Y any random variables with finite means.
parts.D:
CONCEPT: the average of a sum is the sum of averages, regardless of how
   the variables depend on each other. This makes hard problems easy:
   break a complicated variable into a sum of simple indicator variables.
parts.E:
CONDITIONS: holds ALWAYS for sums (the strength of the theorem); the
   product rule needs independence (or zero covariance).
parts.F:
DERIVATION: E[X + Y] = sum_x sum_y (x + y) p(x, y) = sum x p_X(x) + sum y p_Y(y),
   using only the definition of marginals.
parts.G:
EXAMPLES
   Simple: sum of two dice: E = 3.5 + 3.5 = 7.
   Moderate (indicator trick): binomial mean. X = X_1 + ... + X_n with E[X_i]
      = p: E[X] = n p (no PMF sums needed).
   Moderate 2 (dependent variables): n people put their hats in a box and
      each takes one at random. Let X_i = 1 if person i gets their own
      hat; E[X_i] = 1/n. Expected number of matches = n * (1/n) = 1 for
      EVERY n, even though the X_i are dependent.
   Moderate 3 (affine): temperature X in C with mean 20; in F: 1.8 * 20 + 32
      = 68.
parts.H:
INTERPRETATION: the mean of a sample mean is the population mean:
   E[X_bar] = mu (unbiasedness, Module 37).
parts.I:
MISTAKES: thinking independence is needed for the sum rule; extending the
   rule to variances (it needs independence/covariance); applying to
   non-linear functions.
parts.J:
RELATED: variance of sums (F36.3), binomial mean (F35.7),
   unbiasedness of the sample mean (F37.2).

sections.title: VARIANCE AND STANDARD DEVIATION OF RANDOM VARIABLES

blocks.title: VARIANCE
blocks.formulaBody:
Var(X) = E[ (X - mu)^2 ] = E[X^2] - (E[X])^2
     sd(X) = sigma = sqrt(Var(X))
     Var(a X + b) = a^2 Var(X);   sd(a X + b) = |a| sd(X)
     Var(X + Y) = Var(X) + Var(Y) + 2 Cov(X, Y)
     If X_1..X_n are INDEPENDENT (or uncorrelated):
        Var(sum X_i) = sum Var(X_i);    Var(a X + b Y) = a^2 Var X + b^2 Var Y
     Mean of n iid values with variance sigma^2: Var(X_bar) = sigma^2/n.

parts.A: NAME: Variance and standard deviation of a random variable.
parts.B:
FORMULAS
     Var(X) = E[ (X - mu)^2 ] = E[X^2] - (E[X])^2
     sd(X) = sigma = sqrt(Var(X))
     Var(a X + b) = a^2 Var(X);   sd(a X + b) = |a| sd(X)
     Var(X + Y) = Var(X) + Var(Y) + 2 Cov(X, Y)
     If X_1..X_n are INDEPENDENT (or uncorrelated):
        Var(sum X_i) = sum Var(X_i);    Var(a X + b Y) = a^2 Var X + b^2 Var Y
     Mean of n iid values with variance sigma^2: Var(X_bar) = sigma^2/n.
parts.C: SYMBOLS: mu = E[X]; Cov covariance; X_bar the sample mean.
parts.D:
CONCEPT: the expected squared distance from the mean: the average
   amount of "wobble". It is the population analog of the sample
   variance of Module 31; the sample variance s^2 ESTIMATES it.
parts.E:
CONDITIONS: needs a finite second moment. Variances add only when
   covariances vanish (otherwise include 2 Cov). Standard deviations do
   NOT add.
parts.F:
DERIVATION of the shortcut: E[(X - mu)^2] = E[X^2 - 2 mu X + mu^2] =
   E[X^2] - 2 mu^2 + mu^2 = E[X^2] - mu^2 (using linearity).
parts.G:
EXAMPLES
   Simple: fair die: E[X^2] = (1 + 4 + 9 + 16 + 25 + 36)/6 = 91/6 = 15.167;
      Var = 91/6 - 3.5^2 = 15.167 - 12.25 = 2.917 = 35/12.
   Moderate: sum of two dice (independent): Var = 35/12 + 35/12 = 35/6 = 5.833;
      sd = 2.415. (Check by enumeration: variance of the 36 sums is 5.833.)
   Moderate 2: Bernoulli: p - p^2; binomial n p (1 - p) (sum of n independent
      Bernoulli); X ~ U(a, b): (b - a)^2/12; exponential 1/lambda^2.
   Moderate 3: Y = 2X + 3 with Var(X) = 4: Var(Y) = 4 * 4 = 16; sd(Y) = 4 (the
      shift 3 does not matter).
   Moderate 4 (negative association): Var(X - Y) = Var X + Var Y - 2 Cov(X, Y):
      for portfolios, covariance (diversification) reduces risk.
parts.H:
INTERPRETATION: the sd is in the original units; Chebyshev: P(|X - mu| >=
   k sigma) <= 1/k^2 for any distribution (k = 2: at most 25%).
parts.J:
RELATED: covariance (Module 32); standard error sigma/sqrt(n) (Module
   37); bias-variance decomposition (Module 46).

sections.title: MOMENTS

blocks.title: MOMENTS AND THE MOMENT GENERATING FUNCTION
blocks.formulaBody:
k-th RAW moment:       m_k = E[X^k]
     k-th CENTRAL moment:   mu_k = E[(X - mu)^k]
     Mean = m_1; variance = mu_2.
     SKEWNESS: gamma_1 = mu_3/sigma^3 (asymmetry);
     KURTOSIS: mu_4/sigma^4 (tail heaviness; normal = 3; EXCESS kurtosis =
        mu_4/sigma^4 - 3).
     MGF: M(t) = E[e^(tX)]; the k-th moment is the k-th derivative at 0:
        E[X^k] = M^(k)(0).

parts.A: NAME: Raw moments, central moments, standardized moments, MGF.
parts.B:

sections.title: TRANSFORMATIONS OF RANDOM VARIABLES

blocks.title: LINEAR AND NONLINEAR TRANSFORMATIONS
blocks.formulaBody:
LINEAR: Y = a X + b:  E[Y] = a E[X] + b;  Var(Y) = a^2 Var(X);
        sd(Y) = |a| sd(X). If X ~ N(mu, sigma^2) then Y ~ N(a mu + b, a^2 sigma^2).
        Standardizing: Z = (X - mu)/sigma has mean 0 and variance 1.
     CDF METHOD (any g): F_Y(y) = P(g(X) <= y) = P(X in {x : g(x) <= y}); then
        differentiate to get f_Y.
     MONOTONE g (strictly increasing or decreasing, differentiable) with
        inverse x = g^(-1)(y):
          f_Y(y) = f_X( g^(-1)(y) ) * | d g^(-1)(y)/dy |.
        (A one-dimensional change of variables; the factor is the
        Jacobian, F13.3.)
     INVERSE-TRANSFORM SAMPLING: if U ~ U(0, 1) and F is a CDF, then
        X = F^(-1)(U) has CDF F.

parts.B:
FORMULAS
     LINEAR: Y = a X + b:  E[Y] = a E[X] + b;  Var(Y) = a^2 Var(X);
        sd(Y) = |a| sd(X). If X ~ N(mu, sigma^2) then Y ~ N(a mu + b, a^2 sigma^2).
        Standardizing: Z = (X - mu)/sigma has mean 0 and variance 1.
     CDF METHOD (any g): F_Y(y) = P(g(X) <= y) = P(X in {x : g(x) <= y}); then
        differentiate to get f_Y.
     MONOTONE g (strictly increasing or decreasing, differentiable) with
        inverse x = g^(-1)(y):
          f_Y(y) = f_X( g^(-1)(y) ) * | d g^(-1)(y)/dy |.

parts.C:
SYMBOLS: g a function; g^(-1) its inverse; |dx/dy| the absolute
   derivative of the inverse (Jacobian factor).
parts.D:
CONCEPT: transforming a random variable changes its distribution; for
   linear maps only the location and scale change, for nonlinear maps
   the SHAPE changes.
parts.E:
CONDITIONS: the density formula needs g monotone on the support (else
   split into monotone pieces and add contributions). Expectation of a
   nonlinear transform: use LOTUS, not g(E[X]).
parts.G:
EXAMPLES
   Simple (linear): temperature X ~ N(20, 4^2) C. In F: Y = 1.8 X + 32 ~
      N(68, 7.2^2) (sd = 1.8 * 4 = 7.2).
   Moderate 1 (inverse transform): U ~ U(0, 1) and Y = -ln(U)/lambda. Then
      F_Y(y) = P(-ln U/lambda <= y) = P(U >= e^(-lambda y)) = 1 - e^(-lambda y):
      Y ~ Exponential(lambda). Used to generate exponential random numbers.
   Moderate 2 (squaring): U ~ U(0, 1), Y = U^2: F_Y(y) = P(U <= sqrt(y))
      = sqrt(y) for 0 < y < 1; f_Y(y) = 1/(2 sqrt(y)) (unbounded near 0).
      E[Y] = 1/3 (LOTUS), not (1/2)^2 = 1/4.
   Moderate 3 (log-normal): if X ~ N(mu, sigma^2), Y = e^X is log-normal with
      mean e^(mu + sigma^2/2) (greater than e^mu: Jensen).
parts.H:
INTERPRETATION: log transforms turn multiplicative effects into additive
   ones and make right-skewed data more symmetric; back-transforming a
   mean of logs gives the geometric mean, not the arithmetic mean.
parts.I:
MISTAKES: E[g(X)] = g(E[X]); forgetting the Jacobian factor; applying the
   monotone formula to non-monotone g; forgetting that standardization
   changes the scale of the units.

sections.title: PROBABILITY OF INTERVALS; ZERO PROBABILITY AT POINTS

blocks.title: INTERVAL PROBABILITIES
blocks.formulaBody:
Continuous X with CDF F and PDF f:
     P(a <= X <= b) = P(a < X < b) = P(a < X <= b) = F(b) - F(a)
                    = int[a..b] f(x) dx.
   Discrete X: endpoints MATTER: P(a < X <= b) = F(b) - F(a);
     P(a <= X <= b) = F(b) - F(a-) = F(b) - F(a) + p(a).
   One-sided: P(X <= b) = F(b); P(X > a) = 1 - F(a).

parts.B:
Continuous X with CDF F and PDF f:
     P(a <= X <= b) = P(a < X < b) = P(a < X <= b) = F(b) - F(a)
                    = int[a..b] f(x) dx.
   Discrete X: endpoints MATTER: P(a < X <= b) = F(b) - F(a);
     P(a <= X <= b) = F(b) - F(a-) = F(b) - F(a) + p(a).
   One-sided: P(X <= b) = F(b); P(X > a) = 1 - F(a).
parts.C:
SYMBOLS: F the CDF; F(a-) the left limit of F at a; p(a) the point
   probability.
parts.D:
CONCEPT: the probability of an interval is the probability
   accumulated between its endpoints: a difference of CDF values.
parts.E:
CONDITIONS: for continuous X the endpoints are irrelevant; for
   discrete X they matter.
parts.G:
EXAMPLES: Exponential(lambda = 0.5): P(1 < X < 4) = 0.4712 (whether or not
   the endpoints are included).
   Binomial(10, 0.5): P(3 <= X <= 5) = p(3) + p(4) + p(5)
   = (120 + 210 + 252)/1024 = 582/1024 = 0.5684; P(3 < X <= 5) = 462/1024.
parts.H:
INTERPRETATION: lets us read 'between' probabilities directly from a
   CDF table or function.
parts.I:
MISTAKE: ignoring endpoint inclusion for discrete variables ("at least 3"
   vs "more than 3").

C. SYMBOLS: F the CDF; F(a-) the left limit of F at a; p(a) the point

D. CONCEPT: the probability of an interval is the probability

   Binomial(10, 0.5): P(3 <= X <= 5) = p(3) + p(4) + p(5)

I. MISTAKE: ignoring endpoint inclusion for discrete variables ("at least 3"
   vs "more than 3").

WHY CONTINUOUS RANDOM VARIABLES HAVE ZERO PROBABILITY AT INDIVIDUAL POINTS
STATEMENT: if X is continuous with density f, then P(X = x) = 0 for every
single value x.
EXPLANATION
   1. By the definition of the PDF, P(X = x) = P(x <= X <= x) = int[x..x] f(t) dt
      = 0: an integral over an interval of zero width has zero area.
   2. Limit argument: for any h > 0, P(X = x) <= P(x - h <= X <= x + h)
      = int[x-h..x+h] f(t) dt <= 2 h max f. Let h -> 0: the bound -> 0.
   3. Counting/total-mass argument: there are uncountably many possible
      values and total probability is 1. If each point had positive
      probability, then for any c > 0 only finitely many (at most 1/c)
      points can have probability at least c, so at most countably many
      points could have positive probability. A continuous variable
      spreads its probability over a continuum, so each point gets 0.
   4. Measurement view: "exactly 1.80000... m tall" with infinite precision
      is an event no real person satisfies; real statements concern
      INTERVALS (to the nearest cm).
J. RELATED: CDF (F35.4), density (F35.3), p-values (F39.5).
IMPORTANT CONSEQUENCES AND CLARIFICATIONS
   - Probability ZERO does NOT mean IMPOSSIBLE. For X ~ U(0, 1) the value 0.5 is
     possible, yet P(X = 0.5) = 0 ("almost surely" X != 0.5).
     Impossible events have probability 0, but not conversely in the
     continuous setting.
   - The density f(x) is NOT P(X = x). f(x) dx approx P(x <= X <= x + dx): for a
     tiny window of width h, probability approx f(x) h.
     Example: U(0, 1): P(0.5 <= X <= 0.5 + h) = h.
   - Hence P(X <= x) = P(X < x), and for continuous variables the
     inclusion of endpoints is irrelevant.
   - Likelihood of continuous data uses DENSITIES (not probabilities) as
     the quantity to maximize (Module 38).
   - In practice, rounding makes real measurements discrete: probabilities
     of observed values are positive because the value represents an
     interval.
COMMON MISTAKES: reading f(x) as "the probability of x"; concluding that
"P = 0" events never happen; summing densities instead of integrating;
asking for P(X = x) of a continuous variable instead of an interval.

DATA SCIENCE LINK (Modules 35-36): loss functions derive from distributions
(squared error from the normal, cross-entropy from Bernoulli/categorical);
probability calibration; predicted distributions; expectation underlies
risk (expected loss), bias-variance, and policy value in reinforcement
learning; sampling from distributions underlies Monte Carlo simulation,
bootstrapping and generative models.

   - The density f(x) is NOT P(X = x). f(x) dx approx P(x <= X <= x + dx): for a
     tiny window of width h, probability approx f(x) h.
     Example: U(0, 1): P(0.5 <= X <= 0.5 + h) = h.
   - Hence P(X <= x) = P(X < x), and for continuous variables the
     inclusion of endpoints is irrelevant.
   - Likelihood of continuous data uses DENSITIES (not probabilities) as
     the quantity to maximize (Module 38).
   - In practice, rounding makes real measurements discrete: probabilities
     of observed values are positive because the value represents an
     interval.

"P = 0" events never happen; summing densities instead of integrating;
asking for P(X = x) of a continuous variable instead of an interval.

title: SAMPLING AND ESTIMATION
introRaw:
BASIC IDEA (plain English)
We rarely observe everyone. We observe a SAMPLE and use it to learn
about the whole POPULATION. Statistical inference is the science of
doing this honestly: quantifying how far the sample result may be from
the truth, and how that error shrinks as the sample grows.

introBlocks.rawText:
BASIC IDEA (plain English)
We rarely observe everyone. We observe a SAMPLE and use it to learn
about the whole POPULATION. Statistical inference is the science of
doing this honestly: quantifying how far the sample result may be from
the truth, and how that error shrinks as the sample grows.

sections.title: POPULATION vs SAMPLE; PARAMETERS vs STATISTICS

blocks.rawText:
DEFINITIONS
   POPULATION: the complete collection of units we want to learn about
      (all customers, all future transactions, all possible measurements).
      It can be a hypothetical infinite process.
   SAMPLE: the subset actually observed, size n.
   PARAMETER: a fixed (usually unknown) numerical summary of the
      population: mu, sigma^2, proportion p, regression coefficient beta.
   STATISTIC: a numerical summary computed from the sample: x_bar, s^2, p_hat.
      A statistic is a RANDOM VARIABLE: a different sample would give a
      different value.
   ESTIMATOR: a rule/function of the sample used to estimate a parameter;
      written with a hat: theta_hat = g(X_1, ..., X_n). It is random.
   ESTIMATE: the specific number obtained from one observed sample.
      Example: x_bar = (1/n) sum X_i is the ESTIMATOR of mu; x_bar = 5.2
      from your data is the ESTIMATE.
  Quantity                Population (parameter)   Sample (statistic)
  Mean                    mu                       x_bar
  Variance                sigma^2                  s^2
  Standard deviation      sigma                    s
  Proportion              p                        p_hat
  Correlation             rho                      r
  Size                    N                        n
  Fixed or random?        fixed, unknown           random (varies by sample)
SAMPLING METHODS
   SIMPLE RANDOM SAMPLE (SRS): every subset of size n is equally likely.
   STRATIFIED: split the population into homogeneous strata, sample within
      each (reduces variance, guarantees group coverage).
   CLUSTER: sample whole groups (schools, villages): cheaper, usually
      higher variance.
   SYSTEMATIC: every k-th unit.
   CONVENIENCE/VOLUNTARY-RESPONSE samples are NOT random and are typically
      biased.
   IID ASSUMPTION: observations Independent and Identically Distributed:
      the standard model behind most formulas in this module.
SAMPLING ERROR vs BIAS
   SAMPLING ERROR: random variation from using a sample; shrinks with n.
   SAMPLING BIAS (selection bias, non-response, survivorship): systematic
      error from HOW the sample was obtained; does NOT shrink with n.
      Famous example: a huge biased poll can be worse than a small random
      one. A large n makes a biased estimate precisely wrong.

blocks.title: SAMPLING DISTRIBUTION OF A STATISTIC
blocks.formulaBody:
the probability distribution of a statistic (e.g. x_bar) over
   all possible samples of size n from the population.

parts.B:
DEFINITION: the probability distribution of a statistic (e.g. x_bar) over
   all possible samples of size n from the population.
parts.C:
SYMBOLS: n the sample size; x_bar the statistic; the sampling
   distribution lives over all possible samples of size n.
parts.D:
CONCEPT: imagine repeating the sampling process many times, computing the
   statistic each time; the histogram of those values is the sampling
   distribution. It describes the REPEATED-SAMPLING behavior of the
   statistic, not the variability of individual data points. All
   frequentist inference (standard errors, confidence intervals, p-values)
   relies on it.
parts.E: CONDITIONS: it depends on the population, the sampling scheme and n.
parts.G:
WORKED EXAMPLE (exact enumeration): population {2, 4, 6, 8}
   (N = 4: mu = 5, sigma^2 = (9 + 1 + 1 + 9)/4 = 5). Draw samples of size
   n = 2 WITH replacement: 16 equally likely ordered pairs.
     Sample means: 2 (once), 3 (twice), 4 (three times), 5 (four times),
     6 (three), 7 (twice), 8 (once)  -> probabilities /16.
     E[x_bar] = (2*1 + 3*2 + 4*3 + 5*4 + 6*3 + 7*2 + 8*1)/16 = 80/16 = 5 = mu.
     Var(x_bar) = (9*1 + 4*2 + 1*3 + 0 + 1*3 + 4*2 + 9*1)/16 = 40/16 = 2.5
     = sigma^2/n = 5/2. OK.
   So the sampling distribution is centered at mu with spread sigma/sqrt(n);
   it is triangular here, more bell-like than the (uniform) population.
parts.H:
INTERPRETATION: it is the reference distribution for standard errors,
   confidence intervals and tests.
parts.I:
COMMON MISTAKES: confusing the sampling distribution of x_bar with
   the distribution of the data; thinking only one sample exists.
parts.J:
RELATED: CLT (F37.4), standard error (F37.8), bootstrap (section
   37.6).

blocks.formulaBody:
If X_1..X_n are iid with mean mu and variance sigma^2:
        E[x_bar] = mu;   Var(x_bar) = sigma^2/n;   sd(x_bar) = sigma/sqrt(n).

SYMBOLS: mu, sigma^2 the population mean and variance; n the sample
   size; X_i the observations.
parts.D:
CONCEPT: averaging cancels random errors: the mean stays centered at
   mu while its spread shrinks like 1/sqrt(n).
parts.F:
DERIVATION: E[x_bar] = (1/n) sum E[X_i] = mu (linearity, F36.2);
   Var(x_bar) = (1/n^2) sum Var(X_i) = n sigma^2/n^2 (independence).
parts.E:
CONDITIONS: independence (clustered or serially correlated data have a
   larger variance of x_bar). If sampling WITHOUT replacement from a finite
   population: Var(x_bar) = (sigma^2/n) (N - n)/(N - 1), the FINITE
   POPULATION CORRECTION (fpc); negligible when n << N.
parts.G:
EXAMPLE: sigma = 15, n = 36: sd(x_bar) = 15/6 = 2.5; n = 144: 1.25.
   For the population {2, 4, 6, 8} with n = 2: Var(x_bar) = 5/2 = 2.5
   (F37.1).

INTERPRETATION: quadrupling the sample size halves the standard
   error.

   with sigma; using it for dependent data.

blocks.title: LAW OF LARGE NUMBERS (LLN)
blocks.formulaBody:
If X_i are iid with finite mean mu then x_bar_n -> mu in probability as
   n -> infinity: for every epsilon > 0, P(|x_bar_n - mu| > epsilon) -> 0.

parts.B:
If X_i are iid with finite mean mu then x_bar_n -> mu in probability as
   n -> infinity: for every epsilon > 0, P(|x_bar_n - mu| > epsilon) -> 0.
parts.C:
SYMBOLS: x_bar_n the mean of n observations; mu the true mean;
   epsilon > 0 a tolerance.
parts.D:
CONCEPT: sample averages settle down to the true mean as n grows
   (justifies simulation and the frequency interpretation of
   probability). It says nothing about short runs ("law of averages"
   fallacy: past heads do not "owe" tails).
parts.E:
PROOF IDEA (Chebyshev): P(|x_bar - mu| > eps) <= Var(x_bar)/eps^2 =
   sigma^2/(n eps^2) -> 0.
parts.G:
EXAMPLE: the proportion of heads in n tosses of a fair coin: for n =
   10 it typically lies between 0.3 and 0.7; for n = 10,000 it is within
   about +/-0.01 of 0.5 (sd = 0.005).
parts.H:
INTERPRETATION: justifies Monte Carlo estimates and the frequency
   meaning of probability.
parts.I:
COMMON MISTAKES: the gambler's fallacy (past deviations are not
   'corrected'); applying it to distributions without a finite mean
   (Cauchy).
parts.J: RELATED: consistency (F37.7), CLT (F37.4), simulation (section 41.6).

blocks.title: CENTRAL LIMIT THEOREM (CLT)
blocks.formulaBody:
let X_1..X_n be iid with mean mu and finite variance sigma^2.
   Then as n grows
        Z_n = (x_bar - mu) / (sigma/sqrt(n))  ->  N(0, 1) in distribution,
   i.e. for large n, x_bar is approximately N(mu, sigma^2/n); the sum
   S_n = sum X_i is approximately N(n mu, n sigma^2).

parts.B:
STATEMENT: let X_1..X_n be iid with mean mu and finite variance sigma^2.
   Then as n grows
        Z_n = (x_bar - mu) / (sigma/sqrt(n))  ->  N(0, 1) in distribution,
   i.e. for large n, x_bar is approximately N(mu, sigma^2/n); the sum
   S_n = sum X_i is approximately N(n mu, n sigma^2).
parts.C: SYMBOLS: Z_n the standardized sample mean; "->" convergence in distribution.
parts.D:
CONCEPT: averaging many independent contributions washes out the
   peculiarities of the underlying distribution, leaving a bell shape
   whatever the original shape (as long as the variance is finite).
parts.E:
CONDITIONS & CAUTIONS
   - Independence and finite variance (the Cauchy distribution has no
     variance: its sample mean is as variable as one observation).
   - The speed of convergence depends on the population: symmetric
     distributions converge quickly; heavily skewed ones need larger n.
     Rule of thumb n >= 30 (not a law).
   - The CLT is about the distribution of the MEAN (or sum), NOT about the
     data becoming normal.
   - Proportions: p_hat approx N(p, p(1 - p)/n) when n p >= 10 and
     n(1 - p) >= 10 (the binomial CLT).
parts.G:
EXAMPLES
   Simple: roll a fair die n = 50 times. mu = 3.5, sigma^2 = 35/12 = 2.917.
      x_bar approx N(3.5, 2.917/50 = 0.0583): sd = 0.2415.
      P(x_bar > 3.8) = P(Z > 0.3/0.2415 = 1.242) = 0.107.
   Moderate (skewed population): waiting times Exponential with mean 2
      (sigma = 2), n = 40: x_bar approx N(2, 4/40 = 0.1) (sd 0.316).
      P(x_bar > 2.5) approx P(Z > 1.581) = 0.057. The exact value
      (the sum is Gamma(40)) is 0.065: the approximation is decent but
      not perfect at n = 40 for skewed data.
parts.H:
INTERPRETATION: why the normal distribution and the z/t procedures are
   used so widely for means.
parts.I:
MISTAKES: "with n > 30 the data are normal"; applying it to
   heavy-tailed data without checking; ignoring dependence.
parts.J:
RELATED: sampling distribution (F37.1), normal distribution (F35.8),
   confidence intervals (F39.7).

        Z_n = (x_bar - mu) / (sigma/sqrt(n))  ->  N(0, 1) in distribution,
   i.e. for large n, x_bar is approximately N(mu, sigma^2/n); the sum
   S_n = sum X_i is approximately N(n mu, n sigma^2).
C. SYMBOLS: Z_n the standardized sample mean; "->" convergence in distribution.
D. CONCEPT: averaging many independent contributions washes out the
   peculiarities of the underlying distribution, leaving a bell shape
   whatever the original shape (as long as the variance is finite).
E. CONDITIONS & CAUTIONS
   - Independence and finite variance (the Cauchy distribution has no
     variance: its sample mean is as variable as one observation).
   - The speed of convergence depends on the population: symmetric
     distributions converge quickly; heavily skewed ones need larger n.
     Rule of thumb n >= 30 (not a law).
   - The CLT is about the distribution of the MEAN (or sum), NOT about the
     data becoming normal.
   - Proportions: p_hat approx N(p, p(1 - p)/n) when n p >= 10 and
     n(1 - p) >= 10 (the binomial CLT).
G. EXAMPLES
   Simple: roll a fair die n = 50 times. mu = 3.5, sigma^2 = 35/12 = 2.917.
      x_bar approx N(3.5, 2.917/50 = 0.0583): sd = 0.2415.
      P(x_bar > 3.8) = P(Z > 0.3/0.2415 = 1.242) = 0.107.
   Moderate (skewed population): waiting times Exponential with mean 2
      (sigma = 2), n = 40: x_bar approx N(2, 4/40 = 0.1) (sd 0.316).
      P(x_bar > 2.5) approx P(Z > 1.581) = 0.057. The exact value
      (the sum is Gamma(40)) is 0.065: the approximation is decent but
      not perfect at n = 40 for skewed data.
H. INTERPRETATION: why the normal distribution and the z/t procedures are
   used so widely for means.
I. MISTAKES: "with n > 30 the data are normal"; applying it to
   heavy-tailed data without checking; ignoring dependence.
J. RELATED: sampling distribution (F37.1), normal distribution (F35.8),
   confidence intervals (F39.7).

sections.title: ESTIMATORS, BIAS AND UNBIASEDNESS

blocks.title: BIAS AND UNBIASED ESTIMATORS
blocks.formulaBody:
Bias(theta_hat) = E[theta_hat] - theta
     UNBIASED: E[theta_hat] = theta for every possible value of theta.

parts.B:
FORMULAS
     Bias(theta_hat) = E[theta_hat] - theta
     UNBIASED: E[theta_hat] = theta for every possible value of theta.
parts.C:
SYMBOLS: theta the true parameter; theta_hat the estimator (a random
   variable); the expectation is over repeated samples (the sampling
   distribution).
parts.D:
CONCEPT: on average over many samples an unbiased estimator hits the
   target; a biased one is systematically too high or low. Bias is a
   property of the PROCEDURE, not of a single estimate.
parts.E:
CONDITIONS: unbiasedness refers to the sampling distribution, with the
   model assumptions (e.g. iid). It is NOT sufficient for a good
   estimator (see variance) nor necessary (see MSE).
parts.G:
EXAMPLES
   Simple (unbiased): x_bar for mu: E[x_bar] = mu. Sample variance s^2 (divisor
      n - 1) is unbiased for sigma^2 (F31.4). The sample proportion p_hat is
      unbiased for p.
   Moderate 1 (biased): divide-by-n variance has E = (n - 1)/n sigma^2: bias =
      -sigma^2/n (too small). Sample sd s is slightly biased low for
      sigma (E[s] < sigma, Jensen).
   Moderate 2: X_i ~ U(0, theta); the sample maximum M estimates theta. E[M]
      = n theta/(n + 1): biased low (always below theta). For n = 3,
      E[M] = 0.75 theta (simulation: 0.7504 for theta = 1). The corrected
      estimator ((n + 1)/n) M is unbiased.
   Moderate 3: estimating mu with 0.9 x_bar: bias = -0.1 mu (biased).
parts.H:
INTERPRETATION: unbiasedness is a repeated-sampling guarantee; you only
   have one sample.
parts.I:
MISTAKES: calling an estimate (a number) biased (bias belongs to the
   estimator); assuming unbiased means accurate; thinking all
   "natural" estimators are unbiased; forgetting that s is not unbiased
   even though s^2 is.
parts.J:
RELATED: variance and MSE (F37.6), consistency (F37.7), the n - 1
   divisor (F31.4).

sections.title: VARIANCE OF ESTIMATORS; MEAN SQUARED ERROR

blocks.title: VARIANCE OF AN ESTIMATOR, EFFICIENCY AND MSE
blocks.formulaBody:
Var(theta_hat) = E[ (theta_hat - E[theta_hat])^2 ]
     MSE(theta_hat) = E[ (theta_hat - theta)^2 ] = Var(theta_hat) + Bias(theta_hat)^2
     RELATIVE EFFICIENCY of two unbiased estimators: Var(T_2)/Var(T_1)
        (the one with smaller variance is more efficient).

parts.A:
NAME: Estimator variance; mean squared error (MSE) and the
   bias-variance decomposition.
parts.B:
FORMULAS
     Var(theta_hat) = E[ (theta_hat - E[theta_hat])^2 ]
     MSE(theta_hat) = E[ (theta_hat - theta)^2 ] = Var(theta_hat) + Bias(theta_hat)^2
     RELATIVE EFFICIENCY of two unbiased estimators: Var(T_2)/Var(T_1)
        (the one with smaller variance is more efficient).
parts.C:
SYMBOLS: Var describes the spread of the estimator over repeated samples;
   MSE is the expected squared distance from the truth.
parts.D:
CONCEPT: accuracy has two ingredients: SYSTEMATIC error (bias) and RANDOM
   error (variance). MSE combines them. A slightly biased estimator
   with much lower variance can beat an unbiased noisy one: the
   BIAS-VARIANCE TRADE-OFF (also Module 46).
parts.E:
CONDITIONS: MSE needs finite second moments; the decomposition holds
   for any estimator with finite variance.
parts.F:
DERIVATION: write theta_hat - theta = (theta_hat - E[theta_hat]) +
   (E[theta_hat] - theta) = (random part) + (bias, a constant). Squaring and
   taking expectations, the cross term vanishes because
   E[theta_hat - E theta_hat] = 0. Hence MSE = Var + Bias^2.
parts.G:
EXAMPLES
   Simple (precision grows with n): Var(x_bar) = sigma^2/n. For normal data the
      sample MEDIAN has variance about (pi/2) sigma^2/n = 1.57 sigma^2/n,
      so the mean has relative efficiency 64% (simulation: variances 0.0399
      vs 0.0616 for n = 25). The mean is better for normal data; the
      median wins for heavy-tailed data.
   Moderate (shrinkage): estimate mu with T = 0.9 x_bar when mu = 1, sigma^2 = 4,
      n = 10. x_bar: bias 0, Var 0.4, MSE 0.4. T: bias -0.1, Var 0.81 * 0.4
      = 0.324; MSE = 0.324 + 0.01 = 0.334 < 0.4. The biased estimator has
      LOWER MSE here (shrinkage; ridge regression and James-Stein
      estimation work this way).
parts.H:
INTERPRETATION: choose estimators by MSE (or by out-of-sample prediction
   error), not by unbiasedness alone. Cramer-Rao bound (Module 38): no
   unbiased estimator can have variance below 1/(n I(theta)).
parts.I:
MISTAKES: ignoring variance; thinking low bias alone justifies an
   estimator; confusing the variance of the estimator with the variance of
   the data.
parts.J:
RELATED: bias-variance decomposition for predictions (F46.1),
   Cramer-Rao bound (F38.4), regularization (section 43.8).

sections.title: CONSISTENCY

blocks.title: CONSISTENCY
blocks.formulaBody:
theta_hat_n is CONSISTENT for theta if theta_hat_n converges to
   theta in probability as n -> infinity: for every eps > 0,
   P(|theta_hat_n - theta| > eps) -> 0.
   SUFFICIENT CONDITION: Bias(theta_hat_n) -> 0 and Var(theta_hat_n) -> 0 (then
   MSE -> 0).

parts.B:
DEFINITION: theta_hat_n is CONSISTENT for theta if theta_hat_n converges to
   theta in probability as n -> infinity: for every eps > 0,
   P(|theta_hat_n - theta| > eps) -> 0.
   SUFFICIENT CONDITION: Bias(theta_hat_n) -> 0 and Var(theta_hat_n) -> 0 (then
   MSE -> 0).
parts.C:
SYMBOLS: theta_hat_n the estimator based on n observations; theta the
   true value; 'in probability' means P(|theta_hat_n - theta| > eps)
   tends to 0.
parts.D:
CONCEPT: with enough data the estimator closes in on the truth. It is a
   large-sample property, distinct from unbiasedness (a finite-sample
   average property).
parts.E:
CONDITIONS: a large-sample property; bias tending to 0 and variance
   tending to 0 is sufficient.
parts.G:
EXAMPLES
   Consistent: x_bar (LLN); s^2; p_hat; the divide-by-n variance
      (biased but consistent: bias -sigma^2/n -> 0); the MLE (under
      regularity conditions).
   Unbiased but NOT consistent: use only the FIRST observation X_1 to estimate
      mu: E[X_1] = mu (unbiased) but Var = sigma^2 never shrinks.
   Biased and consistent: the sample maximum for U(0, theta): bias = -theta/(n + 1)
      -> 0.
parts.H:
INTERPRETATION: consistency is the minimal requirement ("more data should
   help"); an inconsistent estimator is useless however long you collect.
parts.I: MISTAKES: equating consistency with unbiasedness.
parts.J:
RELATED: LLN (F37.3), MLE properties (F38.4).

COMPARISON: UNBIASED vs CONSISTENT
   Unbiased: E[theta_hat] = theta for each fixed n (average over samples).
   Consistent: theta_hat_n -> theta as n grows (single-sample behavior).
   Neither implies the other (see examples above).

sections.title: STANDARD ERROR

blocks.title: STANDARD ERROR
blocks.formulaBody:
SE(theta_hat) = sd(theta_hat) = sqrt(Var(theta_hat))  (sd of the SAMPLING
        distribution)
     Sample mean:        SE(x_bar) = sigma/sqrt(n), estimated by s/sqrt(n)
     Sample proportion:  SE(p_hat) = sqrt( p (1 - p) / n ), estimated by
        sqrt( p_hat (1 - p_hat) / n )
     Difference of two independent means: sqrt( s_1^2/n_1 + s_2^2/n_2 )
     With finite population correction: multiply by sqrt((N - n)/(N - 1)).

parts.B:
FORMULAS
     SE(theta_hat) = sd(theta_hat) = sqrt(Var(theta_hat))  (sd of the SAMPLING
        distribution)
     Sample mean:        SE(x_bar) = sigma/sqrt(n), estimated by s/sqrt(n)
     Sample proportion:  SE(p_hat) = sqrt( p (1 - p) / n ), estimated by
        sqrt( p_hat (1 - p_hat) / n )
     Difference of two independent means: sqrt( s_1^2/n_1 + s_2^2/n_2 )
     With finite population correction: multiply by sqrt((N - n)/(N - 1)).
parts.C: SYMBOLS: s the sample sd (estimating sigma); n sample size.
parts.D:
CONCEPT: the typical size of the sampling error: how far the estimate is
   likely to be from the parameter. Precision improves with sqrt(n):
   to HALVE the SE you need FOUR times the data.
parts.E:
CONDITIONS: the formulas assume iid sampling (no clustering/serial
   correlation); sigma replaced by s adds uncertainty (t distribution
   for small n).
parts.G:
EXAMPLES
   Simple: s = 15, n = 36: SE = 15/6 = 2.5. With n = 144: SE = 15/12 = 1.25.
   Moderate: a poll finds p_hat = 0.40 with n = 100: SE = sqrt(0.4 * 0.6/100)
      = 0.049. A rough 95% margin of error is 1.96 * 0.049 = 0.096 (about 9.6
      percentage points). For n = 1,000 the margin is about 3 points.
   Moderate 2: difference of two means: group 1: s = 10, n = 25; group 2:
      s = 12, n = 36: SE = sqrt(100/25 + 144/36) = sqrt(4 + 4) = 2.83.
parts.H:
INTERPRETATION: SE tells how precise the estimate is; it is the building
   block of confidence intervals (estimate +/- critical value x SE) and
   test statistics (estimate/SE).
parts.I:
COMMON MISTAKES: confusing standard DEVIATION (spread of the data) with
   standard ERROR (spread of the estimate); reporting SD when SE is
   meant; assuming the SE shrinks with more data that is biased or
   dependent; using SE of a mean to describe individual variation.
parts.J:
RELATED: confidence intervals (F39.7), test statistics (F39.2),
   regression standard errors (F40.4).

   Moderate: a poll finds p_hat = 0.40 with n = 100: SE = sqrt(0.4 * 0.6/100)
      = 0.049. A rough 95% margin of error is 1.96 * 0.049 = 0.096 (about 9.6
      percentage points). For n = 1,000 the margin is about 3 points.
   Moderate 2: difference of two means: group 1: s = 10, n = 25; group 2:
      s = 12, n = 36: SE = sqrt(100/25 + 144/36) = sqrt(4 + 4) = 2.83.
H. INTERPRETATION: SE tells how precise the estimate is; it is the building
   block of confidence intervals (estimate +/- critical value x SE) and
   test statistics (estimate/SE).
I. COMMON MISTAKES: confusing standard DEVIATION (spread of the data) with
   standard ERROR (spread of the estimate); reporting SD when SE is
   meant; assuming the SE shrinks with more data that is biased or
   dependent; using SE of a mean to describe individual variation.
J. RELATED: confidence intervals (F39.7), test statistics (F39.2),
   regression standard errors (F40.4).

BOOTSTRAP [SUPPLEMENTARY]: estimate the sampling distribution by RESAMPLING
the observed sample WITH replacement (B = 1000-10,000 times), computing the
statistic each time. The sd of the bootstrap statistics estimates the SE;
the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles give a percentile confidence interval.
Works for medians, correlations, model metrics (no formula needed).
   rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
   boots = [np.median(rng.choice(x, size=len(x), replace=True))
            for _ in range(5000)]
   se = np.std(boots, ddof=1); ci = np.percentile(boots, [2.5, 97.5])
Limits: needs a representative sample and iid observations; poor for
extremes (max).

   means = [rng.exponential(2, size=40).mean() for _ in range(20000)]
   np.mean(means) -> about 2.0;  np.std(means) -> about 0.316 (= 2/sqrt(40)).

F37.8  STANDARD ERROR
A. NAME: Standard error (SE).
B. FORMULAS
     SE(theta_hat) = sd(theta_hat) = sqrt(Var(theta_hat))  (sd of the SAMPLING
        distribution)
     Sample mean:        SE(x_bar) = sigma/sqrt(n), estimated by s/sqrt(n)
     Sample proportion:  SE(p_hat) = sqrt( p (1 - p) / n ), estimated by
        sqrt( p_hat (1 - p_hat) / n )
     Difference of two independent means: sqrt( s_1^2/n_1 + s_2^2/n_2 )
     With finite population correction: multiply by sqrt((N - n)/(N - 1)).

title: PARAMETER ESTIMATION
introRaw:
BASIC IDEA (plain English)
We believe the data come from a distribution family (normal, Bernoulli,
exponential) with unknown parameters. Parameter estimation chooses
parameter values that make the model fit the observed data. Two classic
recipes: match moments (method of moments) or choose the parameter that
makes the observed data most probable (maximum likelihood).

sections.title: METHOD OF MOMENTS (MoM)

blocks.title: METHOD OF MOMENTS
blocks.formulaBody:
PROCEDURE: for a model with k parameters theta_1..theta_k:
     1. Compute the first k population moments E[X^j] as functions of the
        parameters.
     2. Compute the sample moments m_j = (1/n) sum x_i^j.
     3. Solve the equations E[X^j](theta) = m_j (j = 1..k) for the parameters.

parts.B:
PROCEDURE: for a model with k parameters theta_1..theta_k:
     1. Compute the first k population moments E[X^j] as functions of the
        parameters.
     2. Compute the sample moments m_j = (1/n) sum x_i^j.
     3. Solve the equations E[X^j](theta) = m_j (j = 1..k) for the parameters.
parts.C:
SYMBOLS: E[X^j] theoretical j-th raw moment (F36.4); m_j its sample
   counterpart.
parts.D:
CONCEPT: the sample moments are good estimates of the true moments (by
   the LLN), so choose parameters whose theoretical moments equal the
   observed ones. Simple, often closed-form.
parts.E:
CONDITIONS: needs finite moments; the resulting estimates may lie
   outside the allowed parameter space; MoM estimators are consistent but
   usually less efficient than MLEs.
parts.G:
EXAMPLES
   Simple (exponential): E[X] = 1/lambda. Data 1.2, 0.8, 2.5, 0.4, 1.6: x_bar =
      6.5/5 = 1.3 -> lambda_hat = 1/1.3 = 0.769.
   Moderate 1 (normal, k = 2): E[X] = mu and E[X^2] = sigma^2 + mu^2. Equate:
      mu_hat = x_bar; sigma_hat^2 = m_2 - x_bar^2 = (1/n) sum (x_i - x_bar)^2
      (divide by n!). For 2, 4, 4, 4, 5, 5, 7, 9: mu_hat = 5, m_2 = 232/8 = 29,
      sigma_hat^2 = 29 - 25 = 4.
   Moderate 2 (uniform): X ~ U(0, theta): E[X] = theta/2 -> theta_hat = 2 x_bar.
      Sample 3.1, 4.7, 2.2, 5.0, 3.8: x_bar = 3.76 -> theta_hat = 7.52 (>= max
      5.0, fine). But sample 1, 1, 1, 9: x_bar = 3 -> theta_hat = 6, LESS than
      the observed 9: impossible! (A well-known weakness: MoM can give
      infeasible values; the MLE, the sample maximum, never does.)
parts.H:
INTERPRETATION: a quick, intuitive estimator and a good starting value for
   iterative MLE algorithms.
parts.I:
MISTAKES: using the wrong number of equations; using central/raw moments
   inconsistently; forgetting that the second moment includes mu^2.
parts.J: RELATED: MLE (below); generalized method of moments in econometrics.

sections.title: LIKELIHOOD AND LOG-LIKELIHOOD

blocks.title: LIKELIHOOD FUNCTION

parts.B:
FORMULA: for iid observations x_1..x_n from a density (or PMF) f(x; theta):
        L(theta) = prod[i=1..n] f(x_i; theta)
   Log-likelihood:  l(theta) = ln L(theta) = sum[i=1..n] ln f(x_i; theta).
parts.C:
SYMBOLS: theta the parameter(s); f(x; theta) the density/PMF evaluated at the
   observed x_i, treated as a function of theta; prod the product.
parts.D:
CONCEPT: the same expression as the joint density of the data, but read
   the other way round: the DATA ARE FIXED and the PARAMETER VARIES. L(theta)
   says how plausible each parameter value is, given what was
   observed. For discrete data L(theta) is the probability of the observed
   sample under theta.
   !! WARNING !! L(theta) is NOT a probability distribution over theta (it does
   not integrate to 1 over theta) and is NOT P(theta | data). Likelihood
   values are meaningful only in COMPARISONS (ratios).
parts.G:
EXAMPLE (Bernoulli): 20 trials, 7 successes. L(p) = p^7 (1 - p)^13.
   l(p) = 7 ln p + 13 ln(1 - p).
   p = 0.35: l = 7(-1.0498) + 13(-0.4308) = -12.949.
   p = 0.50: l = 20 ln 0.5 = -13.863.
   The ratio L(0.35)/L(0.5) = e^(0.914) = 2.49: the data are about 2.5 times
   more probable under p = 0.35 than under p = 0.5.
parts.H:
INTERPRETATION: the parameter value with the highest likelihood is
   the one under which the observed data are least surprising.
parts.I:
COMMON MISTAKES: treating L(theta) as a probability of theta;
   multiplying densities of dependent observations.
parts.J: RELATED: MLE (F38.3), cross-entropy loss (F46.5), Bayes (F34.5).

F38.2  LIKELIHOOD FUNCTION
A. NAME: Likelihood function.
B. FORMULA: for iid observations x_1..x_n from a density (or PMF) f(x; theta):
        L(theta) = prod[i=1..n] f(x_i; theta)
   Log-likelihood:  l(theta) = ln L(theta) = sum[i=1..n] ln f(x_i; theta).
C. SYMBOLS: theta the parameter(s); f(x; theta) the density/PMF evaluated at the
   observed x_i, treated as a function of theta; prod the product.
D. CONCEPT: the same expression as the joint density of the data, but read
   the other way round: the DATA ARE FIXED and the PARAMETER VARIES. L(theta)
   says how plausible each parameter value is, given what was
   observed. For discrete data L(theta) is the probability of the observed
   sample under theta.
   !! WARNING !! L(theta) is NOT a probability distribution over theta (it does
   not integrate to 1 over theta) and is NOT P(theta | data). Likelihood
   values are meaningful only in COMPARISONS (ratios).
E. WHY THE LOGARITHM
   (1) ln is increasing, so L and l have the SAME maximizer;
   (2) it turns the product of n factors into a sum: far easier to
       differentiate (F3.8) and add;
   (3) numerical stability: a product of 1,000 small densities underflows
       to 0, a sum of logs does not;
   (4) the negative log-likelihood is the usual LOSS function (cross-entropy
       for classification, squared error for Gaussian regression).
   Independence is what makes L a product; for dependent data use the
   joint density (chain rule).
G. EXAMPLE (Bernoulli): 20 trials, 7 successes. L(p) = p^7 (1 - p)^13.
   l(p) = 7 ln p + 13 ln(1 - p).
   p = 0.35: l = 7(-1.0498) + 13(-0.4308) = -12.949.
   p = 0.50: l = 20 ln 0.5 = -13.863.
   The ratio L(0.35)/L(0.5) = e^(0.914) = 2.49: the data are about 2.5 times
   more probable under p = 0.35 than under p = 0.5.

   the one under which the observed data are least surprising.

sections.title: MAXIMUM LIKELIHOOD ESTIMATION (MLE)

blocks.title: MAXIMUM LIKELIHOOD ESTIMATOR
blocks.formulaBody:
AND RECIPE
     theta_hat_MLE = argmax over theta of L(theta) = argmax l(theta).
     Recipe (smooth, interior maximum):
       1. Write l(theta) = sum ln f(x_i; theta).
       2. Solve the SCORE EQUATION  dl/dtheta = 0 (system of equations for
          several parameters).
       3. Check it is a maximum: second derivative < 0 (negative definite
          Hessian for several parameters); compare with boundary values.
       4. If there is no closed form, maximize numerically (gradient
          methods, Newton, Module 43), e.g. minimize -l(theta).
     INVARIANCE: the MLE of g(theta) is g(theta_hat).

parts.B:
DEFINITION AND RECIPE
     theta_hat_MLE = argmax over theta of L(theta) = argmax l(theta).
     Recipe (smooth, interior maximum):
       1. Write l(theta) = sum ln f(x_i; theta).
       2. Solve the SCORE EQUATION  dl/dtheta = 0 (system of equations for
          several parameters).
       3. Check it is a maximum: second derivative < 0 (negative definite
          Hessian for several parameters); compare with boundary values.
       4. If there is no closed form, maximize numerically (gradient
          methods, Newton, Module 43), e.g. minimize -l(theta).
     INVARIANCE: the MLE of g(theta) is g(theta_hat).
parts.C:
SYMBOLS: argmax the argument at which the function is largest; dl/dtheta the
   score (derivative of the log-likelihood).
parts.D:
CONCEPT: choose the parameter value under which the observed data are
   most probable (least surprising).
parts.E:
CONDITIONS: model correctly specified (family); iid (or specified
   dependence); the maximum may lie on the boundary of the parameter space
   (derivative methods fail, see uniform below); the likelihood may have
   several local maxima (mixtures, neural nets) or none.
parts.G:
WORKED MLE DERIVATIONS
   (1) BERNOULLI(p), k successes in n trials:
       l(p) = k ln p + (n - k) ln(1 - p).
       l'(p) = k/p - (n - k)/(1 - p) = 0 -> k(1 - p) = (n - k) p -> p_hat = k/n.
       l''(p) = -k/p^2 - (n - k)/(1 - p)^2 < 0: maximum.
       Data: n = 20, k = 7: p_hat = 0.35 (the sample proportion).
   (2) EXPONENTIAL(lambda): f = lambda e^(-lambda x).
       l(lambda) = n ln lambda - lambda sum x_i.
       l' = n/lambda - sum x_i = 0 -> lambda_hat = n/sum x_i = 1/x_bar.
       l'' = -n/lambda^2 < 0. Data 1.2, 0.8, 2.5, 0.4, 1.6: lambda_hat = 5/6.5
       = 0.769 (same as the MoM here).
   (3) NORMAL(mu, sigma^2):
       l(mu, sigma^2) = -(n/2) ln(2 pi) - (n/2) ln sigma^2 - sum (x_i - mu)^2/(2 sigma^2).
       d/d mu: sum (x_i - mu)/sigma^2 = 0 -> mu_hat = x_bar.
       d/d(sigma^2): -n/(2 sigma^2) + sum (x_i - mu)^2/(2 sigma^4) = 0
          -> sigma_hat^2 = (1/n) sum (x_i - x_bar)^2.
       !! The MLE of the variance divides by n, so it is BIASED (bias
       -sigma^2/n) but consistent; s^2 (divide by n - 1) is the unbiased
       alternative. !!
       Data 2, 4, 4, 4, 5, 5, 7, 9: mu_hat = 5; sigma_hat^2 = 4 (s^2 = 4.571).
       scipy.stats.norm.fit(data) returns (5.0, 2.0): sd uses divisor n.
   (4) POISSON(lambda) [SUPPLEMENTARY]: l = sum x_i ln lambda - n lambda -
       sum ln x_i!; lambda_hat = x_bar.
   (5) UNIFORM(0, theta) (boundary case): L(theta) = theta^(-n) for theta >=
       max x_i, and 0 if theta < max x_i. L DECREASES in theta, so it is
       maximized at the smallest allowed value: theta_hat = max(x_i). Setting
       the derivative to zero would give no solution. LESSON: always check the
       support. (This MLE is biased: E = n theta/(n + 1).)
   (6) LINEAR REGRESSION with Gaussian errors: y_i = x_i^T beta + eps_i,
       eps_i ~ N(0, sigma^2): maximizing l over beta is equivalent to
       MINIMIZING sum (y_i - x_i^T beta)^2: ordinary least squares (Module
       40). Gaussian noise <=> squared-error loss; Laplace noise <=>
       absolute-error loss.
   (7) LOGISTIC REGRESSION: negative Bernoulli log-likelihood =
       cross-entropy loss; no closed form: gradient descent / Newton
       (IRLS), Module 43.
parts.H:

blocks.rawText:
F38.3  MAXIMUM LIKELIHOOD ESTIMATOR
A. NAME: Maximum likelihood estimator.
B. DEFINITION AND RECIPE
     theta_hat_MLE = argmax over theta of L(theta) = argmax l(theta).
     Recipe (smooth, interior maximum):
       1. Write l(theta) = sum ln f(x_i; theta).
       2. Solve the SCORE EQUATION  dl/dtheta = 0 (system of equations for
          several parameters).
       3. Check it is a maximum: second derivative < 0 (negative definite
          Hessian for several parameters); compare with boundary values.
       4. If there is no closed form, maximize numerically (gradient
          methods, Newton, Module 43), e.g. minimize -l(theta).
     INVARIANCE: the MLE of g(theta) is g(theta_hat).
C. SYMBOLS: argmax the argument at which the function is largest; dl/dtheta the
   score (derivative of the log-likelihood).
D. CONCEPT: choose the parameter value under which the observed data are
   most probable (least surprising).
E. CONDITIONS: model correctly specified (family); iid (or specified
   dependence); the maximum may lie on the boundary of the parameter space
   (derivative methods fail, see uniform below); the likelihood may have
   several local maxima (mixtures, neural nets) or none.
G. WORKED MLE DERIVATIONS
   (1) BERNOULLI(p), k successes in n trials:
       l(p) = k ln p + (n - k) ln(1 - p).
       l'(p) = k/p - (n - k)/(1 - p) = 0 -> k(1 - p) = (n - k) p -> p_hat = k/n.
       l''(p) = -k/p^2 - (n - k)/(1 - p)^2 < 0: maximum.
       Data: n = 20, k = 7: p_hat = 0.35 (the sample proportion).
   (2) EXPONENTIAL(lambda): f = lambda e^(-lambda x).
       l(lambda) = n ln lambda - lambda sum x_i.
       l' = n/lambda - sum x_i = 0 -> lambda_hat = n/sum x_i = 1/x_bar.
       l'' = -n/lambda^2 < 0. Data 1.2, 0.8, 2.5, 0.4, 1.6: lambda_hat = 5/6.5
       = 0.769 (same as the MoM here).
   (3) NORMAL(mu, sigma^2):
       l(mu, sigma^2) = -(n/2) ln(2 pi) - (n/2) ln sigma^2 - sum (x_i - mu)^2/(2 sigma^2).
       d/d mu: sum (x_i - mu)/sigma^2 = 0 -> mu_hat = x_bar.
       d/d(sigma^2): -n/(2 sigma^2) + sum (x_i - mu)^2/(2 sigma^4) = 0
          -> sigma_hat^2 = (1/n) sum (x_i - x_bar)^2.
       !! The MLE of the variance divides by n, so it is BIASED (bias
       -sigma^2/n) but consistent; s^2 (divide by n - 1) is the unbiased
       alternative. !!
       Data 2, 4, 4, 4, 5, 5, 7, 9: mu_hat = 5; sigma_hat^2 = 4 (s^2 = 4.571).
       scipy.stats.norm.fit(data) returns (5.0, 2.0): sd uses divisor n.
   (4) POISSON(lambda) [SUPPLEMENTARY]: l = sum x_i ln lambda - n lambda -
       sum ln x_i!; lambda_hat = x_bar.
   (5) UNIFORM(0, theta) (boundary case): L(theta) = theta^(-n) for theta >=
       max x_i, and 0 if theta < max x_i. L DECREASES in theta, so it is
       maximized at the smallest allowed value: theta_hat = max(x_i). Setting
       the derivative to zero would give no solution. LESSON: always check the
       support. (This MLE is biased: E = n theta/(n + 1).)
   (6) LINEAR REGRESSION with Gaussian errors: y_i = x_i^T beta + eps_i,
       eps_i ~ N(0, sigma^2): maximizing l over beta is equivalent to
       MINIMIZING sum (y_i - x_i^T beta)^2: ordinary least squares (Module
       40). Gaussian noise <=> squared-error loss; Laplace noise <=>
       absolute-error loss.
   (7) LOGISTIC REGRESSION: negative Bernoulli log-likelihood =
       cross-entropy loss; no closed form: gradient descent / Newton
       (IRLS), Module 43.
H. INTERPRETATION: the MLE is the best-supported parameter under the model;
   with the Fisher information it also gives standard errors.
I. COMMON MISTAKES: maximizing L(theta) when the support depends on theta
   without checking boundaries; forgetting to verify a maximum; confusing the
   MLE of sigma^2 (divide by n) with s^2; treating the likelihood as a
   probability of the parameter; using non-independent data in a product
   likelihood; reporting a local maximum.
J. RELATED: MoM, Bayesian (MAP) estimation, cross-entropy loss (Module 48),
   Newton's method (Module 43).

sections.title: PROPERTIES OF ESTIMATORS (INCLUDING MLE PROPERTIES)

blocks.rawText:
GENERAL CRITERIA
   UNBIASEDNESS (F37.5); CONSISTENCY (F37.7); EFFICIENCY (low variance among
   unbiased estimators, F37.6); LOW MSE; SUFFICIENCY (the statistic
   retains all the information about theta; e.g. x_bar and s^2 for the
   normal); ROBUSTNESS (insensitivity to outliers or model misspecification).

blocks.title: FISHER INFORMATION AND THE CRAMER-RAO BOUND
blocks.formulaBody:
Fisher information (per observation): I(theta) = -E[ d^2 ln f(X; theta)/
   d theta^2 ] = E[ (d ln f/d theta)^2 ].
   CRAMER-RAO LOWER BOUND: any UNBIASED estimator satisfies
        Var(theta_hat) >= 1 / ( n I(theta) ).
   ASYMPTOTIC PROPERTIES OF THE MLE (under regularity conditions):
     - CONSISTENT: theta_hat -> theta.
     - ASYMPTOTICALLY NORMAL: theta_hat approx N( theta, 1/(n I(theta)) ).
     - ASYMPTOTICALLY EFFICIENT: attains the Cramer-Rao bound as n grows.
     - INVARIANT under reparameterization.
   Finite-sample caveats: may be biased (sigma^2 for the normal; the
   uniform maximum); may be hard to compute; sensitive to misspecification.

parts.B:

   d theta^2 ] = E[ (d ln f/d theta)^2 ].

        Var(theta_hat) >= 1 / ( n I(theta) ).

     - INVARIANT under reparameterization.
   Finite-sample caveats: may be biased (sigma^2 for the normal; the
   uniform maximum); may be hard to compute; sensitive to misspecification.
parts.C:
SYMBOLS: I(theta) the information a single observation carries about theta:
   large curvature of the log-likelihood = sharp peak = precise estimate.
parts.D:
CONCEPT: the curvature of l at its peak measures how precisely the data
   pin down theta; its reciprocal is the variance.
parts.E:
CONDITIONS: regularity conditions (smooth model, support independent
   of theta, interior parameter); the bound applies to unbiased
   estimators; asymptotic results need large n.
parts.G:
EXAMPLE (Bernoulli): ln f = x ln p + (1 - x) ln(1 - p); second derivative
   -x/p^2 - (1 - x)/(1 - p)^2; expectation: I(p) = 1/p + 1/(1 - p) =
   1/(p(1 - p)). Bound: Var(p_hat) >= p(1 - p)/n, which the sample proportion
   attains exactly: p_hat is efficient. (n = 100, p = 0.4: SE = 0.049.)
parts.H:
INTERPRETATION: standard error of an MLE = 1/sqrt(n I(theta_hat)); the
   observed information (negative Hessian of l at theta_hat) is used in
   practice (software output of standard errors for logistic regression).
parts.I:
MISTAKES: expecting the MLE to be unbiased; applying asymptotic results
   with tiny n; ignoring that the bound applies to UNBIASED estimators
   only.
parts.J:
RELATED: standard errors of coefficients, Hessian (F12.6), efficiency
   (F37.6).

blocks.title: COMPARISON TABLE: METHOD OF MOMENTS vs MAXIMUM LIKELIHOOD
blocks.rawText:
Aspect               Method of moments           Maximum likelihood
  Principle            match sample and            maximize probability
                       theoretical moments         of observed data
  Needs                moments as functions of     full distribution f(x; theta)
                       parameters
  Closed form          usually easy                often, sometimes not
  Efficiency           often lower                 asymptotically optimal
  Infeasible values    possible (uniform example)  respects the parameter space
  Bias                 can be biased               can be biased (normal variance)
  Computation          solve equations             optimization (Module 43)
  Use                  quick/starting values       standard in practice (GLMs,
                                                   neural net losses)

sections.title: IDENTIFIABILITY

blocks.title: IDENTIFIABILITY
blocks.formulaBody:
a model is IDENTIFIABLE if different parameter values give
   different distributions: f(x; theta_1) = f(x; theta_2) for all x implies
   theta_1 = theta_2. If not, no amount of data can tell the parameters apart.

parts.B:
DEFINITION: a model is IDENTIFIABLE if different parameter values give
   different distributions: f(x; theta_1) = f(x; theta_2) for all x implies
   theta_1 = theta_2. If not, no amount of data can tell the parameters apart.
parts.C:
SYMBOLS: theta_1, theta_2 two parameter values; f(x; theta) the model
   distribution.
parts.D:
CONCEPT: the parameters must have distinct observable consequences. When
   they do not, the likelihood has a flat ridge or several equal peaks and
   the MLE is not unique.
parts.G:
EXAMPLES
   Simple: X ~ N(a + b, sigma^2) with two parameters a and b: only the SUM
      a + b affects the distribution; a and b are NOT separately
      identifiable. Reparameterize with c = a + b (identifiable).
   Moderate 1 (collinearity): regression y = b0 + b1 x1 + b2 x2 where x2 = 2 x1
      exactly: only b1 + 2 b2 is identified; X^T X is singular (Module 8:
      dependent columns, nullity > 0): infinitely many least-squares
      solutions. The "dummy-variable trap" (including all category dummies
      plus an intercept) is the same problem.
   Moderate 2 (label switching): a two-component Gaussian mixture is
      unchanged by swapping the component labels: the labeled parameters
      are not identifiable (fix by ordering the means).
   Moderate 3 (neural networks): permuting hidden units, or scaling
      weights up in one layer and down in the next with ReLU, gives the
      same function: parameters are not identifiable, yet predictions
      are fine (identifiability matters for interpretation, less for
      prediction).
   Moderate 4: Y ~ Poisson(alpha beta): only the product alpha beta is
      identified.
parts.H:
CONSEQUENCES: non-unique MLE; infinite or huge standard errors;
   numerical instability; coefficients that cannot be interpreted.
   PRACTICAL (weak) NON-IDENTIFIABILITY: near-collinear features make
   parameters barely distinguishable and estimates unstable.
   FIXES: reparameterize; add constraints (sum-to-zero, drop a dummy);
   add regularization (ridge shifts eigenvalues, Module 9); collect more
   informative data (vary the inputs); use priors.
parts.I:
MISTAKES: reading individual coefficients of a non-identified model;
   assuming optimization failure when the likelihood is genuinely flat.
parts.J:
RELATED: rank and nullity (Module 8), Hessian singularity (Module 12),
   Fisher information being singular.

BAYESIAN ESTIMATION [SUPPLEMENTARY]: treat theta as random with a PRIOR
p(theta); POSTERIOR p(theta | data) is proportional to L(theta) p(theta)
(Bayes, F34.5). MAP estimate = argmax of the posterior. Example
(Beta-Bernoulli): prior Beta(2, 2); data 7 successes in 20: posterior
Beta(9, 15); posterior mean 9/24 = 0.375; MAP (a + k - 1)/(a + b + n - 2)
= 8/22 = 0.364; MLE 0.35: the prior pulls the estimate toward 0.5
(shrinkage). Gaussian prior on regression coefficients gives ridge
regression; Laplace prior gives lasso.

PYTHON: NUMERICAL MLE
   from scipy import stats, optimize
   x = np.array([1.2, 0.8, 2.5, 0.4, 1.6])
   nll = lambda lam: -np.sum(stats.expon.logpdf(x, scale=1/lam))
   optimize.minimize_scalar(nll, bounds=(1e-3, 10), method="bounded").x
