F38.5  IDENTIFIABILITY
A. NAME: Parameter identifiability.
B. DEFINITION: a model is IDENTIFIABLE if different parameter values give
   different distributions: f(x; theta_1) = f(x; theta_2) for all x implies
   theta_1 = theta_2. If not, no amount of data can tell the parameters apart.
C. SYMBOLS: theta_1, theta_2 two parameter values; f(x; theta) the model
   distribution.
D. CONCEPT: the parameters must have distinct observable consequences. When
   they do not, the likelihood has a flat ridge or several equal peaks and
   the MLE is not unique.
E. CONDITIONS: identifiability can be global or local;
   near-non-identifiability (weak identification) is also harmful in
   practice.
G. EXAMPLES
   Simple: X ~ N(a + b, sigma^2) with two parameters a and b: only the SUM
      a + b affects the distribution; a and b are NOT separately
      identifiable. Reparameterize with c = a + b (identifiable).
   Moderate 1 (collinearity): regression y = b0 + b1 x1 + b2 x2 where x2 = 2 x1
      exactly: only b1 + 2 b2 is identified; X^T X is singular (Module 8:
      dependent columns, nullity > 0): infinitely many least-squares
      solutions. The "dummy-variable trap" (including all category dummies
      plus an intercept) is the same problem.
   Moderate 2 (label switching): a two-component Gaussian mixture is
      unchanged by swapping the component labels: the labeled parameters
      are not identifiable (fix by ordering the means).
   Moderate 3 (neural networks): permuting hidden units, or scaling
      weights up in one layer and down in the next with ReLU, gives the
      same function: parameters are not identifiable, yet predictions
      are fine (identifiability matters for interpretation, less for
      prediction).
   Moderate 4: Y ~ Poisson(alpha beta): only the product alpha beta is
      identified.
H. CONSEQUENCES: non-unique MLE; infinite or huge standard errors;
   numerical instability; coefficients that cannot be interpreted.
   PRACTICAL (weak) NON-IDENTIFIABILITY: near-collinear features make
   parameters barely distinguishable and estimates unstable.
   FIXES: reparameterize; add constraints (sum-to-zero, drop a dummy);
   add regularization (ridge shifts eigenvalues, Module 9); collect more
   informative data (vary the inputs); use priors.
I. MISTAKES: reading individual coefficients of a non-identified model;
   assuming optimization failure when the likelihood is genuinely flat.
J. RELATED: rank and nullity (Module 8), Hessian singularity (Module 12),
   Fisher information being singular.

BAYESIAN ESTIMATION [SUPPLEMENTARY]: treat theta as random with a PRIOR
p(theta); POSTERIOR p(theta | data) is proportional to L(theta) p(theta)
(Bayes, F34.5). MAP estimate = argmax of the posterior. Example
(Beta-Bernoulli): prior Beta(2, 2); data 7 successes in 20: posterior
Beta(9, 15); posterior mean 9/24 = 0.375; MAP (a + k - 1)/(a + b + n - 2)
= 8/22 = 0.364; MLE 0.35: the prior pulls the estimate toward 0.5
(shrinkage). Gaussian prior on regression coefficients gives ridge
regression; Laplace prior gives lasso.

PYTHON: NUMERICAL MLE
   from scipy import stats, optimize
   x = np.array([1.2, 0.8, 2.5, 0.4, 1.6])
   nll = lambda lam: -np.sum(stats.expon.logpdf(x, scale=1/lam))
   optimize.minimize_scalar(nll, bounds=(1e-3, 10), method="bounded").x
   -> 0.7692 (matches 1/x_bar). Library fits: stats.norm.fit(x),
   stats.expon.fit(x, floc=0).

DATA SCIENCE LINK (Modules 37-38): model training = estimating parameters
(MLE or penalized MLE); loss functions are negative log-likelihoods;
standard errors/confidence intervals of coefficients; the Fisher
information matrix underlies natural-gradient methods and Laplace
approximations; identifiability explains unstable coefficients under
multicollinearity.

title: HYPOTHESIS TESTING
introRaw:
BASIC IDEA (plain English)
A hypothesis test is a structured way to ask: "Is what I observed in my
sample surprising enough, if nothing special were going on, that I
should doubt that 'nothing special' explanation?" It is proof by
probabilistic contradiction: assume the boring explanation (the null),
see how unlikely the data would be under it, and reject it if the data
would be too surprising.

sections.title: NULL AND ALTERNATIVE HYPOTHESES

blocks.rawText:
DEFINITIONS
   NULL HYPOTHESIS H0: the default claim to be tested: no effect, no
      difference, parameter equals a specified value (mu = 100,
      p1 = p2, beta = 0). It always contains the "equals" sign.
   ALTERNATIVE HYPOTHESIS H1 (or Ha): what we conclude if the data
      contradict H0: the research claim.
   TWO-SIDED:   H0: mu = mu0   vs   H1: mu != mu0   (any difference)
   ONE-SIDED:   H0: mu = mu0 (or <=) vs H1: mu > mu0 (right-tailed), or
                H1: mu < mu0 (left-tailed).
   The direction of H1 must be chosen BEFORE seeing the data, from the
   question being asked. Choosing a one-sided test after seeing which way
   the data point is cheating (it halves the p-value).
LOGIC OF TESTING
   - We never "prove" H0. The result is either REJECT H0 (evidence against
     it) or FAIL TO REJECT H0 (insufficient evidence). Failing to reject is
     not the same as "H0 is true": the sample may simply be too small.
   - Analogy: a court. H0: "innocent". Evidence insufficient: "not guilty"
     (not "proved innocent").
EXAMPLES
   A machine should fill bottles with 500 ml: H0: mu = 500, H1: mu != 500.
   A new website design should raise the conversion rate above the current
      4%: H0: p = 0.04, H1: p > 0.04.
   A model's mean error is claimed to be at most 10: H0: mu <= 10, H1: mu > 10.
COMMON MISTAKES: putting the claim you hope to prove in H0; writing
hypotheses about SAMPLE statistics (x_bar) instead of PARAMETERS (mu);
choosing the direction after seeing the data.

sections.title: SIGNIFICANCE LEVEL

blocks.title: SIGNIFICANCE LEVEL ALPHA
blocks.formulaBody:
alpha = P(reject H0 | H0 is true) = P(Type I error). It is
   chosen BEFORE the analysis; conventional values 0.05, 0.01, 0.10.
   Decision rule: reject H0 if the test statistic falls in the REJECTION
   (critical) REGION, equivalently if p-value <= alpha.

parts.B:
DEFINITION: alpha = P(reject H0 | H0 is true) = P(Type I error). It is
   chosen BEFORE the analysis; conventional values 0.05, 0.01, 0.10.
   Decision rule: reject H0 if the test statistic falls in the REJECTION
   (critical) REGION, equivalently if p-value <= alpha.
parts.C:
SYMBOLS: alpha the significance level; H0 the null hypothesis;
   'reject' means the test statistic falls in the rejection region.
parts.D:
CONCEPT: alpha is the long-run false-alarm rate we are willing to
   accept when H0 is actually true. Smaller alpha means stricter evidence
   but more Type II errors (missed effects).
parts.E:
CONDITIONS: alpha is a threshold set by the analyst based on the cost of
   false positives (drug approval: small; exploratory screening: larger).
   0.05 is a convention, not a law of nature.
parts.G:
EXAMPLE: alpha = 0.05, two-sided z-test: reject when |z| > 1.96;
   across 100 true null hypotheses about 5 will be rejected by chance.
parts.H: INTERPRETATION: alpha is the false-alarm rate accepted in advance.
parts.I:
MISTAKES: choosing alpha after seeing the p-value; reading alpha as the
   probability that H0 is true; treating 0.05 as a magic boundary.
parts.J:
RELATED: p-value (F39.5), power (F39.6), confidence level 1 - alpha
   (F39.7).

sections.title: TEST STATISTICS

blocks.title: GENERAL FORM OF A TEST STATISTIC
blocks.formulaBody: test statistic = (estimate - value claimed under H0) / (standard error)

parts.B: test statistic = (estimate - value claimed under H0) / (standard error)
parts.C:
SYMBOLS: 'estimate' the sample statistic; 'value under H0' the
   hypothesized value; SE its standard error.
parts.D:
CONCEPT: measures how many standard errors the observed estimate lies from
   what H0 predicts. Its sampling distribution when H0 is true is known
   (normal, t, chi-square, F), which lets us compute probabilities.
parts.E:
CONDITIONS: the null distribution of the statistic must be known
   (normal, t, chi-square, F), which requires the test's assumptions.
parts.G:
EXAMPLE: estimate x_bar = 104, H0: mu = 100, SE = 2.5: statistic =
   (104 - 100)/2.5 = 1.6.
parts.H:
INTERPRETATION: the statistic counts how many standard errors the
   data are from H0.
parts.I:
COMMON MISTAKES: using the sd instead of the SE in the denominator;
   using the wrong null distribution.
parts.J:
RELATED: z-test (F39.3), t-statistic (F39.4), regression t-tests
   (F40.4).

blocks.title: z-TEST FOR A MEAN (sigma known, or large n)
blocks.formulaBody: Z = (x_bar - mu0) / (sigma / sqrt(n))   ~  N(0, 1) when H0: mu = mu0 holds.

parts.B: Z = (x_bar - mu0) / (sigma / sqrt(n))   ~  N(0, 1) when H0: mu = mu0 holds.
parts.C:
SYMBOLS: x_bar sample mean; mu0 hypothesized mean; sigma population sd
   (known); n sample size.
parts.D:
CONCEPT: how many standard errors the sample mean lies from the
   hypothesized mean, assuming the population sd is known.
parts.E:
CONDITIONS: random sample; population normal OR n large (CLT); sigma known
   (rare in practice).
parts.G:
EXAMPLE: H0: mu = 100 vs H1: mu != 100; n = 36, x_bar = 104, sigma = 15.
   SE = 15/6 = 2.5; z = (104 - 100)/2.5 = 1.6. Two-sided p = 2 P(Z >= 1.6)
   = 0.1096 > 0.05: fail to reject. (One-sided p = 0.0548: still above
   0.05.)
parts.H:
INTERPRETATION: z = 1.6 is below 1.96, so the evidence is not strong
   enough at the 5% level.
parts.I:
COMMON MISTAKES: using z when sigma is estimated from a small sample
   (use t); confusing one-sided and two-sided p-values.
parts.J: RELATED: t-test (F39.4), confidence interval (F39.7), CLT (F37.4).

blocks.title: t-STATISTIC (sigma unknown)
blocks.formulaBody:
T = (x_bar - mu0) / (s / sqrt(n))  ~  t with n - 1 degrees of freedom
   under H0 (population normal).

parts.B:
T = (x_bar - mu0) / (s / sqrt(n))  ~  t with n - 1 degrees of freedom
   under H0 (population normal).
parts.C: SYMBOLS: s sample sd; n - 1 the degrees of freedom (df).
parts.D:
CONCEPT: replacing the unknown sigma by s adds extra randomness; the
   Student t distribution has HEAVIER TAILS than the normal to account for
   it. As df grows t approaches N(0, 1).
   Critical values for a two-sided test with alpha = 0.05 (t_(0.975, df)):
        df = 5: 2.571;  9: 2.262;  14: 2.145;  24: 2.064;  29: 2.045;
        100: 1.984;  infinity: 1.960.
   Two-sided 99%: df = 9: 3.250; infinity: 2.576.
parts.E:
CONDITIONS: independent observations; population approximately normal (or n
   large; t is fairly robust except with strong skew or outliers in
   small samples).
parts.H:
INTERPRETATION: T = 2.025 is below the 5% critical value 2.262: not
   significant.
parts.I:
COMMON MISTAKES: using n instead of n - 1 for the degrees of freedom;
   using z critical values with small samples.
parts.J: RELATED: z-statistic (F39.3), t-tests (F39.8), regression (F40.4).

sections.title: p-VALUES

blocks.title: p-VALUE
blocks.formulaBody:
the probability, ASSUMING H0 IS TRUE, of obtaining a test
   statistic at least as extreme as the one observed (in the direction(s) of
   H1).
     right-tailed: p = P(T >= t_obs | H0)
     left-tailed:  p = P(T <= t_obs | H0)
     two-sided:    p = P(|T| >= |t_obs| | H0) = 2 P(T >= |t_obs|) for
                   symmetric distributions.
   Decision: reject H0 if p <= alpha.

parts.B:
DEFINITION: the probability, ASSUMING H0 IS TRUE, of obtaining a test
   statistic at least as extreme as the one observed (in the direction(s) of
   H1).
     right-tailed: p = P(T >= t_obs | H0)
     left-tailed:  p = P(T <= t_obs | H0)
     two-sided:    p = P(|T| >= |t_obs| | H0) = 2 P(T >= |t_obs|) for
                   symmetric distributions.
   Decision: reject H0 if p <= alpha.
parts.C:
SYMBOLS: t_obs the value computed from the data; T the random statistic
   under H0.
parts.D:
CONCEPT: "How surprising are data like these if nothing is going on?" A small
   p means such data would be rare under H0, which is evidence against H0.
parts.E:
CONDITIONS: p-values are valid only if the model/assumptions behind the
   null distribution hold and the test was specified in advance. If H0 is
   true and the test statistic is continuous, p is UNIFORMLY distributed on
   (0, 1): a p-value below 0.05 happens 5% of the time by design
   (simulation with 5,000 t-tests on null data gives 5.1%).
parts.G:
EXAMPLES
   Simple: z = 1.6 (above): p = 2(1 - 0.9452) = 0.1096.
   Moderate: t = 2.025 with df = 9: two-sided p = 0.0735 (software). Since
      2.025 < the critical value 2.262, we fail to reject at 5%; the
      p-value and the critical-value method always agree.
parts.H:
INTERPRETATION: a small p means the data would be unusual if H0 were
   true; it is not a probability about H0.
parts.J:
RELATED: alpha (F39.1), duality with confidence intervals (F39.7),
   multiple testing (section 39.5).
WHAT A p-VALUE IS NOT (the most important list in this module)
   - It is NOT the probability that H0 is true. (p = 0.03 does not mean a 3%
     chance that H0 holds; that needs a prior: Bayes, F34.5.)
   - It is NOT the probability that the result occurred "by chance".
   - It is NOT the probability that a repeat experiment would agree.
   - It is NOT the size or importance of the effect.
   - 1 - p is NOT the probability that H1 is true.
   - A large p does NOT show that H0 is true ("absence of evidence is not
     evidence of absence"; the test may lack power).
   - p-values depend on sample size: with huge n trivial effects get tiny
     p-values.

blocks.rawText:
F39.5  p-VALUE
A. NAME: p-value.
B. DEFINITION: the probability, ASSUMING H0 IS TRUE, of obtaining a test
   statistic at least as extreme as the one observed (in the direction(s) of
   H1).
     right-tailed: p = P(T >= t_obs | H0)
     left-tailed:  p = P(T <= t_obs | H0)
     two-sided:    p = P(|T| >= |t_obs| | H0) = 2 P(T >= |t_obs|) for
                   symmetric distributions.
   Decision: reject H0 if p <= alpha.
C. SYMBOLS: t_obs the value computed from the data; T the random statistic
   under H0.
D. CONCEPT: "How surprising are data like these if nothing is going on?" A small
   p means such data would be rare under H0, which is evidence against H0.
E. CONDITIONS: p-values are valid only if the model/assumptions behind the
   null distribution hold and the test was specified in advance. If H0 is
   true and the test statistic is continuous, p is UNIFORMLY distributed on
   (0, 1): a p-value below 0.05 happens 5% of the time by design
   (simulation with 5,000 t-tests on null data gives 5.1%).
G. EXAMPLES
   Simple: z = 1.6 (above): p = 2(1 - 0.9452) = 0.1096.
   Moderate: t = 2.025 with df = 9: two-sided p = 0.0735 (software). Since
      2.025 < the critical value 2.262, we fail to reject at 5%; the
      p-value and the critical-value method always agree.
H. INTERPRETATION: a small p means the data would be unusual if H0 were
   true; it is not a probability about H0.
I. COMMON MISTAKES: see the list 'What a p-value is not' in this
   section.
J. RELATED: alpha (F39.1), duality with confidence intervals (F39.7),
   multiple testing (section 39.5).
WHAT A p-VALUE IS NOT (the most important list in this module)
   - It is NOT the probability that H0 is true. (p = 0.03 does not mean a 3%
     chance that H0 holds; that needs a prior: Bayes, F34.5.)
   - It is NOT the probability that the result occurred "by chance".
   - It is NOT the probability that a repeat experiment would agree.
   - It is NOT the size or importance of the effect.
   - 1 - p is NOT the probability that H1 is true.
   - A large p does NOT show that H0 is true ("absence of evidence is not
     evidence of absence"; the test may lack power).
   - p-values depend on sample size: with huge n trivial effects get tiny
     p-values.
I. COMMON MISTAKES: the dichotomy p = 0.049 "significant" vs p = 0.051 "not";
   reporting only "p < 0.05" without estimate and interval; p-hacking
   (trying many analyses and reporting the one with p < 0.05);
   one-sided p after peeking.

sections.title: TYPE I AND TYPE II ERRORS; POWER

blocks.rawText:
THE FOUR OUTCOMES
                       Truth: H0 true          Truth: H0 false
   Reject H0           TYPE I ERROR            Correct (power = 1 - beta)
                       (false positive), prob. alpha
   Fail to reject H0   Correct (prob. 1-alpha) TYPE II ERROR
                                               (false negative), prob. beta

blocks.title: ERROR RATES AND POWER
blocks.formulaBody:
alpha = P(reject H0 | H0 true)
   beta  = P(fail to reject H0 | H1 true: a specific alternative)
   POWER = 1 - beta = P(reject H0 | H1 true).
   Power depends on: effect size (true difference delta), population
   variability sigma, sample size n, significance level alpha, and
   one- vs two-sided test. For the one-sided z-test with true mean
   mu1 = mu0 + delta:
       power = P( Z > z_alpha - delta sqrt(n)/sigma ),
   and the sample size for target power 1 - beta is
       n = ( (z_alpha + z_beta) sigma / delta )^2   (one-sided)
       n = ( (z_(alpha/2) + z_beta) sigma / delta )^2   (two-sided).

parts.B:
alpha = P(reject H0 | H0 true)
   beta  = P(fail to reject H0 | H1 true: a specific alternative)
   POWER = 1 - beta = P(reject H0 | H1 true).
   Power depends on: effect size (true difference delta), population
   variability sigma, sample size n, significance level alpha, and
   one- vs two-sided test. For the one-sided z-test with true mean
   mu1 = mu0 + delta:
       power = P( Z > z_alpha - delta sqrt(n)/sigma ),
   and the sample size for target power 1 - beta is
       n = ( (z_alpha + z_beta) sigma / delta )^2   (one-sided)
       n = ( (z_(alpha/2) + z_beta) sigma / delta )^2   (two-sided).
parts.C:
SYMBOLS: z_alpha the upper-alpha point of N(0,1) (1.645 for 0.05; 1.960 for
   alpha/2 = 0.025); z_beta the point for the Type II error (0.8416 for 80%
   power; 1.2816 for 90%).
parts.D:
CONCEPT: alpha controls false alarms when nothing is going on; power is
   the chance to detect a real effect of a given size. Lowering alpha
   (stricter) lowers power unless n grows; more data, bigger effects,
   less noise all raise power.
parts.E:
CONDITIONS: power is computed for a specific alternative; the
   formulas shown are for the z-test with known sigma (approximate for
   t-tests).
parts.G:
EXAMPLE (power): H0: mu = 100 vs H1: mu > 100; sigma = 15, n = 36, alpha =
   0.05 (one-sided). Reject when x_bar > 100 + 1.645 * 2.5 = 104.11.
   If the TRUE mean is 105 (delta = 5): power = P(x_bar > 104.11 | mu = 105)
   = P(Z > (104.11 - 105)/2.5 = -0.355) = 0.639. So there is only a 64%
   chance to detect a 5-point effect; beta = 0.361.
   SAMPLE SIZE for 80% power (delta = 5, sigma = 15): one-sided
   n = ((1.645 + 0.8416) * 15/5)^2 = (7.46)^2 = 55.6 -> 56 (two-sided,
   alpha = 0.05: ((1.96 + 0.8416) * 3)^2 = 70.6 -> 71).
parts.H:
INTERPRETATION: an underpowered study (low power) rarely finds real effects
   and, when it does find "significant" ones, tends to overestimate them.
   Plan sample size BEFORE collecting data (power analysis).
parts.I:
MISTAKES: calling "not significant" a proof of no effect in a low-power
   study; confusing alpha with beta or with power; computing "post-hoc
   power" from the observed p-value (uninformative).
parts.J:
RELATED: sample size and CI width (F39.7), Type I and II errors
   (table above).
MULTIPLE TESTING: testing m independent true nulls at alpha = 0.05 each gives
P(at least one false positive) = 1 - 0.95^m: m = 20 gives 64%.
   Bonferroni: use alpha/m per test (0.0025 for 20 tests); Benjamini-
   Hochberg controls the false discovery rate (less conservative). Data
   science: testing hundreds of features, many model variants or many
   A/B segments inflates false positives; use corrections or hold-out
   confirmation.

blocks.title: COMPARISON TABLE: TYPE I vs TYPE II ERROR
blocks.rawText:
Aspect         Type I                      Type II
  Meaning        reject a TRUE H0            fail to reject a FALSE H0
  Also called    false positive, false alarm false negative, miss
  Probability    alpha (set by analyst)      beta (depends on effect, n, alpha)
  Control        choose alpha                increase n, effect, reduce noise
  Trade-off      lowering alpha raises beta (for fixed n)
  Example        declaring a useless drug    missing a useful drug
                 effective                   (confirming it is "no different")
  ML analog      false positive rate         false negative rate (1 - recall)

sections.title: CONFIDENCE INTERVALS

blocks.title: CONFIDENCE INTERVAL FOR A MEAN
blocks.formulaBody:
sigma known (or large n):   x_bar +/- z_(alpha/2) * sigma/sqrt(n)
     sigma unknown:              x_bar +/- t_(alpha/2, n-1) * s/sqrt(n)
     General:  estimate +/- critical value x standard error;
     the quantity "critical value x SE" is the MARGIN OF ERROR E.
     Proportion (large-sample, Wald): p_hat +/- z_(alpha/2) sqrt(p_hat (1 - p_hat)/n).
     Sample size for a margin E (mean): n = (z_(alpha/2) sigma / E)^2;
        (proportion, worst case p = 0.5): n = z^2 * 0.25/E^2.

parts.A: NAME: Confidence interval (CI) for a population mean.
parts.B:
FORMULAS
     sigma known (or large n):   x_bar +/- z_(alpha/2) * sigma/sqrt(n)
     sigma unknown:              x_bar +/- t_(alpha/2, n-1) * s/sqrt(n)
     General:  estimate +/- critical value x standard error;
     the quantity "critical value x SE" is the MARGIN OF ERROR E.
     Proportion (large-sample, Wald): p_hat +/- z_(alpha/2) sqrt(p_hat (1 - p_hat)/n).
     Sample size for a margin E (mean): n = (z_(alpha/2) sigma / E)^2;
        (proportion, worst case p = 0.5): n = z^2 * 0.25/E^2.
parts.C:
SYMBOLS: confidence level 1 - alpha (e.g. 95%); t_(alpha/2, n-1) the upper
   alpha/2 point of t with n - 1 df; SE the standard error (F37.8).
parts.D:
CONCEPT: a range of plausible parameter values. The "95%" describes the
   PROCEDURE: if you repeated the sampling many times and built an interval
   each time, about 95% of those intervals would contain the true
   parameter.
parts.E:
CONDITIONS: same as the corresponding test (random sample, near-normal
   or large n). Wald proportion intervals need n p_hat >= 10 and
   n(1 - p_hat) >= 10; otherwise use Wilson or exact methods.
parts.H:
INTERPRETATION: width shrinks like 1/sqrt(n), grows with s and with the
   confidence level (99% is wider than 95%). The interval conveys effect
   size AND uncertainty; it is more informative than a bare p-value.
   CORRECT: "We are 95% confident that mu lies between 47.87 and 56.13 (the
   method captures the truth in 95% of repetitions)."
   INCORRECT (frequentist): "there is a 95% probability that mu lies in this
   particular interval" (mu is fixed; the interval is the random object
   before data are collected). A Bayesian credible interval does have
   that probability interpretation, under a prior.
   DUALITY WITH TESTS: a two-sided test of H0: mu = mu0 at level alpha rejects
   exactly when mu0 lies OUTSIDE the (1 - alpha) CI. In the example above,
   H0: mu = 12 is NOT rejected because 12 lies inside (11.973, 12.487).
parts.I:
MISTAKES: reading 95% as the proportion of DATA inside the interval (that
   is a prediction interval, much wider); comparing two CIs for overlap as
   a substitute for testing the difference (overlap is not a reliable test);
   using z instead of t for small n; applying Wald proportions to tiny
   counts.
parts.J:
RELATED: duality with tests (this section), standard error (F37.8),
   prediction intervals (F40.5).

G. EXAMPLES

      CI = 52 +/- 4.13 = (47.87, 56.13).
   Moderate 1 (from data): sample 12.1, 11.8, 12.6, 12.3, 11.9, 12.8, 12.2,
      12.5, 11.7, 12.4 (n = 10): x_bar = 12.23, s = 0.359, SE = 0.1136,

   Moderate 2 (proportion): p_hat = 0.40, n = 100: margin = 1.96 * 0.049 =
      0.096: CI = (0.304, 0.496).

      at 95%: n = (1.96 * 15/3)^2 = 96.04 -> 97.

   exactly when mu0 lies OUTSIDE the (1 - alpha) CI. In the example above,

   INCORRECT (frequentist): "there is a 95% probability that mu lies in this
   particular interval" (mu is fixed; the interval is the random object
   before data are collected). A Bayesian credible interval does have
   that probability interpretation, under a prior.
   DUALITY WITH TESTS: a two-sided test of H0: mu = mu0 at level alpha rejects
   exactly when mu0 lies OUTSIDE the (1 - alpha) CI. In the example above,
   H0: mu = 12 is NOT rejected because 12 lies inside (11.973, 12.487).
I. MISTAKES: reading 95% as the proportion of DATA inside the interval (that
   is a prediction interval, much wider); comparing two CIs for overlap as
   a substitute for testing the difference (overlap is not a reliable test);
   using z instead of t for small n; applying Wald proportions to tiny
   counts.
J. RELATED: duality with tests (this section), standard error (F37.8),
   prediction intervals (F40.5).

sections.title: t-TESTS

blocks.title: THE THREE t-TESTS
blocks.formulaBody:
TWO-SAMPLE (INDEPENDENT-GROUPS) t-TEST: compares two means from separate,
   unrelated groups. H0: mu_1 = mu_2.
     WELCH (unequal variances allowed; the safe default):
        T = (x_bar_1 - x_bar_2) / sqrt( s_1^2/n_1 + s_2^2/n_2 ),
        df from the Welch-Satterthwaite formula (non-integer).
     POOLED (assumes equal variances):
        T = (x_bar_1 - x_bar_2) / ( s_p sqrt(1/n_1 + 1/n_2) ),
        s_p^2 = ((n_1 - 1) s_1^2 + (n_2 - 1) s_2^2)/(n_1 + n_2 - 2),
        df = n_1 + n_2 - 2.

parts.A:
ONE-SAMPLE t-TEST: compares a mean with a fixed value.
     H0: mu = mu0.  T = (x_bar - mu0)/(s/sqrt(n)),  df = n - 1.
parts.B:
TWO-SAMPLE (INDEPENDENT-GROUPS) t-TEST: compares two means from separate,
   unrelated groups. H0: mu_1 = mu_2.
     WELCH (unequal variances allowed; the safe default):
        T = (x_bar_1 - x_bar_2) / sqrt( s_1^2/n_1 + s_2^2/n_2 ),
        df from the Welch-Satterthwaite formula (non-integer).
     POOLED (assumes equal variances):
        T = (x_bar_1 - x_bar_2) / ( s_p sqrt(1/n_1 + 1/n_2) ),
        s_p^2 = ((n_1 - 1) s_1^2 + (n_2 - 1) s_2^2)/(n_1 + n_2 - 2),
        df = n_1 + n_2 - 2.
parts.C:
PAIRED t-TEST: compares two measurements on the SAME units (before/after,
   matched pairs). Compute differences d_i = after_i - before_i, then do a
   one-sample t-test on the d_i with H0: mu_d = 0:
        T = d_bar / (s_d/sqrt(n)),  df = n - 1.
parts.D:
CONCEPT: all three divide an estimated difference by its standard error.
   Pairing removes between-subject variability and is usually far more
   powerful when the pairs are correlated.
parts.E:
CONDITIONS: see 39.8. CHOOSE the test by the DESIGN: same units measured
   twice -> paired; two separate groups -> two-sample.
parts.G:
WORKED EXAMPLES
   (1) ONE-SAMPLE: data in 39.6 (n = 10, x_bar = 12.23, s = 0.359).
       H0: mu = 12 vs H1: mu != 12, alpha = 0.05.
       T = (12.23 - 12)/0.1136 = 2.025, df = 9, p = 0.0735. Since p > 0.05
       (and |T| < 2.262) we FAIL TO REJECT H0: no convincing evidence that
       the mean differs from 12 (the 95% CI (11.97, 12.49) contains 12).
   (2) WELCH TWO-SAMPLE: group A (n = 8): 23, 25, 21, 27, 24, 26, 22, 25 ->
       mean 24.125, s^2 = 4.125. Group B (n = 8): 20, 22, 19, 24, 21, 23, 20,
       22 -> mean 21.375, s^2 = 2.839.
       Difference = 2.75. SE = sqrt(4.125/8 + 2.839/8) = sqrt(0.8705) = 0.933.
       T = 2.75/0.933 = 2.947; Welch df = 13.5; p = 0.0109 -> REJECT H0 at 5%:
       evidence that the means differ.
       (Pooled version: same T because n_1 = n_2; df = 14; p = 0.0106.)
       Effect size: Cohen's d = 2.75/s_p = 2.75/1.866 = 1.47 (large).
       95% CI for the difference: 2.75 +/- t_(0.975, 13.5) * 0.933 = 2.75 +/- 2.0
       -> about (0.75, 4.75).
   (3) PAIRED: 6 subjects' scores before: 80, 85, 90, 78, 92, 88; after: 75,
       83, 86, 79, 87, 84. Differences (after - before): -5, -2, -4, 1, -5,
       -4. d_bar = -3.167, s_d = 2.317, SE = 2.317/sqrt(6) = 0.946.
       T = -3.167/0.946 = -3.348, df = 5, p = 0.0204 < 0.05: REJECT H0: the
       scores dropped by about 3.2 points on average (95% CI: -3.167 +/-
       2.571 * 0.946 = (-5.60, -0.73)).
       (Treating these as independent groups would ignore the pairing and
       give a much larger SE: the paired test is the right one here.)
parts.H:
INTERPRETATION: report the estimate, CI, effect size and p-value together
   ("scores fell by 3.2 points, 95% CI 0.7 to 5.6, p = 0.02").
parts.I:
COMMON MISTAKES: using an independent test on paired data (or vice
   versa); using the pooled test with very unequal variances and unequal
   sample sizes; dropping the sign when interpreting direction; deciding
   the test after seeing the results; running t-tests on many features
   without correction.
parts.J:
RELATED: z-test, ANOVA (more than two groups), chi-square tests for
   categorical data [SUPPLEMENTARY], nonparametric alternatives: Wilcoxon
   signed-rank (paired/one-sample), Mann-Whitney U (two independent
   groups), permutation tests.

sections.title: ASSUMPTIONS OF STATISTICAL TESTS

blocks.rawText:
Every test is valid only under assumptions. Know them, check them, and
know which violations are serious.
  ASSUMPTION                     WHY IT MATTERS / HOW TO CHECK / REMEDY
  Random sampling or randomized  Inference to a population needs it; bias
  assignment                     cannot be fixed by n. Check design.
  INDEPENDENCE of observations   MOST critical. Repeated measures on the same
                                 person, clusters, time series, or duplicated
                                 rows make SEs too small and p-values too
                                 low (pseudo-replication; Type I inflated).
                                 Remedy: paired/mixed models, clustered SEs,
                                 aggregate to the independent unit.
  Normality (t-tests)            Of the population for small n; for large n
                                 the CLT makes the mean nearly normal. Check
                                 histogram/Q-Q plot, never rely only on a
                                 Shapiro-Wilk p-value (with large n it flags
                                 trivial deviations; with small n has no
                                 power). Remedy: transform, nonparametric
                                 test, bootstrap, larger n.
  Equal variances (pooled t,     Check ratio of sds (> 2 suspicious); remedy:
  ANOVA)                         Welch.
  Measurement scale              Means need interval/ratio data; ordinal data
                                 (Likert) often use rank tests.
  No extreme outliers            Inflate s and distort x_bar; investigate, use
                                 robust methods.
  Adequate sample size           Large-sample z and Wald methods need n large;
                                 small samples need exact methods.
  Pre-specified analysis         Choose hypotheses, test and alpha before
                                 looking; avoid p-hacking, optional stopping.
ROBUSTNESS SUMMARY: t-tests tolerate mild non-normality (especially with
equal n and symmetric data); they are NOT robust to non-independence,
and moderately sensitive to outliers/heavy skew with small n; Welch is
robust to unequal variances.

sections.title: INTERPRETATION OF STATISTICAL SIGNIFICANCE

blocks.rawText:
KEY PRINCIPLES
   1. STATISTICAL SIGNIFICANCE != PRACTICAL IMPORTANCE.
      Significance says the effect is unlikely to be exactly zero; it says
      nothing about whether it is large or useful.
      Example: two groups each of 1,000,000 observations; true difference of
      0.01 standard deviations (d = 0.01). The test statistic is about
      z = d sqrt(n/2) = 0.01 * 707 = 7.07, p approx 1.5 x 10^-12: "highly
      significant" yet practically nil. With n = 20 per group a real,
      important effect of d = 0.5 may not reach significance (power about
      34%).
   2. NOT SIGNIFICANT != NO EFFECT. Report the CI: a wide interval
      containing both zero and important values means "inconclusive".
   3. EFFECT SIZES give magnitude: raw difference in natural units;
      Cohen's d = (x_bar_1 - x_bar_2)/s_p (rough benchmarks 0.2 small,
      0.5 medium, 0.8 large; context matters); r or R^2; odds ratios.
   4. The difference between "significant" and "not significant" is not
      itself statistically significant (comparing two p-values is not a
      test of the difference).
   5. ALPHA = 0.05 is a convention; consider costs of errors; avoid
      treating p = 0.049 and p = 0.051 differently.
   6. MULTIPLE COMPARISONS and the garden of forking paths inflate false
      positives; pre-register or hold out data; adjust.
   7. REPLICATION and prior plausibility matter: a surprising result with p =
      0.03 has a high chance of being a false positive (Bayes: low prior
      probability of a true effect).
   8. Report: estimate, CI, effect size, test, df, exact p-value, n, and
      assumption checks. The American Statistical Association (2016)
      statement: a p-value does not measure the probability that the
      studied hypothesis is true, and scientific conclusions should not
      be based only on whether p passes a threshold.
STEP-BY-STEP CHECKLIST FOR A TEST
   1. State H0 and H1 (parameters, direction) and alpha before the data.
   2. Choose the test from the design and data type.
   3. Check assumptions (independence first).
   4. Compute the statistic, df, p-value, and the CI/effect size.
   5. Decide (reject / fail to reject) and state it in context, in words.
   6. Discuss limitations (power, bias, multiplicity).
DATA SCIENCE LINKS
   - A/B testing: two-proportion z-test or Welch t-test on a metric;
     pre-compute sample size from power analysis; do not stop the moment
     p < 0.05 (optional stopping inflates Type I error); use corrections
     for many metrics/segments.
   - Comparing models: cross-validation folds are NOT independent (they share
     training data); use corrected paired t-tests, repeated CV with
     corrections, or McNemar's test on the same test set.
   - Feature screening with hundreds of tests: control the false discovery
     rate.
   - A statistically significant improvement of 0.001 in AUC may be
     practically irrelevant.
   - Regression coefficients: t-test of H0: beta_j = 0 (Module 40).
   - Drift detection: KS test or chi-square tests on feature distributions;
     with huge data everything is "significant": use effect sizes.

title: LINEAR REGRESSION
introRaw:
BASIC IDEA (plain English)
Regression models how the AVERAGE value of an outcome y changes with
one or more predictors x. Linear regression assumes the average changes
in a straight-line (linear) way and finds the line (or plane) that
fits the data best in the least-squares sense. It is the workhorse of
statistics and the foundation of many machine learning methods.

blocks.title: THE SIMPLE LINEAR REGRESSION MODEL
blocks.formulaBody:
Population model:   y_i = beta_0 + beta_1 x_i + eps_i,   i = 1..n
        with errors eps_i independent, E[eps_i] = 0, Var(eps_i) = sigma^2
        (and, for exact small-sample inference, eps_i ~ N(0, sigma^2)).
     Fitted (regression) line:  y_hat = b_0 + b_1 x

parts.A: NAME: Simple linear regression model (one predictor).
parts.B:
FORMULA

        with errors eps_i independent, E[eps_i] = 0, Var(eps_i) = sigma^2
        (and, for exact small-sample inference, eps_i ~ N(0, sigma^2)).

parts.C:
SYMBOLS

   x_i      predictor (independent variable, feature, regressor).
   beta_0   INTERCEPT (population): mean of y when x = 0.
   beta_1   SLOPE (population): change in the mean of y per 1-unit increase
            in x.
   eps_i    error term: everything else affecting y (unmodeled factors,
            noise).
   b_0, b_1 ESTIMATES of beta_0, beta_1 from data (also written beta_hat).
   y_hat_i  fitted value (prediction) for observation i.
parts.D:
CONCEPT: the model says E[y | x] = beta_0 + beta_1 x: the conditional mean is a
   straight line; individual y values scatter around it with constant
   spread sigma.
parts.E:
CONDITIONS: see 40.7 (assumptions). Regression describes the average
   relationship; it does not by itself say that x causes y (40.9).
parts.G:
EXAMPLE: the study-hours data are modeled as score = beta_0 + beta_1
   hours + eps; the fit gives 46.86 + 4.476 hours (next formula).
parts.H:
INTERPRETATION: the line gives the mean of y for each x; the residual
   scatter is sigma.
parts.I:
COMMON MISTAKES: treating the error eps and the residual e as the
   same thing; forgetting that the model is about the conditional mean.

   Gaussian errors (F38.3).

blocks.title: LEAST SQUARES ESTIMATES FOR SIMPLE REGRESSION
blocks.formulaBody:
Choose b_0, b_1 to minimize  SSE = sum (y_i - b_0 - b_1 x_i)^2.
     b_1 = sum (x_i - x_bar)(y_i - y_bar) / sum (x_i - x_bar)^2 = S_xy/S_xx
         = r * s_y / s_x
     b_0 = y_bar - b_1 x_bar
     Residual standard error (estimate of sigma):
        sigma_hat = s_e = sqrt( SSE/(n - 2) ),   MSE = SSE/(n - 2).

parts.B:
FORMULAS
     Choose b_0, b_1 to minimize  SSE = sum (y_i - b_0 - b_1 x_i)^2.
     b_1 = sum (x_i - x_bar)(y_i - y_bar) / sum (x_i - x_bar)^2 = S_xy/S_xx
         = r * s_y / s_x
     b_0 = y_bar - b_1 x_bar
     Residual standard error (estimate of sigma):
        sigma_hat = s_e = sqrt( SSE/(n - 2) ),   MSE = SSE/(n - 2).
parts.D:
CONCEPT: the line that makes the total squared vertical distance from the
   points as small as possible. Slope = correlation rescaled by the ratio
   of spreads, so a positive correlation gives a positive slope. The
   line always passes through the center of the data (x_bar, y_bar).
parts.E:
CONDITIONS: needs variation in x (S_xx > 0); outliers and leverage points
   strongly affect it.
parts.F:
DERIVATION (calculus, Module 12): SSE(b_0, b_1) is a quadratic bowl.
     dSSE/db_0 = -2 sum (y_i - b_0 - b_1 x_i) = 0  ->  sum e_i = 0
        ->  b_0 = y_bar - b_1 x_bar.
     dSSE/db_1 = -2 sum x_i (y_i - b_0 - b_1 x_i) = 0  ->  sum x_i e_i = 0.
   Substituting b_0 into the second equation and solving gives b_1 = S_xy/S_xx.
   These are the NORMAL EQUATIONS (matrix form in 40.2).
parts.G:
WORKED EXAMPLE (hours studied vs exam score)
   x (hours): 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8
   y (score): 52, 55, 61, 64, 70, 72, 79, 83
   x_bar = 4.5, y_bar = 67. S_xx = 42, S_xy = 188.
   b_1 = 188/42 = 4.476;  b_0 = 67 - 4.476 * 4.5 = 46.857.
   Fitted line: score = 46.86 + 4.476 * hours.
   Fitted values: 51.33, 55.81, 60.29, 64.76, 69.24, 73.71, 78.19, 82.67.
   Residuals (y - y_hat): 0.667, -0.810, 0.714, -0.762, 0.762, -1.714, 0.810,
   0.333. They sum to 0 and are orthogonal to x (sum x e = 0).
   SSE = 6.476; SST = sum (y - 67)^2 = 848; SSR = SST - SSE = 841.52.
   Residual standard error = sqrt(6.476/6) = 1.039 points.
parts.H:
INTERPRETATION
   Slope: each additional hour of study is associated with an average
   increase of about 4.5 points in the score (within the observed range 1-8
   hours).
   Intercept: predicted score at 0 hours is 46.9. (Meaningful only if
   x = 0 is within or near the data; otherwise it is just a positioning
   constant: e.g. regressing weight on height gives an "intercept" for
   height 0 which is nonsense. Centering x makes the intercept the
   prediction at the mean.)
   Residual sd 1.04: typical prediction errors are about 1 point.
parts.I:
COMMON MISTAKES: interpreting the slope as causal; extrapolating beyond
   the data (see 40.2); interpreting the intercept literally; mixing up y
   on x with x on y (the two regression lines are different unless r = +/-
   1: b_1(y on x) = r s_y/s_x but b_1(x on y) = r s_x/s_y); reversing the
   order of x and y in S_xy/S_xx.
parts.J: RELATED: correlation r (F32.2): r^2 = R^2 here; least squares (F10.5).

blocks.title: GOODNESS OF FIT: SST, SSR, SSE AND R^2
blocks.formulaBody:
SST = sum (y_i - y_bar)^2   (total variation)
   SSR = sum (y_hat_i - y_bar)^2 (variation explained by the regression)
   SSE = sum (y_i - y_hat_i)^2   (unexplained variation)
   SST = SSR + SSE   (holds for OLS with an intercept)
   R^2 = SSR/SST = 1 - SSE/SST  (coefficient of determination)
   Simple regression: R^2 = r^2.
   Multiple regression: ADJUSTED R^2 = 1 - (1 - R^2)(n - 1)/(n - p - 1),
      with p predictors.

parts.B:
SST = sum (y_i - y_bar)^2   (total variation)
   SSR = sum (y_hat_i - y_bar)^2 (variation explained by the regression)
   SSE = sum (y_i - y_hat_i)^2   (unexplained variation)
   SST = SSR + SSE   (holds for OLS with an intercept)
   R^2 = SSR/SST = 1 - SSE/SST  (coefficient of determination)
   Simple regression: R^2 = r^2.
   Multiple regression: ADJUSTED R^2 = 1 - (1 - R^2)(n - 1)/(n - p - 1),
      with p predictors.
parts.C:
SYMBOLS: y_i the observations; y_bar their mean; y_hat_i the fitted
   values; p the number of predictors.
parts.D:
CONCEPT: R^2 is the proportion of the variance of y accounted for by the
   model (relative to predicting y_bar always). Adding any predictor never
   decreases R^2, so adjusted R^2 penalizes needless predictors.
parts.E:
CONDITIONS: SST = SSR + SSE requires OLS with an intercept; R^2 can
   be negative for predictions on new data.
parts.G:
EXAMPLE: R^2 = 841.52/848 = 0.9924: the model explains 99.2% of the
   variation in scores (r = 0.9962).
parts.H:
INTERPRETATION: R^2 = 0.9924 means that 99.2% of the variance of y is
   explained by the model.
parts.I:
MISTAKES: "high R^2 means a correct/causal model" (no); "low R^2 means
   the model is useless" (in noisy social data R^2 = 0.1 can still be
   informative; the slope may be well determined); comparing R^2 across
   different response transformations; using training R^2 as evidence of
   predictive performance (use held-out data, Module 46); forgetting that
   R^2 can be negative on test data.
parts.J:
RELATED: correlation (F32.2), adjusted R^2, F-test, test-set R^2
   (F46.6).

blocks.title: INFERENCE FOR THE SLOPE AND INTERCEPT

parts.C:
SYMBOLS: sigma_hat the residual standard error; SE the standard error of
   the estimate (F37.8).
parts.D:
CONCEPT: the slope estimate varies from sample to sample; its
   standard error shrinks when there is more data, more spread in x
   (larger S_xx), or less noise (smaller sigma_hat). Spreading the x
   values widely is the best way to pin down the slope.
parts.E:
CONDITIONS: the assumptions of 40.7 (normal errors for exact t inference;
   otherwise approximate by the CLT).
parts.H:
INTERPRETATION: "an extra hour of study is associated with 4.1 to 4.9 more
   points (95% CI)".
parts.I:
MISTAKES: reading a small p-value for the slope as a large effect or good
   prediction; confusing the p-value of the slope with the overall
   goodness of fit; ignoring the CI.
parts.J:
RELATED: standard error (F37.8), t-tests (F39.4), confidence
   intervals (F39.7), multiple regression (F40.6).

blocks.rawText:
F40.4  INFERENCE FOR THE SLOPE AND INTERCEPT
B. SE(b_1) = sigma_hat / sqrt(S_xx);
   SE(b_0) = sigma_hat sqrt( 1/n + x_bar^2/S_xx );
   t-statistic for H0: beta_j = 0:  t = b_j / SE(b_j) ~ t_(n - 2) under H0;
   (1 - alpha) CI: b_j +/- t_(alpha/2, n - 2) SE(b_j).
   Overall F-test (simple regression): F = t^2 = MSR/MSE with (1, n - 2) df.
C. SYMBOLS: sigma_hat the residual standard error; SE the standard error of
   the estimate (F37.8).
D. CONCEPT: the slope estimate varies from sample to sample; its
   standard error shrinks when there is more data, more spread in x
   (larger S_xx), or less noise (smaller sigma_hat). Spreading the x
   values widely is the best way to pin down the slope.
E. CONDITIONS: the assumptions of 40.7 (normal errors for exact t inference;
   otherwise approximate by the CLT).
G. EXAMPLE (study data): sigma_hat = 1.039, S_xx = 42:
   SE(b_1) = 1.039/sqrt(42) = 0.1603; t = 4.476/0.1603 = 27.92 with 6 df,
   p = 1.4 x 10^-7: very strong evidence that the slope is not 0.
   95% CI for beta_1: 4.476 +/- 2.447 * 0.1603 = (4.08, 4.87).
   SE(b_0) = 1.039 * sqrt(1/8 + 20.25/42) = 0.810; t = 57.9.
H. INTERPRETATION: "an extra hour of study is associated with 4.1 to 4.9 more
   points (95% CI)".
I. MISTAKES: reading a small p-value for the slope as a large effect or good
   prediction; confusing the p-value of the slope with the overall
   goodness of fit; ignoring the CI.
J. RELATED: standard error (F37.8), t-tests (F39.4), confidence
   intervals (F39.7), multiple regression (F40.6).

blocks.title: PREDICTION: MEAN RESPONSE vs NEW OBSERVATION
blocks.formulaBody:
At predictor value x_0: y_hat_0 = b_0 + b_1 x_0.
   CI for the MEAN response E[y | x_0]:
       y_hat_0 +/- t * sigma_hat sqrt( 1/n + (x_0 - x_bar)^2/S_xx ).
   PREDICTION INTERVAL for a NEW individual observation:
       y_hat_0 +/- t * sigma_hat sqrt( 1 + 1/n + (x_0 - x_bar)^2/S_xx ).

parts.B:
At predictor value x_0: y_hat_0 = b_0 + b_1 x_0.
   CI for the MEAN response E[y | x_0]:
       y_hat_0 +/- t * sigma_hat sqrt( 1/n + (x_0 - x_bar)^2/S_xx ).
   PREDICTION INTERVAL for a NEW individual observation:
       y_hat_0 +/- t * sigma_hat sqrt( 1 + 1/n + (x_0 - x_bar)^2/S_xx ).
parts.D:
CONCEPT: the mean can be pinned down precisely with enough data, but a new
   single observation still carries its own noise sigma^2 (the extra "1"
   inside the square root), so prediction intervals are wider and do not
   shrink to zero with n. Both widen as x_0 moves away from x_bar.
parts.E:
CONDITIONS: assumes the model assumptions of section 40.7;
   extrapolation voids the guarantee.
parts.G:
EXAMPLE (study data) at x_0 = 5.5 hours: y_hat = 46.857 + 4.476 * 5.5 = 71.48.
   95% CI for the mean score: 71.48 +/- 2.447 * 0.4008 = (70.50, 72.46).
   95% prediction interval for one student: 71.48 +/- 2.447 * 1.1135 =
   (68.75, 74.20).
   EXTRAPOLATION WARNING: at x_0 = 12 hours (outside 1-8) the line predicts
   100.57 points (> 100: impossible!) with the PI center at an
   unreliable location; the linear relationship probably saturates.
parts.H:
INTERPRETATION: the CI says where the AVERAGE response lies; the PI
   says where a SINGLE new observation will fall.
parts.I:
MISTAKES: using the CI for the mean when a prediction for one case is
   needed; extrapolating; reporting the prediction without uncertainty.
   (Note: the standard prediction interval assumes normal, constant-
   variance errors.)
parts.J:
RELATED: standard error (F37.8), leverage (F40.7), CI versus PI table
   (Appendix A).

     b_0 = y_bar - b_1 x_bar
     Residual standard error (estimate of sigma):
        sigma_hat = s_e = sqrt( SSE/(n - 2) ),   MSE = SSE/(n - 2).
C. SYMBOLS: S_xx = sum (x_i - x_bar)^2; S_xy = sum (x_i - x_bar)(y_i - y_bar);
   r the correlation (Module 32); s_x, s_y sample SDs; n - 2 degrees of
   freedom (two parameters estimated).
D. CONCEPT: the line that makes the total squared vertical distance from the
   points as small as possible. Slope = correlation rescaled by the ratio
   of spreads, so a positive correlation gives a positive slope. The
   line always passes through the center of the data (x_bar, y_bar).
E. CONDITIONS: needs variation in x (S_xx > 0); outliers and leverage points
   strongly affect it.
F. DERIVATION (calculus, Module 12): SSE(b_0, b_1) is a quadratic bowl.
     dSSE/db_0 = -2 sum (y_i - b_0 - b_1 x_i) = 0  ->  sum e_i = 0
        ->  b_0 = y_bar - b_1 x_bar.
     dSSE/db_1 = -2 sum x_i (y_i - b_0 - b_1 x_i) = 0  ->  sum x_i e_i = 0.
   Substituting b_0 into the second equation and solving gives b_1 = S_xy/S_xx.
   These are the NORMAL EQUATIONS (matrix form in 40.2).
G. WORKED EXAMPLE (hours studied vs exam score)
   x (hours): 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8
   y (score): 52, 55, 61, 64, 70, 72, 79, 83
   x_bar = 4.5, y_bar = 67. S_xx = 42, S_xy = 188.
   b_1 = 188/42 = 4.476;  b_0 = 67 - 4.476 * 4.5 = 46.857.
   Fitted line: score = 46.86 + 4.476 * hours.
   Fitted values: 51.33, 55.81, 60.29, 64.76, 69.24, 73.71, 78.19, 82.67.
   Residuals (y - y_hat): 0.667, -0.810, 0.714, -0.762, 0.762, -1.714, 0.810,
   0.333. They sum to 0 and are orthogonal to x (sum x e = 0).
   SSE = 6.476; SST = sum (y - 67)^2 = 848; SSR = SST - SSE = 841.52.
   Residual standard error = sqrt(6.476/6) = 1.039 points.
H. INTERPRETATION
   Slope: each additional hour of study is associated with an average
   increase of about 4.5 points in the score (within the observed range 1-8
   hours).
   Intercept: predicted score at 0 hours is 46.9. (Meaningful only if
   x = 0 is within or near the data; otherwise it is just a positioning
   constant: e.g. regressing weight on height gives an "intercept" for
   height 0 which is nonsense. Centering x makes the intercept the
   prediction at the mean.)
   Residual sd 1.04: typical prediction errors are about 1 point.
I. COMMON MISTAKES: interpreting the slope as causal; extrapolating beyond
   the data (see 40.2); interpreting the intercept literally; mixing up y
   on x with x on y (the two regression lines are different unless r = +/-
   1: b_1(y on x) = r s_y/s_x but b_1(x on y) = r s_x/s_y); reversing the
   order of x and y in S_xy/S_xx.
J. RELATED: correlation r (F32.2): r^2 = R^2 here; least squares (F10.5).

F40.3  GOODNESS OF FIT: SST, SSR, SSE AND R^2
B. SST = sum (y_i - y_bar)^2   (total variation)
   SSR = sum (y_hat_i - y_bar)^2 (variation explained by the regression)
   SSE = sum (y_i - y_hat_i)^2   (unexplained variation)
   SST = SSR + SSE   (holds for OLS with an intercept)
   R^2 = SSR/SST = 1 - SSE/SST  (coefficient of determination)
   Simple regression: R^2 = r^2.
   Multiple regression: ADJUSTED R^2 = 1 - (1 - R^2)(n - 1)/(n - p - 1),
      with p predictors.
C. SYMBOLS: y_i the observations; y_bar their mean; y_hat_i the fitted
   values; p the number of predictors.
D. CONCEPT: R^2 is the proportion of the variance of y accounted for by the
   model (relative to predicting y_bar always). Adding any predictor never
   decreases R^2, so adjusted R^2 penalizes needless predictors.
E. CONDITIONS: SST = SSR + SSE requires OLS with an intercept; R^2 can
   be negative for predictions on new data.
G. EXAMPLE: R^2 = 841.52/848 = 0.9924: the model explains 99.2% of the
   variation in scores (r = 0.9962).
H. INTERPRETATION: R^2 = 0.9924 means that 99.2% of the variance of y is
   explained by the model.
I. MISTAKES: "high R^2 means a correct/causal model" (no); "low R^2 means
   the model is useless" (in noisy social data R^2 = 0.1 can still be
   informative; the slope may be well determined); comparing R^2 across
   different response transformations; using training R^2 as evidence of
   predictive performance (use held-out data, Module 46); forgetting that
   R^2 can be negative on test data.
J. RELATED: correlation (F32.2), adjusted R^2, F-test, test-set R^2
   (F46.6).

F40.4  INFERENCE FOR THE SLOPE AND INTERCEPT
B. SE(b_1) = sigma_hat / sqrt(S_xx);
   SE(b_0) = sigma_hat sqrt( 1/n + x_bar^2/S_xx );
   t-statistic for H0: beta_j = 0:  t = b_j / SE(b_j) ~ t_(n - 2) under H0;
   (1 - alpha) CI: b_j +/- t_(alpha/2, n - 2) SE(b_j).
   Overall F-test (simple regression): F = t^2 = MSR/MSE with (1, n - 2) df.
C. SYMBOLS: sigma_hat the residual standard error; SE the standard error of
   the estimate (F37.8).
D. CONCEPT: the slope estimate varies from sample to sample; its
   standard error shrinks when there is more data, more spread in x
   (larger S_xx), or less noise (smaller sigma_hat). Spreading the x
   values widely is the best way to pin down the slope.
E. CONDITIONS: the assumptions of 40.7 (normal errors for exact t inference;
   otherwise approximate by the CLT).
G. EXAMPLE (study data): sigma_hat = 1.039, S_xx = 42:
   SE(b_1) = 1.039/sqrt(42) = 0.1603; t = 4.476/0.1603 = 27.92 with 6 df,
   p = 1.4 x 10^-7: very strong evidence that the slope is not 0.
   95% CI for beta_1: 4.476 +/- 2.447 * 0.1603 = (4.08, 4.87).
   SE(b_0) = 1.039 * sqrt(1/8 + 20.25/42) = 0.810; t = 57.9.
H. INTERPRETATION: "an extra hour of study is associated with 4.1 to 4.9 more
   points (95% CI)".
I. MISTAKES: reading a small p-value for the slope as a large effect or good
   prediction; confusing the p-value of the slope with the overall
   goodness of fit; ignoring the CI.
J. RELATED: standard error (F37.8), t-tests (F39.4), confidence
   intervals (F39.7), multiple regression (F40.6).

F40.5  PREDICTION: MEAN RESPONSE vs NEW OBSERVATION
B. At predictor value x_0: y_hat_0 = b_0 + b_1 x_0.
   CI for the MEAN response E[y | x_0]:
       y_hat_0 +/- t * sigma_hat sqrt( 1/n + (x_0 - x_bar)^2/S_xx ).
   PREDICTION INTERVAL for a NEW individual observation:
       y_hat_0 +/- t * sigma_hat sqrt( 1 + 1/n + (x_0 - x_bar)^2/S_xx ).
C. SYMBOLS: x_0 the new predictor value; y_hat_0 the prediction;
   sigma_hat the residual standard error; t the critical value with n -
   2 df.
D. CONCEPT: the mean can be pinned down precisely with enough data, but a new
   single observation still carries its own noise sigma^2 (the extra "1"
   inside the square root), so prediction intervals are wider and do not
   shrink to zero with n. Both widen as x_0 moves away from x_bar.
E. CONDITIONS: assumes the model assumptions of section 40.7;
   extrapolation voids the guarantee.
G. EXAMPLE (study data) at x_0 = 5.5 hours: y_hat = 46.857 + 4.476 * 5.5 = 71.48.
   95% CI for the mean score: 71.48 +/- 2.447 * 0.4008 = (70.50, 72.46).
   95% prediction interval for one student: 71.48 +/- 2.447 * 1.1135 =
   (68.75, 74.20).
   EXTRAPOLATION WARNING: at x_0 = 12 hours (outside 1-8) the line predicts
   100.57 points (> 100: impossible!) with the PI center at an
   unreliable location; the linear relationship probably saturates.
H. INTERPRETATION: the CI says where the AVERAGE response lies; the PI
   says where a SINGLE new observation will fall.
I. MISTAKES: using the CI for the mean when a prediction for one case is
   needed; extrapolating; reporting the prediction without uncertainty.
   (Note: the standard prediction interval assumes normal, constant-
   variance errors.)
J. RELATED: standard error (F37.8), leverage (F40.7), CI versus PI table
   (Appendix A).

sections.title: MULTIPLE LINEAR REGRESSION AND LEAST SQUARES IN MATRIX FORM

blocks.title: MULTIPLE LINEAR REGRESSION
blocks.formulaBody:
Model:  y_i = beta_0 + beta_1 x_i1 + ... + beta_p x_ip + eps_i
     Matrix form:  y = X beta + eps
        y   (n x 1) responses; X (n x (p + 1)) DESIGN MATRIX whose first
        column is all ones (intercept) and whose other columns are the
        predictors; beta ((p + 1) x 1) coefficients; eps (n x 1) errors.
     OLS estimator (normal equations X^T X beta = X^T y):
        beta_hat = (X^T X)^(-1) X^T y
     Fitted values y_hat = X beta_hat = H y with HAT MATRIX
        H = X (X^T X)^(-1) X^T  (projection onto the column space of X,
        F10.3);  residuals e = y - y_hat = (I - H) y.
     Error variance estimate: sigma_hat^2 = SSE/(n - p - 1).
     Covariance of the estimator: Cov(beta_hat) = sigma^2 (X^T X)^(-1);
        SE(b_j) = sigma_hat sqrt( [(X^T X)^(-1)]_jj ).
     Interpretation of each coefficient: the expected change in y for a
        1-unit increase in x_j HOLDING THE OTHER PREDICTORS FIXED.
     Overall F-test: H0: beta_1 = ... = beta_p = 0;
        F = (SSR/p)/(SSE/(n - p - 1)).
     Gauss-Markov theorem: under linearity, E[eps | X] = 0, constant
        variance and uncorrelated errors, and X of full column rank, OLS is
        the Best Linear Unbiased Estimator (BLUE): smallest variance among
        all linear unbiased estimators. NORMALITY is NOT needed for this; it
        is needed only for exact t and F distributions.

parts.A: NAME: Multiple linear regression model and the OLS solution.
parts.B:
FORMULAS

        F = (SSR/p)/(SSE/(n - p - 1)).
     Gauss-Markov theorem: under linearity, E[eps | X] = 0, constant
        variance and uncorrelated errors, and X of full column rank, OLS is
        the Best Linear Unbiased Estimator (BLUE): smallest variance among
        all linear unbiased estimators. NORMALITY is NOT needed for this; it
        is needed only for exact t and F distributions.
parts.C:
SYMBOLS: p number of predictors; n - p - 1 residual degrees of freedom;
   H the hat matrix; X^T X the Gram matrix (Module 10).
parts.D:
CONCEPT: y_hat is the projection of y onto the space spanned by the
   columns of X: the best approximation of the response that is a
   linear combination of the predictors. Residuals are orthogonal to every
   predictor column, which is why the residuals are uncorrelated with the
   predictors and sum to zero (intercept present).
parts.E:
CONDITIONS: n > p + 1; X has FULL COLUMN RANK (no perfect collinearity,
   Modules 8 and 38); the assumptions of 40.7. Practical: standardize
   predictors for numerical stability/interpretation; use QR/SVD
   (np.linalg.lstsq) rather than inverting X^T X.
parts.F:
DERIVATION: minimize SSE(beta) = (y - X beta)^T (y - X beta). Gradient:
   -2 X^T (y - X beta) = 0 -> X^T X beta = X^T y (F10.5); the Hessian
   2 X^T X is positive definite when X has full column rank, so it is the
   unique minimum.
   Unbiasedness: beta_hat = (X^T X)^(-1) X^T (X beta + eps) = beta +
   (X^T X)^(-1) X^T eps; expectation beta if E[eps | X] = 0.
parts.G:
WORKED EXAMPLE (house prices; n = 10)
   size x1 (m^2): 50, 60, 70, 80, 90, 100, 110, 120, 130, 140
   age x2 (years): 30, 5, 20, 10, 25, 2, 15, 8, 12, 1
   price y (thousands): 150, 200, 205, 240, 245, 300, 290, 330, 345, 380
   OLS fit (computed by solving the normal equations):
     price = 81.42 + 2.148 size - 1.325 age
     SE:      6.93      0.0562      0.1750
     t:       11.75     38.24       -7.57       (7 df; p-values 7e-6, 2e-9,
                                                 1.3e-4)
     R^2 = 0.9972; adjusted R^2 = 0.9965; residual sd = 4.33 (thousand);
     F = 1267.6 on (2, 7) df.
   INTERPRETATION: Holding age fixed, each extra m^2 is associated with
     2.15 thousand more in price; holding size fixed, each additional year
     of age is associated with 1.33 thousand less. 95% CI for the age
     coefficient: -1.325 +/- 2.365 * 0.175 = (-1.74, -0.91).
   WHY THE COEFFICIENT CHANGES WHEN ADDING VARIABLES: size-only model:
     price = 43.09 + 2.373 size (R^2 = 0.9747). The size coefficient moved
     from 2.37 to 2.15 once age was included, because size and age are
     correlated (r = -0.53: in this sample bigger houses tend to be
     newer). The simple slope mixed the effect of size with part of the
     effect of age (omitted-variable bias, section 40.8).
parts.H:
INTERPRETATION OF OUTPUT (statsmodels / R summary): coef (estimates),
   std err (SE), t, P>|t| (test of each coefficient being 0 GIVEN the other
   variables), [0.025, 0.975] (CI), R-squared, Adj. R-squared, F-statistic
   and its p-value (all slopes zero), residual df, AIC/BIC (model
   comparison, lower better), Durbin-Watson (residual autocorrelation),
   Jarque-Bera/Omnibus (residual normality), Cond. No. (multicollinearity).
parts.I:
COMMON MISTAKES: interpreting a coefficient without "other variables held
   fixed"; comparing raw coefficients of variables on different scales
   (use standardized coefficients); including all dummies for a
   categorical variable plus an intercept (dummy-variable trap): use k - 1
   dummies, the omitted group is the REFERENCE category; adding variables
   until R^2 is high (overfitting); ignoring that t-tests of individual
   coefficients depend on which other variables are included.
parts.J:
RELATED: categorical predictors (dummy coding), interactions (x1 * x2
   lets the slope of x1 depend on x2), polynomial terms (still linear in
   the parameters), regularization (ridge: beta_hat = (X^T X + lambda I)^(-1)
   X^T y; lasso), logistic regression (Module 48) as the extension to
   binary outcomes, MLE under Gaussian errors (F38.3).

blocks.title: COMPARISON TABLE: SIMPLE vs MULTIPLE LINEAR REGRESSION
blocks.rawText:
Aspect             Simple                      Multiple
  Predictors         one                         p >= 2
  Geometry           line in (x, y) plane        hyperplane
  Slope meaning      total association           effect holding others fixed
  Estimation         b_1 = S_xy/S_xx             (X^T X)^(-1) X^T y
  R^2                = r^2                       use adjusted R^2
  Residual df        n - 2                       n - p - 1
  Main risk          omitted variables           multicollinearity, overfitting
  Slope in presence  can differ markedly from the coefficient once other
  of other variables variables are included (Simpson's paradox is the extreme)

   (X^T X)^(-1) X^T eps; expectation beta if E[eps | X] = 0.
G. WORKED EXAMPLE (house prices; n = 10)
   size x1 (m^2): 50, 60, 70, 80, 90, 100, 110, 120, 130, 140
   age x2 (years): 30, 5, 20, 10, 25, 2, 15, 8, 12, 1
   price y (thousands): 150, 200, 205, 240, 245, 300, 290, 330, 345, 380
   OLS fit (computed by solving the normal equations):
     price = 81.42 + 2.148 size - 1.325 age
     SE:      6.93      0.0562      0.1750
     t:       11.75     38.24       -7.57       (7 df; p-values 7e-6, 2e-9,
                                                 1.3e-4)
     R^2 = 0.9972; adjusted R^2 = 0.9965; residual sd = 4.33 (thousand);
     F = 1267.6 on (2, 7) df.
   INTERPRETATION: Holding age fixed, each extra m^2 is associated with
     2.15 thousand more in price; holding size fixed, each additional year
     of age is associated with 1.33 thousand less. 95% CI for the age
     coefficient: -1.325 +/- 2.365 * 0.175 = (-1.74, -0.91).
   WHY THE COEFFICIENT CHANGES WHEN ADDING VARIABLES: size-only model:
     price = 43.09 + 2.373 size (R^2 = 0.9747). The size coefficient moved
     from 2.37 to 2.15 once age was included, because size and age are
     correlated (r = -0.53: in this sample bigger houses tend to be
     newer). The simple slope mixed the effect of size with part of the
     effect of age (omitted-variable bias, section 40.8).
H. INTERPRETATION OF OUTPUT (statsmodels / R summary): coef (estimates),
   std err (SE), t, P>|t| (test of each coefficient being 0 GIVEN the other
   variables), [0.025, 0.975] (CI), R-squared, Adj. R-squared, F-statistic
   and its p-value (all slopes zero), residual df, AIC/BIC (model
   comparison, lower better), Durbin-Watson (residual autocorrelation),
   Jarque-Bera/Omnibus (residual normality), Cond. No. (multicollinearity).
I. COMMON MISTAKES: interpreting a coefficient without "other variables held
   fixed"; comparing raw coefficients of variables on different scales
   (use standardized coefficients); including all dummies for a
   categorical variable plus an intercept (dummy-variable trap): use k - 1
   dummies, the omitted group is the REFERENCE category; adding variables
   until R^2 is high (overfitting); ignoring that t-tests of individual
   coefficients depend on which other variables are included.
J. RELATED: categorical predictors (dummy coding), interactions (x1 * x2
   lets the slope of x1 depend on x2), polynomial terms (still linear in
   the parameters), regularization (ridge: beta_hat = (X^T X + lambda I)^(-1)
   X^T y; lasso), logistic regression (Module 48) as the extension to
   binary outcomes, MLE under Gaussian errors (F38.3).

COMPARISON TABLE: SIMPLE vs MULTIPLE LINEAR REGRESSION
  Aspect             Simple                      Multiple
  Predictors         one                         p >= 2
  Geometry           line in (x, y) plane        hyperplane
  Slope meaning      total association           effect holding others fixed
  Estimation         b_1 = S_xy/S_xx             (X^T X)^(-1) X^T y
  R^2                = r^2                       use adjusted R^2
  Residual df        n - 2                       n - p - 1
  Main risk          omitted variables           multicollinearity, overfitting
  Slope in presence  can differ markedly from the coefficient once other
  of other variables variables are included (Simpson's paradox is the extreme)

sections.title: REGRESSION COEFFICIENTS: INTERCEPT AND SLOPE (SUMMARY)

blocks.rawText:
INTERCEPT b_0: predicted y when ALL predictors equal 0. Often not
      meaningful (age 0, income 0). Center predictors (x - x_bar) to make
      b_0 the prediction at the average case.
   SLOPE b_j: change in predicted y per unit change in x_j, other predictors
      held constant (multiple) or ignoring them (simple).
   UNITS: b_j is in units of (y)/(x_j). Rescaling x_j by c rescales b_j by 1/c
      (predictions unchanged). Standardized coefficient = b_j s_xj/s_y.
   LOG TRANSFORMATIONS: log(y) on x: a 1-unit rise in x multiplies y by about
      e^(b) (100 b percent for small b); log-log: elasticity (a 1% rise in x
      -> b% rise in y).
   CATEGORICAL: coefficient of a dummy = difference in mean y between that
      category and the reference category, other variables fixed.
   BINARY OUTCOME: linear regression (linear probability model) can predict
      outside [0, 1]; use logistic regression.

sections.title: RESIDUALS AND DIAGNOSTICS

blocks.rawText:
DEFINITION: the RESIDUAL e_i = y_i - y_hat_i is the observed minus the fitted
value: the part of y the model does not explain; it ESTIMATES the unobservable
error eps_i (they are not the same thing: residuals are constrained to sum
to zero and have unequal variances Var(e_i) = sigma^2 (1 - h_ii)).
RESIDUAL TYPES: raw; STANDARDIZED r_i = e_i/(sigma_hat sqrt(1 - h_ii));
   studentized (externally, leave-one-out sigma_hat). |r_i| > 3 (or > 2 for
   a loose flag) suggests an outlier.
KEY DIAGNOSTIC PLOTS
   1. Residuals vs fitted values: should look like a random horizontal band
      around 0. Curved pattern -> nonlinearity (add transformations or
      terms). Funnel (spread growing with the fit) -> heteroscedasticity.
   2. Normal Q-Q plot of residuals: points near the line -> approximately
      normal; S-shapes -> heavy tails; curvature -> skew.
   3. Scale-location (sqrt |standardized residuals| vs fitted): flat line
      -> constant variance.
   4. Residuals vs observation order/time: trends or runs -> autocorrelation
      (Durbin-Watson near 2 is fine).
   5. Residuals vs leverage with Cook's distance contours (40.5).
EXAMPLE: study-hours data: residuals 0.67, -0.81, 0.71, -0.76, 0.76, -1.71,
0.81, 0.33: small and without trend (sum 0): the straight-line model is
adequate.
I. MISTAKES: judging fit only by R^2; not plotting; mistaking residuals for
   the true errors; expecting residuals to be exactly normal in small
   samples.

sections.title: OUTLIERS, LEVERAGE AND INFLUENTIAL OBSERVATIONS

blocks.rawText:
DEFINITIONS
   OUTLIER (in regression): a point with an unusually LARGE RESIDUAL: its y
      is far from the fitted line, given its x.
   HIGH-LEVERAGE point: an unusual PREDICTOR value (far from the other x's).
      It has the potential to pull the fit toward itself.
   INFLUENTIAL point: one whose removal CHANGES the fit substantially
      (slope, intercept, predictions). Influence usually requires both a
      leverage and a (sizeable) residual.

blocks.title: LEVERAGE AND COOK'S DISTANCE
blocks.formulaBody:
LEVERAGE: h_ii = i-th diagonal entry of the hat matrix H.
     Simple regression: h_ii = 1/n + (x_i - x_bar)^2/S_xx.
     Properties: 1/n <= h_ii <= 1; sum h_ii = p + 1 (number of parameters).
     Flag: h_ii > 2(p + 1)/n (some use 3(p + 1)/n).
   COOK'S DISTANCE: D_i = ( e_i^2/((p + 1) sigma_hat^2) ) * ( h_ii/(1 - h_ii)^2 )
     (the overall change in all fitted values when observation i is
     dropped). Flag: D_i > 1 (conservative) or D_i > 4/n.
   Other measures: DFFITS, DFBETAS (change in an individual coefficient).

parts.B:
LEVERAGE: h_ii = i-th diagonal entry of the hat matrix H.
     Simple regression: h_ii = 1/n + (x_i - x_bar)^2/S_xx.

   Other measures: DFFITS, DFBETAS (change in an individual coefficient).
parts.C: SYMBOLS: e_i residual; h_ii leverage; sigma_hat^2 MSE; p + 1 parameters.
parts.D:
CONCEPT: OLS treats every point equally in squared error, so extreme
   x-positions act like long levers on the line (like a seesaw); a
   high-leverage point can force the line near itself, giving a small
   residual that HIDES its influence.
parts.E:
CONDITIONS: the thresholds are rules of thumb; compare with the
   distribution of the diagnostics.
parts.G:
WORKED EXAMPLE: base data x = 1, 2, 3, 4, 5; y = 2, 4, 5, 4, 5:
     fit y = 2.2 + 0.6 x, R^2 = 0.60.
   Add one point (15, 3) far to the right (high leverage, y low):
     new fit y = 3.987 - 0.031 x, R^2 = 0.018: the slope flips from +0.6
     to about 0 (slightly negative).
     Leverage of the new point: x_bar = 30/6 = 5 and S_xx = 16 + 9 + 4 + 1
     + 0 + 100 = 130, so h_66 = 1/6 + (15 - 5)^2/130 = 0.167 + 0.769 =
     0.936 (cut-off 2(2)/6 = 0.667): very high leverage.
     Cook's distance of the new point: 18.8 (>> 1): highly influential.
   So a single point controls the whole analysis.
parts.H:
INTERPRETATION: investigate each flagged point: data error? different
   population? genuine extreme? Report the analysis with and without it;
   consider robust regression (Huber, RANSAC, quantile regression). Never
   delete just because it spoils the fit.
parts.I:
MISTAKES: confusing "outlier" (large residual) with "high leverage" (extreme
   x); removing influential points silently; assuming a point with a tiny
   residual is harmless.
parts.J: RELATED: hat matrix (F40.6), residual diagnostics (section 40.4).

sections.title: MULTICOLLINEARITY

blocks.title: MULTICOLLINEARITY AND THE VARIANCE INFLATION FACTOR
blocks.formulaBody:
AND FORMULAS
     Multicollinearity: two or more predictors are strongly linearly related.
        PERFECT: some column of X is an exact linear combination of others:
        X^T X singular (rank deficient), beta not identifiable (F38.5).
        NEAR (imperfect): high but not exact dependence.
     VIF_j = 1/(1 - R_j^2), where R_j^2 is the R^2 from regressing x_j on all
        the OTHER predictors.
     Var(b_j) = sigma^2 / ( (1 - R_j^2) S_(x_j x_j) ) = VIF_j * sigma^2/S_(x_j x_j):
        the VIF is exactly how much the variance of b_j is inflated relative
        to uncorrelated predictors. SE inflates by sqrt(VIF).
     Rules of thumb: VIF > 5 (concern), > 10 (serious); two predictors with
        correlation r have VIF = 1/(1 - r^2): r = 0.5 -> 1.33; r = 0.9 ->
        5.26; r = 0.95 -> 10.26; r = 0.99 -> 50.3.
     Condition number of the (scaled) design matrix > 30 (or eigenvalues of
        the correlation matrix near 0): warning (Module 10: ratio of the
        largest to smallest singular value).

parts.C: SYMBOLS: R_j^2 how well the other predictors explain x_j.
parts.D:
CONCEPT: if two predictors move together, the data cannot separate their
   individual effects: many different combinations of coefficients fit
   about equally well (the SSE surface has a long, nearly flat valley in
   the plane of the two coefficients), so the estimates are unstable and
   their SEs enormous.
parts.E:
CONSEQUENCES: coefficient estimates have HIGH VARIANCE (change wildly with
   small data changes; signs may flip); individual t-tests insignificant
   although the overall F-test and R^2 are strong; interpretation of
   single coefficients unreliable. NOT affected: the fitted values and
   predictions within the range of the collinear pattern, and the
   overall R^2. Predictions break when new data violate the collinear
   pattern.
parts.G:
EXAMPLE: add x3 = 2 x1 + small noise (-2..2) to the house data (corr(x1, x3)
   = 0.9997). Regress price on x1 and x3:
     b_1 = 2.89 (SE 5.88, t = 0.49); b_3 = -0.26 (SE 2.95, t = -0.09);
     R^2 = 0.975 (same as using x1 alone, 0.9747!).
   Neither coefficient is significant, yet the model fits as well as before.
   VIF = 1,659; condition number about 771 (raw design matrix).
   Without x3: the x1 slope was 2.37 with SE 0.135 (t about 17).
   The SE of the size coefficient jumped from 0.135 to 5.88: a factor of
   about 44, close to sqrt(VIF) = sqrt(1659) = 40.7 (the small remaining
   difference comes from the changed residual standard error).
   In the first house model (size and age) the VIFs were 1.39 (r = -0.53):
   harmless.
parts.H:
DETECTION: correlation matrix/heatmap; VIFs; condition number
   (statsmodels summary prints "The condition number is large" warning,
   Module 41); eigenvalues; coefficient instability when adding/removing
   variables or resampling.
   REMEDIES: drop or combine redundant variables (average, ratio, index);
   PCA/partial least squares (orthogonal components); RIDGE regression
   (X^T X + lambda I is better conditioned); center variables before forming
   polynomial/interaction terms; collect more varied data; if the goal
   is prediction only, you may tolerate it.
parts.I:
MISTAKES: removing variables solely because their t-values are low when
   they are collinear (drop one at a time, using domain knowledge);
   thinking multicollinearity biases OLS (it does not bias, it inflates
   variance); the dummy-variable trap (perfect collinearity).
parts.J:
RELATED: rank/identifiability (Modules 8, 38), eigenvalues and condition
   number (Modules 9, 10), ridge regularization (Module 47).

     b_1 = 2.89 (SE 5.88, t = 0.49); b_3 = -0.26 (SE 2.95, t = -0.09);
     R^2 = 0.975 (same as using x1 alone, 0.9747!).
   Neither coefficient is significant, yet the model fits as well as before.
   VIF = 1,659; condition number about 771 (raw design matrix).
   Without x3: the x1 slope was 2.37 with SE 0.135 (t about 17).
   The SE of the size coefficient jumped from 0.135 to 5.88: a factor of
   about 44, close to sqrt(VIF) = sqrt(1659) = 40.7 (the small remaining
   difference comes from the changed residual standard error).

   harmless.

   Module 41); eigenvalues; coefficient instability when adding/removing
   variables or resampling.

   they are collinear (drop one at a time, using domain knowledge);
   thinking multicollinearity biases OLS (it does not bias, it inflates
   variance); the dummy-variable trap (perfect collinearity).

sections.rawText:
F40.8  MULTICOLLINEARITY AND THE VARIANCE INFLATION FACTOR
A. NAME: Multicollinearity; VIF.
B. DEFINITION AND FORMULAS
     Multicollinearity: two or more predictors are strongly linearly related.
        PERFECT: some column of X is an exact linear combination of others:
        X^T X singular (rank deficient), beta not identifiable (F38.5).
        NEAR (imperfect): high but not exact dependence.
     VIF_j = 1/(1 - R_j^2), where R_j^2 is the R^2 from regressing x_j on all
        the OTHER predictors.
     Var(b_j) = sigma^2 / ( (1 - R_j^2) S_(x_j x_j) ) = VIF_j * sigma^2/S_(x_j x_j):
        the VIF is exactly how much the variance of b_j is inflated relative
        to uncorrelated predictors. SE inflates by sqrt(VIF).
     Rules of thumb: VIF > 5 (concern), > 10 (serious); two predictors with
        correlation r have VIF = 1/(1 - r^2): r = 0.5 -> 1.33; r = 0.9 ->
        5.26; r = 0.95 -> 10.26; r = 0.99 -> 50.3.
     Condition number of the (scaled) design matrix > 30 (or eigenvalues of
        the correlation matrix near 0): warning (Module 10: ratio of the
        largest to smallest singular value).
C. SYMBOLS: R_j^2 how well the other predictors explain x_j.
D. CONCEPT: if two predictors move together, the data cannot separate their
   individual effects: many different combinations of coefficients fit
   about equally well (the SSE surface has a long, nearly flat valley in
   the plane of the two coefficients), so the estimates are unstable and
   their SEs enormous.
E. CONSEQUENCES: coefficient estimates have HIGH VARIANCE (change wildly with
   small data changes; signs may flip); individual t-tests insignificant
   although the overall F-test and R^2 are strong; interpretation of
   single coefficients unreliable. NOT affected: the fitted values and
   predictions within the range of the collinear pattern, and the
   overall R^2. Predictions break when new data violate the collinear
   pattern.
G. EXAMPLE: add x3 = 2 x1 + small noise (-2..2) to the house data (corr(x1, x3)
   = 0.9997). Regress price on x1 and x3:
     b_1 = 2.89 (SE 5.88, t = 0.49); b_3 = -0.26 (SE 2.95, t = -0.09);
     R^2 = 0.975 (same as using x1 alone, 0.9747!).

   VIF = 1,659; condition number about 771 (raw design matrix).
   Without x3: the x1 slope was 2.37 with SE 0.135 (t about 17).
   The SE of the size coefficient jumped from 0.135 to 5.88: a factor of
   about 44, close to sqrt(VIF) = sqrt(1659) = 40.7 (the small remaining
   difference comes from the changed residual standard error).
   In the first house model (size and age) the VIFs were 1.39 (r = -0.53):
   harmless.
H. DETECTION: correlation matrix/heatmap; VIFs; condition number
   (statsmodels summary prints "The condition number is large" warning,
   Module 41); eigenvalues; coefficient instability when adding/removing
   variables or resampling.
   REMEDIES: drop or combine redundant variables (average, ratio, index);
   PCA/partial least squares (orthogonal components); RIDGE regression
   (X^T X + lambda I is better conditioned); center variables before forming
   polynomial/interaction terms; collect more varied data; if the goal
   is prediction only, you may tolerate it.
I. MISTAKES: removing variables solely because their t-values are low when
   they are collinear (drop one at a time, using domain knowledge);
   thinking multicollinearity biases OLS (it does not bias, it inflates

sections.title: MODEL ASSUMPTIONS

blocks.rawText:
THE ASSUMPTIONS (mnemonic LINE plus extras)
   L  LINEARITY: E[y | x] is linear in the parameters (the relationship can
      still be curved in x if you include x^2, log x, etc.).
   I  INDEPENDENCE of the errors (no autocorrelation or clustering).
   N  NORMALITY of the errors (needed for exact small-sample t, F, CIs and
      prediction intervals; not for unbiasedness).
   E  EQUAL VARIANCE (homoscedasticity): Var(eps | x) = sigma^2 constant.
   +  EXOGENEITY: E[eps | X] = 0; predictors uncorrelated with the error (no
      omitted confounders, no reverse causation, no measurement error in x).
   +  NO PERFECT MULTICOLLINEARITY (full rank X).
   +  CORRECT SPECIFICATION (no important omitted terms/interactions).
WHAT HAPPENS WHEN ASSUMPTIONS FAIL
  Violation               Detect                 Consequence                 Remedy
  Nonlinearity            residual-vs-fitted     biased fit, wrong           add terms/transform,
                          curvature              predictions                 splines, trees
  Heteroscedasticity      funnel, Breusch-Pagan  OLS still UNBIASED; SEs,    robust (HC) SEs, WLS,
                                                 p-values, PIs WRONG         log-transform y
  Autocorrelation         Durbin-Watson, ACF     SEs too small; p-values     time-series models,
                          of residuals           too optimistic              clustered/HAC SEs
  Non-normal errors       Q-Q plot               small n: CIs/PIs off;       transform, bootstrap,
                                                 large n: CLT mostly ok      robust regression
  Omitted confounder      domain knowledge       BIASED coefficients         add confounders,
  (endogeneity)                                                              design/IV methods
  Multicollinearity       VIF, cond. number      inflated variance           see 40.6
  Outliers/influence      Cook's D               distorted fit               investigate, robust fit
EXAMPLE: income vs spending: variance grows with income (funnel): OLS slope
unbiased but its usual SE is wrong; use robust SEs or model log(spending).

blocks.text:
Assumptions concern the ERRORS (checked via residuals), not the
raw variables: y and x themselves need not be normal.
